Exercise C.39.6.1. In an augmented dg algebra with a closed homogeneous element \(a\) of degree two, evaluate \(dh+hd\) on \(a\otimes1\) in (C.39.10). What root coefficient would fail this identity?

Solution. Formula (C.39.12) gives \(h(a\otimes1)=1\otimes sa\). Its root differential (C.39.11) has coefficient \((-1)^2=1\), so \(dh(a\otimes1)=a\otimes1\); all unary terms vanish and \(hd=0\). Replacing the root coefficient by minus one gives minus the identity on this element, contradicting the claimed contraction. The sign on the unsuspension and the root term must be fixed together.

Exercise C.39.6.2. Take square-zero augmented algebras on closed degree-two elements \(a,b\). Compute the binary shuffle on \(sa\otimes sb\) and the two one-letter products in its target bar differential.

Solution. The two suspended letters are odd, so \[ \mathrm{sh}_2(sa\otimes sb) =s(a\otimes1)|s(1\otimes b) -s(1\otimes b)|s(a\otimes1). \tag{C.39.21} \] The binary bar differential of its first word is \(-s(a\otimes b)\). In its second word it is also \(-s(a\otimes b)\), because the ordinary degree-two factors commute in the tensor algebra. The preceding minus sign cancels these two terms. Thus the shuffle is a cycle. This calculation retains the mixed tensor arrow in the target bar; omitting that arrow would not be the bar of the actual tensor-product input.

Lemma C.39.1.1 and Theorem C.39.2.1 prove the actual module pullback and shared-core coordinate group. Theorem C.39.3.1 proves the original shuffle is a quasi-isomorphism using its explicit free bar-resolution contraction. Lemma C.39.4.1 gives the positive and triangular bar-cobar comparison; Theorem C.39.5.1 recovers the original convolution from the displayed common-input graph. Exercises C.39.6.1-C.39.6.2 check the root and mixed tensor shuffle signs. Editable SVG source. Related free reading: Hess, Parent and Scott, A chain coalgebra model for the James map, Appendix A.

C.40. Simultaneous common-input base change of the nested graph

The base change must keep paths containing several cross arrows, since their differential contains actual grafting. This section replaces every core of one complete directed graph at once. It does not discard the path operations or infer a differential identity from an unproved injectivity of the comparison map.

C.40.1. The full path differential after changing the cores

Theorem C.40.1.1. Let \(\mathcal L_B\) be the reduced bar coalgebra of a finite minimal nested convolution graph from C.38.3. Denote its pure level cores by \(B_i\) and its cross mapping cohomology by \(N_{ij}\), with arrows only from lower to higher height. Let \(f_i:A_i\to B_i\) be chain coalgebra maps retaining the coefficient objects. There is a simultaneous common-core graph coalgebra \(\mathcal L_A\), with its whole grafting differential and a chain coalgebra comparison \[ Q:\mathcal L_A\longrightarrow\mathcal L_B. \tag{C.40.1} \] Its path with levels \(i_0,\ldots,i_q\), ordered from target to source, has graded space \[ A_{i_0}\otimes sN_{i_0i_1}\otimes A_{i_1} \otimes\cdots\otimes sN_{i_{q-1}i_q}\otimes A_{i_q}. \tag{C.40.2} \] On this space \(Q\) applies \(f_{i_r}\) to every core slot and the identity to every cross slot. Its differential retains every original grafting Taylor operation.

For the actual convolution graph take \(A_i=C^{\otimes n_i}\), with \(C=B\mathcal M\) and \(f_i=\sigma_{n_i}\); use \(A_o=C,f_o=1\) for the common output. Thus each arity core is literally a tensor power of the same bar.

Proof. A bar word of the old graph has a unique expression as maximal pure-core runs separated by its cross letters. This is the path expression (C.40.2), with \(B\) in place of \(A\). In a finite directed corner there are at most \(H\) cross letters, where \(H\) is its height range.

Define the coproduct on (C.40.2) by cutting through one core slot and applying that slot's coproduct. The prefix retains the cross letters preceding that slot, the suffix retains those following it, and the two resulting core pieces are their adjacent boundary runs. The tensor signs are the signs in that core coproduct and the canonical graded regrouping. Sum over all slots. This also includes cuts immediately before or after a cross letter, using a coaugmentation piece. If an internal core run is empty, its single group-like coproduct gives exactly one cut between the two adjacent cross letters. On a path with no cross letter it is its core coproduct.

Two successive cuts agree in either order by coassociativity of each \(A_i\); cuts in different slots agree by graded tensor interchange. This proves coassociativity. Counits are the core counits on the zero-cross sectors and zero on all crossed sectors. They satisfy the counit equations. Applying each \(f_i\) in this formula proves that (C.40.1) is a graded coalgebra map.

Describe the old differential by its pure core differentials and its central cross Taylor projection \(\mu_B\). On a path, this projection applies the old bar differential and then projects its output to a single cross letter with both surrounding core runs counited. Its degree is one. The whole differential is reconstructed by applying \(\mu_B\) to every consecutive block of cross letters with their intervening core runs, splitting the two boundary core runs by their coproducts, and retaining the outer pieces. Each term has the sign of its degree-one map passing the preceding part of the word. Together with the pure core differentials this is precisely the old consecutive-word coderivation.

We use the same reconstruction on (C.40.2), with its actual core differential and \[ \mu_A =\mu_B\circ (f_{i_0}\otimes1\otimes f_{i_1} \otimes\cdots\otimes1\otimes f_{i_q}). \tag{C.40.3} \] A term may merge several cross letters, including their entire intervening runs, to the original output cross component. Nothing restricts it to the one-cross module operations. The cut formula shows directly that the reconstructed degree-one map \(D_A\) is a coderivation: a cut outside a selected operation block commutes with that operation, and the two boundary cuts are the two coproduct pieces used in its reconstruction. The pure core terms have the same assertion because their given differentials are coderivations.

We spell out the uniqueness used to check the identities. A coderivation on this path coalgebra, with its pure core values specified, is determined by its central single-cross projections. For the difference of two such maps, first subtract their identical pure core part. On a one-cross input, its two outer coaction equations reconstruct the remaining map from its central projection, just as the cofree formula (C.39.5), with its homogeneous degree sign. On a higher-cross input, project its coproduct to cuts having crossed factors on both sides. All resulting input pieces have fewer cross letters. Induction determines those values. The positive-path cut on a target of two or more cross letters is injective: splitting its intervening core run, then couniting one of the duplicate boundary copies, recovers the original path tensor. Thus those cut values determine every higher-cross output. The remaining one-cross output is again determined by its outer coactions and central projection. This proves uniqueness by induction on the finite cross count. The same argument works for coderivations along a prescribed coalgebra map.

Use it first on \(QD_A-D_BQ\). Its pure core components vanish because each \(f_i\) is a chain map. Its central projection vanishes by the defining formula (C.40.3), counit preservation and coproduct naturality. Both terms are coderivations along \(Q\). Uniqueness gives \[ QD_A=D_BQ. \tag{C.40.4} \] Next \(D_A^2\) is a coderivation: the two cross terms in the square of its coproduct equation cancel because \(D_A\) has odd degree. Its pure core values are zero. Equation (C.40.4) gives \(QD_A^2=0\). The central projection of \(Q\) is the identity on every bare \(sN_{ij}\), since all \(f_i\) preserve their counits. Consequently the central projection of \(D_A^2\) is zero. The uniqueness just proved gives \(D_A^2=0\). This last step uses its central projection and coderivation property; it does not assume \(Q\) is injective.

For the application, choose the input models \(\mathcal M_n\) of C.34.3 as the arity cores of the graph in C.38.3. They are the fixed minimal models of \(\mathcal U^{\otimes n}\); the positive replacement \(\mathcal U\) and its tensor powers compare them with the original enhanced IC input categories, and A.3.1.1 transfers the actual convolution functors through those equivalences. Thus this is a permitted choice of the same actual graph, with unchanged leading mapping cohomology, not an identification of two unchosen models. Form its shared cores and represented modules with these choices from the outset.

C.39.3 now supplies the actual chain coalgebra maps \(\sigma_{n_i}\) to these exact input bars. Insert them in (C.40.3). Each retained nested string and each operation merging strings has its original cross component from C.38.3. The empty string grades the pure cores and the other grades concatenate under grafting; (C.40.3) preserves these grades. Thus the whole labelled nested graph has been changed to the stated common cores, with its complete existing grafting differential retained. Geometric identifications of different string labels are further marked maps, not identifications silently imposed by this construction. ∎

C.40.2. Actual graph recovery and finite height windows

Theorem C.40.2.1. In the actual common-input application of C.40.1, \(Q\) is a quasi-isomorphism on every graph corner. Its cobar recovers the original nested convolution graph, with the common input cores \(\Omega(C^{\otimes n_i})\) and output \(\Omega C\).

On a finite height range \(H\), set \[ W_h(w)=|w|+h(\text{target endpoint})-h(\text{source endpoint}). \tag{C.40.5} \] Weight at most \(D\) is a finite subcoalgebra. It bounds the total number of surrounding positive core-bar letters by \(D\) and the cross count by \(H\). The graph differential raises this weight by one and \(Q\) preserves it. Full finite labelled restrictions retain the construction and its maps.

Proof. First filter the two graph complexes by cross count at most \(q\). Their differentials cannot increase it: a grafting operation merges a consecutive nonempty set of cross letters to one, and pure core differentials retain the count. There are only \(q=0,\ldots,H\) stages.

In the associated cross-count-\(q\) quotient, the remaining cross operations are the one-cross module operations. Filter this quotient further by the sum \(p\) of the ordinary degrees of its \(q\) central \(N\)-letters, at least \(p\). A nonunary one-cross operation consumes positive-degree core input and increases that central degree by the input degree plus one. Bare central unary differentials vanish by minimality. Thus this descending filtration is a subcomplex filtration, as in C.39.5.

On its associated central-degree quotient, the differential acts only on the core slots. The map \(Q\) is the tensor of the maps \(f_i=\sigma_{n_i}\) on those slots, with the fixed central coefficient spaces in between. It is a quasi-isomorphism by C.39.3 and C.30.1's split coefficient tensor argument. For a path in cohomological degree \(r\), \[ r=\sum |\text{core slot}|+ \sum|\text{ordinary central letter}|-q, \tag{C.40.6} \] so \(p\le r+q\). The filtration is finite in each degree and its incoming degree. Finite cone elimination therefore proves \(Q\) is a quasi-isomorphism on each fixed-cross-count quotient. Induction over the finite cross-count filtration proves it on the whole graph. This argument proves equivalence while keeping all grafting terms in the actual differential; they were removed only on an associated quotient in the verification.

For the stated windows, every core slot has nonnegative degree and every nonempty core letter has suspended degree at least one. Each cross letter has suspended degree \(|N|-1\), with \(|N|\ge0\), and strictly raises height. The total height jump is at least \(q\). Hence \[ W_h=\sum|\text{core slot}|+\sum|N|-q+\Delta h \ \ge\ \sum|\text{core slot}|+\sum|N|\ \ge0. \tag{C.40.7} \] Its upper bound \(D\) bounds every ordinary central degree and the total number and degree of positive core letters. The number of central letters is at most \(H\). Each selected arity has finitely many tensor factors, every retained mapping degree is finite, and there are finitely many labels. Thus the window is finite. A cut distributes the endpoint height jump and the cohomological degree additively; both pieces have nonnegative weight by the same calculation, proving the subcoalgebra assertion. Every differential term retains endpoints and has degree one, so raises \(W_h\) by one. Every \(f_i\) and consequently \(Q\) has degree zero and retains them, so preserves it exactly.

We verify the required extension of C.39.4 to a full finite-height graph. A reduced core coalgebra element has degree at least one. A crossed element of height jump \(d\) has degree at least \(-d\), by (C.40.6) and the bound on its own cross count. In a composable cobar word, the sum of all cross height jumps is at most \(H\). If there are \(r\) generators, of which \(q\le H\) are crossed, its degree is therefore at least \[ 2(r-q)+q-H=2r-q-H\ge2r-2H. \tag{C.40.8} \] The descending cobar-length filtration is finite in every fixed degree. Its associated maps are finite balanced tensors of the reduced quasi-isomorphism \(Q\). The split coefficient and finite cone-elimination proof of C.39.4 therefore applies without any unbounded negative-degree tensor products. It proves \(\Omega Q\) is a quasi-equivalence on the graph corners.

For completeness the graph bar-cobar units have the corresponding finite bound. In the fixed-original-element filtration of \(B\Omega\), composability bounds both the number of crossed original elements and their total negative degree by \(H\). With \(r\) original elements their sum of degrees is at least \(r-2H\). Formula (C.39.17) bounds \(r\le t+2H\) in degree \(t\). C.39.4's explicit first-cut homotopy, including its internal signs, still contracts every \(r\ge2\) quotient. The natural unit consequently remains a cornerwise quasi-isomorphism.

The old minimal graph was transferred from the genuine dg graph of C.38.1–C.38.3. Its bar inclusion and projection are actual contraction maps by A.3.1.1; the same finite-height cobar filtration carries their quasi-isomorphisms to the cobars. The dg graph itself is recovered by its bar-cobar counit. To check that last assertion at this height, repeat C.34.1's cut proof on a word of \(r\) original dg arrows and \(v\) cobar blocks. If \(q\le H\) of those arrows are crossed, its degree is at least \(r-2H+v\). Thus \(r\le t+2H-1\) in degree \(t\). The fixed-underlying-arrow cut complex contracts at \(r\ge2\), with the original dg unary differential and its signs; at \(r=1\) the counit is the identity original arrow. The remaining bar multiplication lowers \(r\), so this finite filtration proves the counit is a quasi-isomorphism. This extends the explicit already proved cut argument, rather than assuming positivity of every crossed strict-model arrow.

These comparisons identify the old cobar with the original nested functor graph and its represented modules. Composing with \(\Omega Q\) recovers all those modules and their grafting along the new quasi-equivalent cores. The cores on the new side are exactly \(\Omega(C^{\otimes n_i})\) and \(\Omega C\), so every arity now has the designated common tensor-bar input. Graph recovery is C.33.2's complete represented-module evaluation.

Finally all formulas keep endpoints, string grades and the existing intermediate labels of each word. Choose the finite tuple pools and necessary image summands as in C.38.3, without closing the new output pool under arbitrary tensor products. Full-corner restriction gives the same path words, maps \(f_i\), Taylor substitutions and cut formulas. Their increasing union is the entire prescribed countable nested graph. This verifies the restriction assertion. The full native unit, permutation and comparisons between different graph layouts, with every higher substitution identity used for coefficient descent, are retained in Theorems 78–79 of Rational forest coordinates. ∎

C.40.3. One common-core group on the whole path graph

Theorem C.40.3.1. At a finite corner of the graph in C.40.1–C.40.2, retain a single normalized degree-zero core coordinate \(g\) on \(C=B\mathcal M\). Let \(G\) be a degree-zero coalgebra coordinate on its whole path graph, fixing the coefficient objects and bare cross letters, whose restriction to arity \(n_i\) is exactly \(g^{\otimes n_i}\), and whose output restriction is \(g\). Retain endpoint and concatenated-string grades.

On the finite weight-\(D\) windows, these pairs form a reduced closed subgroup of a finite unitriangular group. Its composition and inverse are \[ (h,H)(g,G)=(hg,HG),\qquad (g,G)^{-1}=(g^{-1},G^{-1}). \tag{C.40.9} \] Core and whole-path differential comparisons are finite polynomial equations on inputs of weight at most \(D-1\), with outputs through \(D\). Whenever a full selected marked comparison has a solution in this group, its reduced solution variety is a torsor under its target stabilizer. Smaller full label, string and weight windows give actual restriction homomorphisms.

Proof. Count the total number of primitive core-bar letters and cross letters in a path. For a core \(C^{\otimes n_i}\), this is the sum of the word lengths in all its tensor factors. On the full path it adds the cross count.

The coproduct filtration by this number is exactly its relative coradical filtration. To verify the assertion rather than assume the core is cofree on one set of letters, apply its iterated reduced coproduct to the top length piece. It records all sequences of primitive letters obtained by interleaving the individual factor words, preserving the order within each factor and the order of cross letters. Project to the term which takes the factors in their fixed index order within each core run. Its coefficient is one of the Koszul signs, hence a unit. Its primitive factor labels and endpoint labels reconstruct every original factor word, central letter and path. This term therefore gives an injection of the top length piece into the corresponding tensor of primitive spaces. In particular no nonzero combination of higher-length terms is primitive.

Every coalgebra map fixing the coefficients preserves this coradical filtration. Its leading primitive map here is the identity: it is the identity on the one-letter component of \(g\), hence on every embedded factor letter in \(g^{\otimes n_i}\), and on each prescribed bare cross letter. Applying its iterated coproduct to the top length piece and using the injection just proved shows that its top length component is the identity too. Thus \(g\) and \(G\) are unitriangular in bases ordered by this total length.

C.40.2 bounds the surrounding core length by \(D\) and the cross count by \(H\), so only lengths through \(D+H\) occur in a graph window. The matrices are finite. A degree-zero map preserving endpoints preserves the height weight exactly; the core coordinate likewise preserves its positive bar degree. Their unitriangular inverses are the finite length recursion and stay in the same windows.

Impose their coalgebra equations, fixed coefficient and leading entries, degree/endpoint and string grades, and \[ G|_{A_i}=g^{\otimes n_i},\qquad G|_{A_o}=g. \tag{C.40.10} \] These are finite polynomial equations; the tensor powers have entries that are products of the corresponding entries of \(g\). Every core factor in a graph window has degree at most \(D\), by (C.40.7), so (C.40.10) uses the retained core window. All cuts in the coalgebra equations likewise use retained windows.

Coalgebra composition preserves the equations. On an arity core its restriction is exactly \(h^{\otimes n_i}g^{\otimes n_i}=(hg)^{\otimes n_i}\). The inverse restrictions are exactly \((g^{-1})^{\otimes n_i}\). Degrees and endpoint/string grades persist under the same finite length recursion. Consequently the reduced polynomial equations define the asserted closed subgroup of the finite unitriangular group, with the genuine operations (C.40.9). This includes higher coordinates on several-cross paths; it is not a product of independently chosen one-cross module groups.

Let \(b,\partial\) and \(b^0,\partial^0\) be two prescribed core/path differentials on the same graded frames. Impose \[ gb=b^0g,\qquad G\partial=\partial^0G \tag{C.40.11} \] on input weights at most \(D-1\). The differentials raise weight by one and coordinates preserve it, so every output through the top window is retained. These are finite polynomial equations.

For two solutions, their quotient (C.40.9) commutes with the target differentials on those same input domains. In the substitution, every inverse preserves the input window, and the only differential outputs lie in the retained next window. Conversely every such target stabilizer sends a solution to a solution. Its equations are closed and preserved by composition and inverse by that calculation. This proves the reduced torsor assertion of C.30.3 inside the actual common-core group. Any extra covariance marks have the same assertion once their complete input/output bounds have been proved and retained. A nonempty ordinary graph comparison outside this common-core group is not substituted for that hypothesis.

Finally use full factor-label corners and the finite selected arity/string system of C.38.3 and C.40.2. The one-core coordinate restricts to its original factor-word labels. Its tensor powers therefore preserve the selected tuple domains. A path component can merge a consecutive block only to its retained endpoint and concatenated-string grade. Those concatenated strings are included in the finite path system; no new unselected intermediate label is introduced. The coalgebra word reconstruction of the higher components uses only the original cuts and these block endpoints. Thus smaller full label and string corners preserve the coordinate maps and their inverses. Smaller weight windows are preserved by the degree argument. Restricting (C.40.10)–(C.40.11) consequently gives actual group and equation restriction maps. This is the compatible finite tower needed once the complete marked extension-field comparison is supplied. ∎

C.40.4. Coradical length and a whole-path coordinate

Exercise C.40.4.1. Let \(C\) be the tensor coalgebra on one primitive odd letter \(u\). In \(A=C\otimes C\), put \(x=u\otimes u\), \(\widehat u_1=u\otimes1\), and \(\widehat u_2=1\otimes u\). Compute the reduced coproduct of \(x\) and its primitive-letter length. Why can the common-core group not treat \(x\) as an extra free primitive?

Solution. Graded tensor interchange gives \[ \bar\Delta x=\widehat u_1\otimes\widehat u_2 -\widehat u_2\otimes\widehat u_1. \tag{C.40.12} \] Both \(\widehat u_i\) are primitive and their factor labels are distinct. The displayed two tensors are independent, so \(x\) is not primitive. Its length is two, detected by the canonical factor-order term of coefficient one. A coalgebra coordinate must retain this equation; freely changing \(x\) while fixing the primitives would generally break it.

Exercise C.40.4.2. In a three-level path coalgebra, take degree-zero cross arrows \(z_{21},z_{10},z_{20}\), with \(z_{20}\) labelled by their composite string, and a middle core letter \(u\) of suspended degree one. Let a normalized whole-path coordinate have its only extra central Taylor term \(sz_{21}|u|sz_{10}\mapsto\lambda sz_{20}\). Check its degree, height weight and inverse. After adjoining a middle letter \(v\) of suspended degree three and a direct cross class \(a_{20}\) of ordinary degree two, exhibit coordinates of this kind which do not commute.

Solution. The input suspended degree is \(-1+1-1=-1\), equal to that of its output. Both have total height jump two, so both have weight one. It reduces primitive-letter length from three to one and respects the concatenated-string label. Its cofree extension leaves any surrounding core runs in place. There is at most one such two-cross block on a three-level path, and its image is a single direct cross arrow on which the extra Taylor term is zero. Thus the extra part \(N\) of the coordinate satisfies \(N^2=0\), and its inverse is \(1-N\), or the same central Taylor term with parameter \(-\lambda\). This is a legitimate whole-path coordinate over the identity core; no claim that it stabilizes a particular differential is needed for this group calculation.

For the noncommuting example, choose the common core coordinate with its one extra component \(g_3(u,u,u)=v\), extended cofreely, and denote its common tensor-power extension to the graph by \(G\). Choose \(\gamma\) with its one extra path term \(sz_{21}|v|sz_{10}\mapsto sa_{20}\). This is homogeneous of degree zero because both terms have suspended degree one. Its inverse subtracts that term, for the same two-cross reason. Put \(w=sz_{21}|u|u|u|sz_{10}\), with these core letters in one chosen middle factor. The common coordinate gives \(G(w)=w+sz_{21}|v|sz_{10}\), while \(\gamma(w)=w\). Bare cross letters are fixed by \(G\), so \[ \gamma G(w)-G\gamma(w)=sa_{20}\ne0. \tag{C.40.13} \] Every term has weight three. This proves noncommutativity inside the actual shared-core path-coordinate group, retaining the same factor labels and composite-string grade.

Theorem C.40.1.1 constructs the actual full graph base change and proves square zero from its central Taylor projections. Theorem C.40.2.1 proves original graph recovery and the finite-height windows. Theorem C.40.3.1 supplies the common-core whole-path coordinate group, inverse restrictions and conditional target-stabilizer torsors. Exercises C.40.4.1-C.40.4.2 verify the mixed tensor coradical, a path-coordinate inverse and the displayed noncommuting coordinates, including equation (C.40.13). Editable SVG source. Related free source: Hess–Parent–Scott, Appendix A.

C.41. Exact block products over the common cores

The partial convolution associated with an ordered partition is the product of its block functors. Its represented module should therefore be constructed as that product, rather than assigned unrelated minimal coordinates. We prove this assertion with the suspension signs, actual common input models and retained multiple-cross operations.

C.41.1. The canonical projection from a common cobar

Theorem C.41.1.1. Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) be the positive relative dg coalgebras used in C.39.4, over their scalar coefficient categories. Write \(A=\bigotimes_i C_i\), \(U_i=\Omega C_i\). There is an actual dg functor \[ \kappa_{\mathbf C}:\Omega A\longrightarrow\bigotimes_i U_i. \tag{C.41.1} \] It fixes the tuple objects and is a quasi-equivalence. On its universal cobar generator its value is the sum of the one-factor twisting cochains, with the other factors counited. These maps regroup strictly under ordered partitions and commute with the graded permutations of the factors. The empty product is the coefficient category and the one-factor map is the identity.

Proof. Denote the universal twisting cochain \(C_i\to\Omega C_i\) by \(t_i\), of degree one. Insert its output in the \(i\)-th target factor, apply counits to all other input factors, and call the resulting degree-one map on \(A\) \(\xi_i\). Put \(\xi=\sum_i\xi_i\).

The internal twisting equation for \(\xi_i\) is the equation for \(t_i\), since the other counits are chain maps. For distinct factors the convolution products satisfy \(\xi_i\star\xi_j=-\xi_j\star\xi_i\). Indeed a contributing input has precisely the two selected factor pieces, with all remaining pieces counited. Interchanging those pieces uses the tensor-coalgebra Koszul sign; interchanging their target images uses the graded tensor-algebra sign. The additional two degree-one shifts leave their total relative sign \((-1)^{1\cdot1}=-1\). Thus the cross terms in \(\xi\star\xi\) cancel in pairs. This proves the twisting equation for \(\xi\).

Extend its values multiplicatively from the free cobar generators. The twisting equation is precisely the equality between the internal and splitting terms of the cobar differential and the target differential. Consequently the extension is the dg functor (C.41.1).

There is also an exact bar identity. With \(\eta_i:C_i\to B\Omega C_i\) the units of C.39.4, set \[ \psi_{\mathbf C}=\operatorname{sh}_m\bigotimes_i\eta_i: A\longrightarrow B\!\left(\bigotimes_i U_i\right). \qquad B\kappa_{\mathbf C}\,\eta_A=\psi_{\mathbf C}. \tag{C.41.2} \] Both sides of the second equality are maps into a cofree relative bar. Their single-letter projections are \(\xi\): in a shuffle a one-letter output can come from just one nonempty factor, with all other factors empty. A coalgebra map into this bar is determined by that projection, by its consecutive-cut reconstruction. This proves the equality, including its higher components.

Each \(\eta_i\) is a quasi-isomorphism by the complete cut proof of C.39.4. The actual shuffle is a quasi-isomorphism by C.39.3; its inputs \(U_i\) are positive by the same cobar degree calculation as C.34.1. Split balanced tensor products over the scalar coefficient categories preserve these quasi-isomorphisms, by C.30.1. Thus \(\psi_{\mathbf C}\) is a quasi-isomorphism. C.39.4 carries it to a quasi-isomorphism on cobars. The bar-cobar counit of the positive dg category \(\bigotimes_i U_i\) is a quasi-isomorphism by C.34.1's fixed-word cut contraction. Its composite with \(\Omega\psi_{\mathbf C}\) is \(\kappa_{\mathbf C}\), since it has the prescribed generator values \(\xi\). This proves the quasi-equivalence assertion.

For regrouping, first project to cobars of groups of adjacent factors, then apply the projections within those groups. On a free generator the resulting twisting cochain is again the sum of all individual \(t_i\), with the other factors counited. It is therefore exactly \(\kappa_{\mathbf C}\), not merely homotopic to it. A graded permutation gives the same statement by tensor naturality and the same one-factor formula. The zero- and one-factor assertions follow directly from that formula and the relative coefficient identities. All constructions preserve the factor and endpoint labels and restrict to full finite corners. ∎

C.41.2. The product module and its fixed-core transfer

Theorem C.41.2.1. Put \(C=B\mathcal M\) and \(A_i=C^{\otimes n_i}\), for positive arities \(n_i\). Let \(F_i:\Omega A_i\to\Omega C\) be strict dg representatives of the actual block convolution functors, with images in the finite additive IC envelope. Set \(N=\sum_i n_i\), and use the projection maps of C.41.1 to define \[ P=(\bigotimes_i F_i)\kappa_{\mathbf A}: \Omega(C^{\otimes N})\longrightarrow(\Omega C)^{\otimes m}, \qquad \nu_m=\kappa_{(C,\ldots,C)}: \Omega(C^{\otimes m})\longrightarrow(\Omega C)^{\otimes m}. \tag{C.41.3} \] The represented dg module with actions through \(P,\nu_m\) has the actual block-product functor as its perfect-envelope interpretation. Its common-core one-cross bar module is exactly the product of the individual common-core modules, with one total cross suspension.

More precisely let \(Z_i=C\otimes sM_i\otimes A_i\) be those modules, where \(M_i(y,x)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Omega C}(F_i x,y)\). For a crossed bar module put \(K(Z)=Z[-1]\), using the usual cochain shift differential and its induced comodule signs. Then the block module is \[ Z_P=\left(\bigotimes_i K(Z_i)\right)[1] \cong C^{\otimes m}\otimes s\!\left(\bigotimes_i M_i\right)\otimes C^{\otimes N}. \tag{C.41.4} \] This is an equality of the full differentials and both coactions after the stated graded regrouping.

Each \(K(Z_i)\) has a contraction, over its fixed cores, to a cofree module on \(H(M_i)\) retaining all higher module operations. Products of these actual contractions give (C.41.4) a contraction onto the product of those minimal modules. An independently transferred minimal block module is isomorphic to this product by an actual bicomodule isomorphism over the identity cores, with identity leading cohomology map.

Proof. The maps \(\kappa_{\mathbf A},\nu_m\) are actual quasi-equivalences by C.41.1. Their equivalences on perfect envelopes follow from the represented-module argument of C.33.2. Thus restricting the target action along \(\nu_m\) and the source along \(\kappa_{\mathbf A}\) gives the original external product of the block functors.

These strict representatives exist in the application: C.38.1 gives a strict block functor on \(\Omega B\mathcal M_{n_i}\). Precompose it with the actual dg quasi-equivalence \(\Omega\sigma_{n_i}\) of C.39.3–C.39.4. Its source is exactly \(\Omega(C^{\otimes n_i})\), and its target is \(\Omega C\). No identification of independently chosen input models is used. Finite additive image matrices are interpreted by the explicit relative matrix balancing of C.38.1.

The dg mapping space in the tensor target of (C.41.3) is literally \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{(\Omega C)^{\otimes m}}(Px,\nu_m y) =\bigotimes_i\operatorname{Hom}_{\Omega C}(F_i x_i,y_i) =\bigotimes_i M_i(y_i,x_i). \tag{C.41.5} \] The object maps of both projections fix the tuple labels. The displayed identification has the ordinary graded tensor differential, not just its cohomology. Every \(M_i\) is nonnegative and degreewise finite because it is a finite matrix of mappings in the positive target core; its cohomology is the actual nonnegative, even IC mapping cohomology of C.33.1.

Pull back the ordinary dg functor graph bars along \(\eta_C,\eta_{A_i}\). The cut-and-central-projection construction of C.40.1 applies equally with a nonzero central unary differential: retain that differential among the specified central operations. Its one-cross sector is the stated \(Z_i\), with its genuine left and right actions. For (C.41.3), the two bar pullbacks are exactly the shuffles of these individual core maps, by (C.41.2).

We spell out the shift in (C.41.4). If \(c,m,a\) are homogeneous, the identification of the ordinary cofree module with \(K(Z_i)\) is \[ c\otimes m\otimes a \longmapsto(-1)^{|c|+|m|}\, u(c\otimes sm\otimes a), \tag{C.41.6} \] where \(u\) is the degree-one shift symbol in \(Z_i[-1]\). Its differential is \(-u\,d_Z\). For the left-core, central and right-core unary terms, respectively, the sign ratios in (C.41.6) are \(-1,-1,+1\). Substitution gives exactly the ordinary tensor differential on \(C\otimes M_i\otimes A_i\). Its induced left coaction moves \(u\) past a core piece with sign \((-1)^{|\text{piece}|}\); its right coaction needs no such interchange. Formula (C.41.6) consequently gives the ordinary two cofree coactions too.

Tensor these ordinary modules, regroup their left cores, central letters and right cores using the Koszul rule, and then restore one cross suspension by the inverse of (C.41.6). This is the isomorphism (C.41.4). It restores degree \(-1\) for a tensor of degree-zero central mappings, irrespective of the number of blocks.

To verify its entire differential, an ordinary dg graph has only its central unary differential and its left and right multiplication Taylor terms on a one-cross sector. In a shuffled one-letter core output, all but one factor are counited. Thus each left or right action on (C.41.5) acts in precisely one factor. Moving that action through the preceding factors gives the ordinary graded tensor sign. The suspended multiplication has the sign \((-1)^{|sa|}\) of C.38.5; after (C.41.6) this is exactly that same sign in the tensor module. The unary terms were checked explicitly above. These are all its central Taylor terms. Its coactions reconstruct the remaining terms from them by C.39.2's cofree formula. This proves equality of the full module differentials and both coactions in (C.41.4), not equality only on bare central letters.

Now choose a normalized contraction \(i_i,p_i,h_i\) of \(M_i\) onto \(H(M_i)\), as in A.3.1.1, retaining its finite multiplicity blocks. Extend it to the ordinary cofree module by identities on its cores and by the graded tensor sign on \(h_i\). Denote the extended maps by \(I_i,P_i,H_i\). The initial differential \(d_0\) includes the full differentials of both cores and the central unary differential. Their tensor signs give \(d_0H_i+H_id_0=1-I_iP_i\) and the normalized side conditions. All three maps are bicomodule maps of their respective degrees over the identity cores.

Let \(\delta_i=d_i-d_0\). Since both differentials have the same core coaction terms, their difference is a degree-one bicomodule map. Every nonzero term consumes a nonempty surrounding core input. Count the total primitive bar-letter length in the two surrounding cores, including every factor in \(A_i\). Such a term strictly lowers that length; \(H_i\) changes only the central letter. Hence all inverses below are finite on each input: \[ I_i^\infty=(1+H_i\delta_i)^{-1}I_i,\quad P_i^\infty=P_i(1+\delta_iH_i)^{-1},\quad H_i^\infty=H_i(1+\delta_iH_i)^{-1}. \tag{C.41.7} \] Their transferred differential is \(d_{\rm core}+P_i\delta_i I_i^\infty\). C.35.1's complete algebraic contraction identities apply with this \(d_0\) and this length filtration; that proof requires local nilpotence and the contraction identities, not a vanishing core differential. Composition of bicomodule maps preserves their coaction equations, so the finite sums in (C.41.7) retain the identity core maps. In particular the transferred differential retains the fixed core differentials and all its higher actions. Its bare central unary term is zero.

Take the tensor product of these already perturbed contractions. Its inclusion and projection are the tensors of \(I_i^\infty,P_i^\infty\), and its homotopy is the ordered sum \[ H_\Pi=\sum_i E_1^\infty\otimes\cdots\otimes E_{i-1}^\infty \otimes H_i^\infty\otimes1\otimes\cdots\otimes1, \qquad E_i^\infty=I_i^\infty P_i^\infty. \tag{C.41.8} \] All evaluations use the tensor degree signs. Commuting the differential through this sum gives the telescope \(\sum_i E_1^\infty\cdots E_{i-1}^\infty(1-E_i^\infty) =1-\bigotimes_i E_i^\infty\). It proves the contraction identity. The side conditions follow from those of the factors; a cross term in \(H_\Pi^2\) contains either \(H_i^\infty E_i^\infty\) or \(E_i^\infty H_i^\infty\) and vanishes. Tensoring the two individual coaction equations gives the product coaction equations. Thus this is an actual contraction of (C.41.4) to the shifted product of the individual minimal modules. We have used the product of actual perturbed maps, not assumed that two different perturbation choices coincide.

If a minimal block module was independently transferred, compose the product inclusion with its projection. This gives a bicomodule chain map from the product model to that model. Its bare central term is the identity under the split Künneth identification \(H(\bigotimes M_i)=\bigotimes H(M_i)\). The cofree bicomodule formula expresses every other term by a central Taylor map consuming at least one surrounding core letter. Its difference from the identity therefore lowers surrounding length. The finite inverse \(\sum_{r\ge0}(-L)^r\), where \(L\) is that difference, is an actual bicomodule inverse. It commutes with the differentials by the chain equation for the original map. This proves the final assertion, retaining the fixed common cores. ∎

C.41.3. Product normalization retains the whole grafting graph

Theorem C.41.3.1. Consider a full finite directed path graph with positive common cores \(C^{\otimes n_i}\) and nonnegative, degreewise finite central dg mapping complexes. Assume its one-cross sectors are the represented modules of C.41.2 whenever a marked operation is an external block product. Its complete differential includes its actual several-cross grafting terms.

There is a transfer to minimal central complexes which fixes every common core. It retains all those grafting terms and their higher identities. Its block-product one-cross sectors can simultaneously be normalized to (C.41.4)'s products of the individual minimal modules. The normalization is an actual whole-path coalgebra isomorphism over the identity cores.

For normalized one-block coordinates \(T_i\) over a single core coordinate \(g\), the induced block-product coordinate is literally their shifted tensor product. Its output restriction is \(g^{\otimes m}\), its input restriction is \(g^{\otimes N}\), and its composition and inverse are the tensor products of the individual compositions and inverses. This is a genuine closed polynomial product mark in the finite windows of C.40.3.

Proof. Split every central mapping complex over its coefficient blocks and choose normalized contractions. On each path extend their inclusions and projections by the identity on every pure core run. They give graded coalgebra maps \(I,P\) between the path coalgebras; all cuts commute with the central tensor maps.

Extend the central homotopies by the ordered tensor sum on the cross positions, using \(ip\) on preceding cross letters, the homotopy on the selected cross letter, and identities afterwards. Pure cores are unchanged. This gives a homotopy \(H\) for the differential \(d_0\) consisting of the full core differentials and all central unary differentials. The telescope of C.41.2 proves \(d_0H+Hd_0=1-IP\) and the side conditions. Cutting before or after the selected central letter proves \(\Delta H=(H\otimes1+IP\otimes H)\Delta\): terms whose selected cross letter lies before the cut give the first summand, and those after the cut give the second. This argument includes a cut within a core run because the core maps are identities.

The remaining differential \(\delta\) is a coderivation. A one-cross action consumes a nonempty core input, whereas a several-cross action replaces at least two cross letters by one. Thus \(\delta\) strictly lowers the total primitive-core-letter plus cross-letter length. \(H\) changes only a central letter. The finite perturbation formulas (C.41.7), now on the whole graph, apply.

Their chain, retraction and homotopy equations are the algebraic identities proved in C.35.1. Their coalgebra equations follow from the same length recursion as A.3.1.1: insert the displayed coproduct identity for \(H\) and the coderivation identity for \(\delta\) in the inclusion and projection recursions; at each length their difference from the required equation has smaller length and hence vanishes inductively. The recursion for the perturbed homotopy is exactly C.36.1's computation, with \(E=I^\infty P^\infty\). No step requires a core run to be cofree on a single set of generators. It uses only the path cuts, the stated identities and strict length decrease.

The pure-core restrictions have \(H=0\) and \(\delta=0\), so remain exactly the identity cores with their original differentials. The transferred differential has zero central unary part. Its square is zero by the contraction identities, and it contains every perturbation term arising from the actual several-cross \(\delta\). On the one-cross sector this is precisely the fixed-core module transfer of C.41.2. On several-cross paths it includes the genuine merging terms; those paths have not been removed or quotiented out.

Use C.41.2's fixed-core isomorphism to replace each independently transferred block module by the prescribed product module. We explain its extension to the full graph. A path with consecutive cross modules \(Z_{i_0i_1},\ldots,Z_{i_{q-1}i_q}\) is their iterated cotensor over the intervening common cores. C.39.1's counit calculation identifies this cotensor with the path tensor having one intervening core run at each level. Therefore bicomodule maps over identity cores give maps on these cotensors and commute with their path cuts. Their inverses give inverse maps on the same cotensors. Together with the identity on pure cores this is a whole-path coalgebra isomorphism \(\Phi\).

Transport the differential by \(\Phi^{-1}d\Phi\). This retains its square-zero identity and the same complete graph recovery. The entire several-cross differential is transported too: only its coordinates have changed, and no grafting operation has been dropped. Its one-cross restrictions are now exactly the product minimal modules because their individual maps were chain isomorphisms.

Finally tensor the actual one-block coordinates after desuspending their single cross letters as in (C.41.6), then restore the single total suspension. Their left coactions are over \(\bigotimes_i g=g^{\otimes m}\), and their right coactions are over \(\bigotimes_i g^{\otimes n_i}=g^{\otimes N}\), with the prescribed regrouping. All coordinates have degree zero. Hence composing two of these product maps is exactly the product of their individual compositions, and their inverse is exactly the product of their individual inverses. Every bare central cohomology map remains the prescribed identity.

In a finite height-weight window the regrouping preserves degree and endpoints. Each core and central factor has bounded degree, by C.40.7, so all tensor entries use retained finite windows. Requiring a block restriction to equal this tensor product is a finite polynomial equation in the individual coordinate entries. The composition and inverse computations show it is preserved by the common-core group operations. The whole-path restrictions and their transported equations therefore give a closed subgroup with this genuine product mark. Smaller full factor-label and weight corners retain the maps and the equation.

This establishes the block-product mark and its full graph normalization. Higher comparisons of differently flattened strings, their coherent ordered-tree and unit diagrams, and the complete marked extension-field solution are additional data; this theorem does not assert them from one-cross product equality. ∎

C.41.4. The one-cross shift and a retained higher action

Exercise C.41.4.1. Take two degree-zero central mappings and empty surrounding core runs. What is the degree of their product cross letter? For ordinary central complexes with \(dx=y\), \(|x|=1,|y|=2\), compute the differential of \(x\otimes x\). Explain the two mistakes prevented by (C.41.4).

Solution. Each separate crossed bar letter has degree \(-1\). Their plain tensor has degree \(-2\). The operation \((K(Z_1)\otimes K(Z_2))[1]\) first raises each degree by one and then lowers their total degree by one; its product cross letter has degree \(-1\), as required for one ordinary degree-zero mapping. Equivalently the plain tensor of the two \(Z_i\)'s requires the shift \([-1]\). The ordinary differential is \[ d(x\otimes x)=y\otimes x-x\otimes y. \tag{C.41.9} \] The minus sign is the degree-one first central factor's tensor sign. Thus plain tensoring suspended cross modules has the wrong degree, while unsigned tensoring central differentials gives the wrong differential. Both signs are retained by (C.41.6).

Exercise C.41.4.2. Let a left core be the tensor coalgebra on three degree-one letters \(u,v,w\), with zero differential. Let the central complex have \(p\) in degree zero, \(x\) in degree one, \(y,t\) in degree two, \(z\) in degree three, and \(q\) in degree four, with \(dx=y,dt=z\). Its cohomology has basis \(p,q\). Take \(h(y)=x,h(z)=t\). Define the degree-one cofree module perturbation by consuming its last core letter \(l\): \[ \delta(a\,l\otimes n)=(-1)^{|a|}a\otimes A_l(n),\qquad A_u(p)=y,\quad A_v(x)=z,\quad A_w(t)=q, \tag{C.41.10} \] and zero on the other central basis inputs. Verify square zero and compute the transferred operation on \(w|v|u\otimes p\). Does vanishing of all one-letter operations on cohomology suffice to discard the higher action?

Solution. Each \(A_l\) has degree two and commutes with the central differential. Their pairwise composites are zero: their images \(y,z,q\) are killed by every \(A_l\). The module tensor signs consequently give \(d_0\delta+\delta d_0=0\) and \(\delta^2=0\), so \((d_0+\delta)^2=0\). The normalized central contraction kills \(x,y,t,z\) in its projection. Its extended homotopy is \(H(a\otimes n)=(-1)^{|a|}a\otimes h(n)\).

All one-letter transferred actions vanish. On the specified three-letter input, the successive nonzero terms are \[ wvup \xrightarrow{\delta} wvy \xrightarrow{H} wvx \xrightarrow{\delta} -wz \xrightarrow{H} wt \xrightarrow{\delta} q. \tag{C.41.11} \] The first prefix has degree two, while the two later prefixes have degree one; those are the two displayed minus signs, which cancel. In \(P\delta(1+H\delta)^{-1}I\), this three-action term has the positive geometric-sum coefficient. Thus the transferred central operation is \(q\ne0\). It has degree one: its input degree is three and its output degree is four. Both cohomology letters have even degrees, as in the IC application.

The example is a finite algebraic module test, not an identification of this complex with an IC mapping complex. It proves that one-letter cohomology actions can all vanish while a higher transferred action remains nonzero. The actual differential and perturbation data of C.41.2 must therefore be retained.

Theorem C.41.1.1 proves the actual common-cobar projection and its strict ordered regrouping. Theorem C.41.2.1 proves the complete shifted product differential and both module coactions, with the explicit sign in equation (C.41.6). Theorem C.41.3.1 gives conditional whole-path product normalization while retaining the several-cross grafting operations. Exercise C.41.4.2 proves the displayed nonzero transferred action, including its exact signs and degrees. Editable SVG source. Complementary free source: Bezrukavnikov–Finkelberg, Equivariant Satake category and Kostant–Whittaker reduction.

C.42. Directed tree indices over the common tensor cores

The ordered-tree comparison is a diagram of functors, not a set of objectwise isomorphisms. Its index has degree-zero arrows, whose bar suspensions have degree minus one. We retain that index and prove the comparison with a height filtration that includes those negative degrees.

C.42.1. The actual index-decorated shuffle

Theorem C.42.1.1. Let \(I\) be a finite poset with an integer height strictly increasing on every nonidentity arrow, and let its height range be \(H_I\). Its linear category \(kI\) is augmented over the scalar identity category \(S_I\). Put \(D_I=B_{S_I}(kI)\). With the fixed \(C=B\mathcal M\), \(\mathcal U=\Omega C\), and the tensor-input minimal models \(\mathcal M_n\) of C.34.3, there is an actual chain coalgebra quasi-isomorphism \[ \sigma_{n,I}:C^{\otimes n}\otimes D_I \longrightarrow B(\mathcal M_n\otimes kI). \tag{C.42.1} \] The source is the literal common tensor core with its fixed index bar. Its restriction to a fixed index object is \(\sigma_n\), and its restriction to the pure index is the identity \(D_I\).

For any of these bars define \(W=|w|+\Delta h_I\). It is nonnegative. Weight at most \(D\) is finite at a finite object corner, and the primitive-letter length is at most \(D+H_I\). The coderivation raises this weight by one and the comparison preserves it.

Proof. A composite of nonidentity arrows in a poset still has different endpoints. Their span is therefore an ideal in \(kI\), complementary to the scalar identity algebra. This proves its augmentation assertion. A reduced index bar word consists of a composable sequence of strict arrows. Its length \(q\) is at most \(H_I\), and its degree is \(-q\). Its height jump is at least \(q\). Hence \[ W(\text{index word})=\Delta h_I-q\ge0. \tag{C.42.2} \] The bar differential merges adjacent arrows with the suspended composition sign. It retains endpoints, increases degree by one and therefore increases weight by one.

We verify the shuffle quasi-isomorphism in this nonpositive bar convention. C.39.3's free resolution proof applies to any augmented dg algebra \(R=S\oplus\bar R\) over a split semisimple \(S\), without a positivity assumption. Indeed its root differential (C.39.11) and contraction (C.39.12) were proved by the Leibniz and multiplication cancellations for homogeneous letters. Those identities do not use their lower degree bound.

The projectivity argument there also does not require that bound. At each finite bar-length stage its graded-free quotient has coefficient complex \((s\bar R)^{\otimes_Sq}\). Mapping into an acyclic module is acyclic because the underlying \(S\)-complex has a split contraction, and postcomposing with that contraction gives a Hom contraction. Restriction to the preceding stage is surjective in every mapping degree. Starting from a compatible cycle, choose a primitive at stage zero; lift it to the next stage, then correct the resulting cycle in the acyclic restriction kernel. Induction produces compatible primitives at all stages. This proves homotopical projectivity for the complete direct-sum bar resolution even when its suspended letters are negative.

For two algebras \(R,T\), use their tensor resolution, filtered by total bar length. Its augmentation has the tensor contraction and it has the same projectivity proof. The actual extended shuffle is a chain map of these two resolutions: the internal-letter identities are the graded cancellations of C.34.2, and its root identities are the two equal sign exponents in C.39.14. They likewise hold for degree-zero ordinary letters. Its map on augmentations is the identity. Its cone is acyclic and homotopically projective, so its identity is null-homotopic by applying that mapping property to the cone itself. The resulting \(R\otimes T\)-linear contraction remains a contraction after augmentation tensor. Thus the resulting actual reduced shuffle is a quasi-isomorphism. This is the complete free-resolution argument, rather than a convergence assertion for a negative bar-length spectral sequence.

Apply it to \(\mathcal U^{\otimes n}\) and \(kI\), and also use the already proved \(n\)-factor shuffle. Normalize the mapping contraction of \(\mathcal U^{\otimes n}\otimes kI\) by tensoring the chosen contraction of \(\mathcal U^{\otimes n}\) with each degree-zero index-arrow line. Its transferred model is exactly \(\mathcal M_n\otimes kI\): every tree term in the transfer has the same \(\mathcal U^{\otimes n}\) contraction and composition term, multiplied by the composite of its index arrows. The latter have degree zero, so add no interchange signs. Scalar identity inputs are normalized as in A.3.1.1. In particular a pure index word has zero homotopy and its ordinary index composition.

Let \(P_{n,I}\) be the resulting actual bar projection. The desired map is \[ \sigma_{n,I} =P_{n,I}\operatorname{sh}_2 \left((\operatorname{sh}_n I_1^{\otimes n})\otimes1_{D_I}\right). \tag{C.42.3} \] Every map here is a chain coalgebra map. The bar inclusion and projection have the finite wordwise contraction of A.3.1.1 and C.35.1, so are quasi-isomorphisms. The shuffle just proved is a quasi-isomorphism, and split finite tensor products preserve it. This proves (C.42.1).

If all index factors are identity arrows at one index object, (C.42.3) is exactly the definition of \(\sigma_n\). On a pure index word, \(I_1\) contributes only its scalar coaugmentations, the shuffle is that same word, and \(P_{n,I}\) is the identity just checked. This proves both restrictions, without presuming naturality of unrelated minimal-model choices.

For the bounds on \(B(\mathcal M_n\otimes kI)\), its ordinary reduced letters have either positive degree at least two, or degree zero on a strict index arrow. If there are \(r_+\) positive letters and \(r_0\) zero-degree letters, then \(r_0\le H_I\). Their suspended degree is at least \(r_+-r_0\), while the height jump is at least \(r_0\). Consequently \(W\ge r_+\), and the total length is at most \(W+H_I\). The same argument applies to \(B(\mathcal U^{\otimes n}\otimes kI)\). On the tensor source, positive \(C\)-letters have suspended degree at least one and (C.42.2) bounds its index letters. This gives the same bound there.

At fixed \(D\), the height range bounds the degree above by \(D\) and below by \(-H_I\). The bound on word length then bounds every ordinary positive letter degree. There are finitely many index arrows and selected object labels, and the mapping spaces are degreewise finite. Thus the windows are finite. Cuts split degrees and heights additively; each piece has nonnegative weight by the same argument, so the windows are subcoalgebras. All comparison maps have degree zero and fixed endpoints, hence preserve \(W\). All coderivations have degree one and fixed endpoints, hence raise it by one. ∎

C.42.2. The weighted recovery of the native tree diagram

Theorem C.42.2.1. Take the actual rational ordered-tree functor graph of C.33.3 for finitely many arities and object labels, with its original coherent finite-frame contraction comparisons. The source core at arity \(n\) can be chosen as \(\mathcal M_n\otimes kT_n\), retaining its whole index. There is an actual common-core graph obtained by replacing that source bar by \(C^{\otimes n}\otimes D_{T_n}\), using \(\sigma_{n,T_n}\), and retaining \(C\) as the common output core.

Its graph comparison and its cobar comparison are quasi-isomorphisms on every corner. They retain the original tree-indexed enhanced functor diagram and all its transferred index-chain components. The same assertion applies to a full finite directed nested graph with such index-decorated cores, nonnegative minimal central mapping spaces, and all its actual several-cross operations.

Proof. First choose the source contractions before transferring the full graph. The enhanced input of C.33.3 is the rational tensor generator category tensored with \(kT_n\). Replace its tensor generator core by the positive \(\mathcal U^{\otimes n}\), using C.34's actual equivalence. Its index remains unchanged. The contraction chosen in C.42.1 gives the exact source model \(\mathcal M_n\otimes kT_n\).

Choose the target core contraction once and choose the cross mapping contractions after those source choices. The full graph transfer restricts to the already chosen source and target transfers on their pure core words. Its cross mapping cohomology is the actual \(\operatorname{Hom}(F_t\mathbf P,Q)\) of C.33.5, nonnegative, even and degreewise finite by C.33.1. Its higher operations retain the native coherent diagram because the transferred bar map is the whole original graph map. This uses the actual graph construction of C.33.2–C.33.3, rather than deducing a natural-transformation complex from the degrees of an object's mappings.

Apply C.40.1's path construction with the chain coalgebra maps \(f_i=\sigma_{n_i,I_i}\) on the decorated inputs and the identity on the output. Its proof of coassociativity, coderivation uniqueness, \(QD_A=D_BQ\) and \(D_A^2=0\) uses the finite path cuts and central projections; it does not assume positivity of a pure core run. Those exact proofs therefore apply here. In particular the path differential still has its operations consuming several cross letters and any intervening index runs.

Choose a total graph height strictly increasing on every strict index arrow and every cross arrow. For the native fixed-arity tree graph use the height of C.31.2 on its source and place its target one step above its maximum. For a finite collection of nested components, separate their level height ranges by constants. No reverse arrow is introduced. Let its range be \(H\), and define \[ W(w)=|w|+h(\text{left endpoint})-h(\text{right endpoint}). \tag{C.42.4} \] Every pure core piece has nonnegative weight, by C.42.1. A central cross letter \(sN\) has degree \(|N|-1\), with \(|N|\ge0\), and its endpoint height jump \(d\) is at least one. It too has nonnegative weight.

Filter the graph by cross count at most \(q\), where \(q\le H\). A grafting term cannot increase this count. On its fixed-count quotient only pure core differentials and one-cross module operations remain.

The ordinary central-degree filtration of C.40.2 no longer suffices: consuming a suspended degree-zero index arrow may leave the ordinary central degree unchanged. Instead use the descending filtration by \[ \nu=\sum_{\text{central cross letters}} \bigl(|N|+\Delta h_{\text{cross}}\bigr). \tag{C.42.5} \] A one-cross operation consuming left and right core pieces of summed cohomological degree \(a\) and summed height jump \(e\) changes the ordinary central degree by \(a+1\), since it is a degree-one suspended Taylor operation. Its output cross letter absorbs those same endpoint jumps, so its change of \(\nu\) is \[ a+1+e=W(\text{consumed cores})+1\ge1. \tag{C.42.6} \] Bare central unary operations vanish by minimality. Thus this is a subcomplex filtration and its associated differential acts only on the pure core slots.

On each associated quotient the graph map \(Q\) is the tensor of the actual quasi-isomorphisms \(f_i\), with the fixed central coefficient spaces. It is a quasi-isomorphism by C.42.1 and the split coefficient contraction of C.30.1. All summands retain their core endpoints, so their fixed \(\nu\) values remain the same in this tensor assertion.

For a path with \(q\) crosses, degrees and endpoint height jumps telescope to \[ W(w)=\sum_{\text{core slots}}W(\text{core slot})+\nu-q. \qquad 0\le\nu\le W(w)+q. \tag{C.42.7} \] In a fixed cohomological degree \(r\), \(W(w)\le r+H\); the same bound holds in its incoming degree. The \(\nu\) filtration is therefore finite there. Associated cone acyclicity can be eliminated finitely, as in C.39.4: solve the cycle's first nonzero filtration component, subtract that boundary, and repeat until the bounded filtration ends. This proves \(Q\) a quasi-isomorphism on the cross-count quotient. Induction on the finite cross-count filtration proves it on the full graph.

We supply the cobar and recovery bounds in the presence of an index. A reduced coalgebra element with zero height jump has degree at least one, because its nonempty core letters are positive and it has no cross or strict index arrow. A reduced element with positive jump \(d\) has degree at least \(-d\), because its weight is nonnegative. In a composable cobar word of \(r\) generators, let \(a\) have positive jump. Then \(a\le H\), and the sum of their jumps is at most \(H\). After desuspension that word's degree is at least \[ 2(r-a)+a-H\ge2r-2H. \tag{C.42.8} \] The descending cobar-length filtration is consequently finite in every fixed degree and its incoming degree. Its associated map is a finite balanced tensor of the reduced cornerwise quasi-isomorphisms \(Q\). The split contraction and finite cone-elimination proof of C.39.4 proves \(\Omega Q\) is a quasi-isomorphism.

For a bar-cobar unit with \(r\) original coalgebra elements, their summed degrees are at least \(r-2H\). Formula (C.39.17) then bounds \(r\le t+2H\) in degree \(t\). The same explicit first-cut contraction of C.39.4 applies at every \(r\ge2\), including its internal signs. Its first quotient is the original coalgebra. This proves the units are quasi-isomorphisms.

We also verify recovery of the minimal graph itself. Its canonical \(A_\infty\) comparison to the cobar of its bar is the consecutive-block formula (C.34.3), applied to the whole directed graph. A word of \(r\) original ordinary arrows has at most \(H\) height-increasing arrows; all other reduced arrows have degree at least two. With \(v\ge1\) cobar blocks its degree is at least \(r-2H+v\). Thus the filtration by original arrow count is finite in each fixed degree. On a fixed-\(r\) quotient, splitting the \(r-1\) possible cuts is the exact exterior complex contracted in C.34.4. At \(r=1\) the comparison's first component is the original arrow; every \(r\ge2\) quotient contracts. The remaining higher bar operations lower \(r\), and minimality makes its original unary differential zero. Finite cone elimination proves that first component is a cornerwise quasi-isomorphism. It gives the required actual \(A_\infty\) equivalence; no strict counit from a cobar to a non-dg minimal category is assumed.

These are maps of the entire graph. Their core restrictions are the specified source/output equivalences, and their cross restrictions are the complete represented module comparisons. C.33.2's evaluation consequently recovers the native enhanced functor and its tree-indexed components. Index words of all lengths through the actual finite tree bound are retained. Their identities are the corresponding components of the full square-zero and chain coalgebra equations; no higher component is set to zero by an objectwise uniqueness argument.

Finally (C.42.7) bounds central ordinary degrees and the total positive core weight. The number of zero-degree index letters and cross letters is at most \(H\). Thus primitive-letter length is at most \(D+H\) in weight \(D\). There are finitely many profiles and coefficients at a finite corner. Cuts have nonnegative weights and all formulas retain their existing labels, so full finite corner and weight restrictions agree. This proves the remaining finite-system assertions. ∎

C.42.3. Coordinate groups and noncollapsing tree grafting

Theorem C.42.3.1. On a finite common-core graph of C.42.2 let \(g\) be a normalized core coordinate on \(C\). Require the whole-path coordinate \(G\) to have restrictions \[ G|_{C^{\otimes n}\otimes D_I} =g^{\otimes n}\otimes1_{D_I}, \qquad G|_C=g. \tag{C.42.9} \] Together with fixed bare cross letters, factor labels and endpoint grades, these equations give a closed finite unitriangular coordinate group on its height-weight windows. Its operations are \((h,H)(g,G)=(hg,HG)\) and componentwise inverse. Full differential-comparison equations use inputs through weight \(D-1\) and outputs through \(D\); whenever a complete selected marked comparison has a point, its reduced solution variety is a target-stabilizer torsor in this actual group.

For positive ordered block sizes \(n_1,\ldots,n_m\), the tree grafting functor gives an actual index coalgebra map \[ \gamma_{\mathbf n}:D_{T_m}\otimes\bigotimes_i D_{T_{n_i}} \longrightarrow D_{T_N},\qquad N=\sum_i n_i. \tag{C.42.10} \] It preserves the summed height weight, regroups associatively, and commutes with all the coordinates (C.42.9). Unit insertion on the common tensor cores is the coaugmentation at the IC unit and likewise commutes strictly with the common core powers. These algebraic statements retain the native diagram of C.42.2; actual cross-arity and geometric unit comparison marks still require their complete module and higher covariance data.

Proof. An index bar is cofree on its strict index-arrow letters, with its given differential. The other pure factors are the same cofree \(C\)'s as in C.40.3. Their tensor cores and path sectors have the same total primitive-letter coradical filtration: the iterated reduced coproduct followed by the canonical factor-order projection recovers every original factor word and cross sequence with coefficient a Koszul unit. This is C.40.3's complete injectivity argument applied also to the index factor.

The prescribed index coordinate is the identity, and all other primitive and bare-cross leading coordinates are fixed as before. Thus every coordinate is the identity on each associated length piece. It is unitriangular. C.42.2 bounds that length by \(D+H\); the matrices and their inverses are finite. Degree-zero, endpoint-preserving maps preserve \(W\). Equation (C.42.9) uses only the degree window of \(g\) already retained: each \(C\) factor's positive degree is at most the total core weight. Its entries are polynomial products of entries of that one \(g\); the index entries are fixed constants.

Coalgebra, degree, leading-entry and restriction equations are closed polynomial equations. Composition gives \(h^{\otimes n}g^{\otimes n}=(hg)^{\otimes n}\) on the decorated source, with the same identity index map. The inverse is \((g^{-1})^{\otimes n}\otimes1\). These calculations and the finite length recursion prove the group assertion. Differential comparisons have exactly the bounded domains stated because differentials raise \(W\) by one. The quotient of two solutions commutes with the target differential on those same domains, while each target stabilizer carries a solution to a solution. This is the actual torsor calculation of C.40.3. Extra marks require their full bounded domains and the stated nonempty point hypothesis; neither is inferred from an unmarked graph comparison.

We verify (C.42.10), including the augmentation condition. Set \(T_1\) to be the one-leaf identity tree, a one-object category of height zero. For \(n\ge2\), represent a tree by its proper intervals as in C.31.1. Grafting replaces outer leaf \(i\) by an interval block \(J_i\) of \(n_i\) consecutive final leaves. Its proper intervals are the following disjoint kinds: the inner proper intervals inside the \(J_i\)'s; each seam interval \(J_i\) with \(n_i\ge2\), when \(m\ge2\); and the expansions of the outer proper intervals into unions of consecutive blocks.

Every variable interval determines its source unambiguously. Inner intervals are properly contained in one \(J_i\), while outer expanded intervals contain at least two blocks. The fixed seams are a third kind. Deleting any source variable interval therefore deletes a distinct proper target interval. Grafting is injective on its tree tuples and sends every nonidentity contraction to a nonidentity contraction. It is a functor because two successive deletions have the same union of deleted intervals. It therefore preserves the augmentation to scalar identity categories. Its actual reduced bar map is defined.

Define \(\gamma_{\mathbf n}\) by the shuffle into the bar of the product index category, followed by that bar grafting map. Its shuffle is a chain coalgebra map by the homogeneous-letter signs of C.34.2, valid also for the degree-zero index algebras by C.42.1. Its bar grafting map is a chain coalgebra map because it preserves arrow composition, identities and nonidentity arrows. This proves (C.42.10).

Give \(T_n\), \(n\ge2\), height \(n-2\) minus the number of proper intervals, and give \(T_1\) height zero. If \(m\ge2\), put \(r=\#\{i:n_i=1\}\). There are \(m-r\) fixed seam intervals, so the grafted height is \[ N-2-\#(\text{outer proper intervals}) -\sum_i\#(\text{inner proper intervals})-(m-r). \tag{C.42.11} \] This is exactly the sum of the outer and inner heights, since \(\sum_i\max(0,n_i-2)=N-2m+r\). For \(m=1\) grafting is just the inner tree and has that same assertion. Hence endpoint height jumps agree. The shuffle preserves total suspended degree, and grafting does not alter the number of letters. Thus (C.42.10) preserves weight.

For nested grafting the final interval collections are identical in both orders: they are the same expanded outer intervals, seams and inner intervals. This proves strict associativity on index categories. The shuffle regrouping identity of C.34.2 consequently proves the same identity for their coalgebra maps. Regrouping \(C\)-factors also preserves their fixed order. Their single coordinate is \(g^{\otimes N}\), independently of grouping; the index coordinates are identities. This proves the strict covariance of the common-core/index maps.

Let \(e_{\mathbf1}\) be the group-like coaugmentation for the simple IC unit object. Its insertion in tensor slot \(r\) defines \[ j_r:C^{\otimes n}\longrightarrow C^{\otimes(n+1)},\qquad j_r(c_1\otimes\cdots\otimes c_n) =c_1\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{\mathbf1}\otimes\cdots\otimes c_n. \tag{C.42.12} \] The inserted element is closed, counital and group-like, so this is a chain coalgebra map preserving positive core degree. Normalized core coordinates fix it. Direct substitution gives \(g^{\otimes(n+1)}j_r=j_rg^{\otimes n}\), including \(n=0\). On finite retained windows these insertion equations use only existing degree-zero coefficient entries.

Positive-arity grafting and the common-core insertion are the maps just proved. A diagram deleting a nullary unit vertex can collapse a nonidentity index arrow to an identity. It is not covered by this augmented reduced-bar grafting proof, and must be retained through its actual unital functor/module diagram. Moreover (C.42.10)–(C.42.12) alone do not identify the two actual convolution modules under a grafting or supply their geometric unit transformation. C.41 gives the exact block-product sectors; their full covariance with the native C.42.2 diagram and its complete extension-field solution are still required. ∎

C.42.4. The height correction and a collapsed arrow

Exercise C.42.4.1. Let \(I\) have objects \(0<1<2\), arrows \(a:0\to1,b:1\to2,c:0\to2\) with \(ba=c\), and height \(h(i)=i\). Compute the differential and weight of \(sb|sa\). Adjoin an output \(y\) of height two and a degree-zero cross letter \(m:1\to y\), whose composition with \(a\) is a nonzero degree-zero cross letter \(m_a:0\to y\). Compute the change in the two central filtrations under \(sm|sa\mapsto -sm_a\).

Solution. Both suspended index arrows have degree minus one. Their bar product is \[ b_2(sb|sa)=-sc. \qquad W(sb|sa)=0,\quad W(sc)=1. \tag{C.42.13} \] The heights are the same total jump two, while the differential raises suspended degree from minus two to minus one. In the crossed calculation both ordinary central mappings have degree zero, so that degree does not increase at all. The original central height jump is \(2-1=1\), and the new one is \(2-0=2\). Thus \(\nu\) increases from one to two. The consumed core has degree minus one and height jump one, hence weight zero; its change \(W+1=1\) is exactly (C.42.6).

An associated quotient retaining only ordinary central degree would still contain this index action. The \(\nu\) quotient removes it while retaining the full action in the original graph. This is why the new filtration proves recovery without deleting native tree comparisons.

Exercise C.42.4.2. Let \(J\) have one nonidentity arrow \(a:0\to1\), and let \(F:J\to\{*\}\) send both objects to \(*\) and \(a\) to the identity. What fails if one tries to represent \(F\) by sending the reduced suspended arrow \(sa\) to zero? Compare the two maps after cobar and the bar-cobar counit.

Solution. There is no nonempty reduced target arrow: its target category is the scalar identity category. A reduced zero-arrow formula therefore kills \(sa\). After cobar it sends the generator \(t(sa)\) to zero. The source bar-cobar counit sends that generator to \(a\), whereas the actual functor sends \(a\) to \(1_*\). Thus the composites are \[ t(sa)\longmapsto0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad t(sa)\longmapsto1_*. \tag{C.42.14} \] They differ already in degree zero. The original arrow lies in the kernel of the source identity augmentation; its image under \(F\) does not lie in the kernel of the target augmentation. Hence the augmented reduced-bar functor formula does not apply. An independently defined zero-arrow coalgebra map, when interpreted after cobar, represents a different functor.

This calculation does not obstruct the normalized unital \(A_\infty\) or represented-module construction of the actual \(F\). It identifies the exact additional datum needed when an index arrow collapses. Positive-arity grafting in C.42.3 was proved noncollapsing; the geometric nullary/unit diagrams must be handled with their actual unital maps.

Theorem C.42.1.1 proves the actual index-decorated shuffle and finite height-weight windows. Theorem C.42.2.1 proves recovery of the complete native indexed graph using the central quantity in equations (C.42.5)–(C.42.7), including the full finite-height bar-cobar comparisons. Theorem C.42.3.1 proves the fixed-index coordinate group, augmentation-preserving positive grafting and common-core unit insertion. Exercises C.42.4.1–C.42.4.2 check the displayed negative degree, corrected filtration and collapsed-arrow distinction. Editable SVG source. Free background on the augmentation and bar conventions: Keller, Introduction to A-infinity algebras and modules, Sections 3.5–3.6.

C.43. Canonical input squares and transfer preserving prescribed modules

Canonical bar-cobar units give a strictly natural common input. Separately chosen contraction inclusions need not have that property. We also transfer a full graph only after choosing its module contractions; this preserves the exact product maps in a comparison, rather than merely identifying the two product models afterwards.

C.43.1. A strictly natural common input

Theorem C.43.1.1. Let \(C,D\) be the positive IC bar coalgebras, and let \(g:C\to D\) be a normalized chain coalgebra map with its prescribed object map. Put \(U_C=\Omega C,U_D=\Omega D,q=\Omega g\). For a finite directed poset \(I\), define \[ \psi^C_{n,I} =\operatorname{sh}_{n+1} \bigl(\eta_C^{\otimes n}\otimes1_{D_I}\bigr): C^{\otimes n}\otimes D_I \longrightarrow B(U_C^{\otimes n}\otimes kI). \tag{C.43.1} \] Here the shuffle includes the index as its last factor, and \(D_I=B(kI)\). This is an actual chain coalgebra quasi-isomorphism and satisfies the strict equality \[ B(q^{\otimes n}\otimes1_{kI})\psi^C_{n,I} =\psi^D_{n,I}(g^{\otimes n}\otimes1_{D_I}). \tag{C.43.2} \] Its additional rectified input map is \[ \widehat\psi^C_{n,I} =\eta_{B(U_C^{\otimes n}\otimes kI)}\psi^C_{n,I}. \tag{C.43.3} \] It has that same strict square with input functor \(\Omega B(q^{\otimes n}\otimes1_{kI})\). These maps retain the fixed index, ordered regrouping, positive tree grafting and coaugmentation insertions. In particular their common input coordinates are literally the indicated tensor powers of \(g\).

Proof. The units are the actual iterated-coproduct maps (C.39.16), not an independently chosen minimal-model inclusion. Their naturality is the identity \[ B(\Omega g)\eta_C=\eta_Dg. \tag{C.43.4} \] Indeed on the component of bar length \(r\), both sides apply \(g\) to the \(r\) original pieces in the iterated coproduct of the input. The coproduct identity of \(g\) makes these the same tensor, including the graded signs. Their coefficient components are the prescribed identity maps. This proves the equality on the whole cofree bar.

The shuffle is natural under strict dg functors: applying such a functor to each embedded single-factor bar letter before or after a shuffle gives the same interleavings, with the same degrees and Koszul signs. Use (C.43.4) on each \(C\)-factor and the identity on the index factor. This proves (C.43.2) as an exact map equality.

C.39.4 proves \(\eta_C\) is a quasi-isomorphism and C.42.1 proves the actual index-decorated shuffle is one. The coefficient tensor contraction proves the finite tensor assertion. Their composite is therefore the stated quasi-isomorphism. Applying C.42.2's finite-height bar-cobar-unit bound to \(B(U_C^{\otimes n}\otimes kI)\) proves that the further unit in (C.43.3) is a quasi-isomorphism too. Naturality of that same unit, now under \(B(q^{\otimes n}\otimes1)\), gives the strict square for (C.43.3).

Ordered regrouping of shuffle words is C.34.2's actual regrouping identity. On index factors use the noncollapsing grafting maps proved in C.42.3; functor naturality and shuffle regrouping give the same maps in both orders. Inserting a common-core coaugmentation contributes only the closed group-like coefficient object to \(\eta\), and contributes no shuffle letter. Thus insertion commutes with (C.43.1) and its \(g\)-square, including the empty input. The same statement holds for graded permutations of the positive factors if those are retained as marked maps. All maps are of degree zero with fixed endpoints, so the height-weight windows of C.42.1 contain their outputs.
