C.41.2 proves the exact canonical shuffle identity and proves that \(\psi_m\) is a quasi-isomorphism. Its source and target reduced coalgebra degrees are positive. C.39.4's complete cobar comparison proof therefore gives that \(\xi_m\) is a quasi-equivalence. On a free generator, the composite \(\epsilon_m\Omega\psi_m\) takes the shuffle's one-letter projection. That projection is exactly the sum of the one-factor twisting cochains with the other factors counited. It is the defining generator formula for \(\kappa_m\), proving the equality everywhere.

The counit generator formula plainly commutes with a strict dg functor \(q^{\otimes m}\), proving the first naturality equation. The second follows by applying \(\Omega\) to the strictly natural canonical shuffle square proved in C.43.1. All formulas retain the empty products and fixed coefficient categories, so the zero-fold statement follows as well. ∎

C.46.4. Solved exercises

Exercise C.46.4.1 (advanced). Take scalar-core levels \(0<1<2\) and closed source arrows \(b:0\to1,a:1\to2,z:0\to2\) of degrees \(0,2,2\), with \(ab=z\). In the target add arrows \(x,y:0\to2\) of degrees \(1,2\), with \(dx=y\), and put \(a'b'=z'+y\). The quotient kills \(x,y\). Keep the one-cross maps \(a\mapsto a',b\mapsto b',z\mapsto z'\). Construct the full bar comparison over the identity quotient.

Solution. Both graphs are dg categories: the only two-cross product is the displayed one, it obeys Leibniz, and a three-cross product is impossible. The kernel pair is acyclic, with \(h(y)=x\). The prescribed one-cross maps are chain maps but fail strict multiplicativity by the nonzero closed kernel element \(y\). In the graph-bar convention of C.38 and C.39, the unary differential is \(b_1(sx)=s(dx)\) and the product is \(b_2(sa|sb)=(-1)^{|sa|}s(ab)\). Thus define \[ T(sa|sb)=sa'|sb'+sx,\qquad T(sa)=sa',\quad T(sb)=sb',\quad T(sz)=sz'. \tag{C.46.EX1} \] The higher output has the right degree: \(sa|sb\) and \(sx\) both have degree zero. It has only the outside core cuts, so this formula preserves the entire coproduct, including the cut between \(sa\) and \(sb\). On the two-cross input, \[ b'T(sa|sb)=-s(z'+y)+sy=-sz'=T b(sa|sb). \tag{C.46.EX2} \] The pure and one-cross chain equations hold too, and there are no further composable cross inputs. Applying the quotient kills \(sx\), so the full square is exactly the identity raw comparison. Dropping that higher component leaves the uncancelled term \(-sy\). This is a supplied full raw square with a necessary higher lift, not an inference from its individual edge maps.

Exercise C.46.4.2 (intermediate). In a free relative dg source let \(u,v\) have degrees two and three, with \(du=v,dv=0\). Let the target quotient have the same generator images \(u_0,v_0\), and let a surjective target extension have an acyclic square-zero kernel \(x,y\), with \(dx=y\) in degrees two and three. Positive quotient elements act as zero on the kernel. A provisional graded generator lift sends \(u\) to \(u_0+x\) and \(v\) to \(v_0\). Correct it, retaining its quotient images.

Solution. The generator complex has a nonzero unary differential. Its Hom defect on \(u\) is \[ o(u)=d(u_0+x)-(v_0)=y,\qquad o(v)=0. \tag{C.46.EX3} \] It is a closed kernel-valued degree-one map. The kernel homotopy sends \(y\) to \(x\), so subtracting its postcomposition sends the corrected \(u\) to \(u_0\) and leaves \(v\) at \(v_0\). It now obeys \(d\widetilde F(u)=\widetilde F(v)\), and its quotient is unchanged. Considering \(d(u_0+x)\) alone would give \(v_0+y\), which is not in the kernel. The incoming generator differential must be retained in the correction complex. Extending multiplicatively gives the dg lift on every source word.

Theorem C.46.1.1 proves the complete relative square, given its full raw comparison. Theorem C.46.2.1 proves the unary-sensitive lifting formula. Theorem C.46.3.1 proves the canonical state counit, common input and strict naturality. Exercises C.46.4.1–C.46.4.2 compute the nonzero higher and unary corrections. The complete prerequisite cut, core and kernel proofs are C.40.1.1, C.43.1.1 and C.45.2.1. Editable SVG source.

C.47. Joint execution and contraction of native trees

C.47.1. Joint arrows and the sharp height

Fix \(n\ge0,L\ge1\). Use C.44.1's formal planar trees with \(n\) external leaves and \(1\le V(t)\le L\) operation vertices. Nullary and unary operation vertices are retained. A contraction remembers its selected original internal edge set \(K\), not just its resulting quotient shape. Write \(\pi_K\) for the map from original operation vertices to their connected contraction clusters, the vertices of \(t/K\).

An object of \(\mathcal E_{n,L}\) is a pair \((t,J)\), where \(J\) is an operation-descendant ideal: executing a vertex requires that all its operation descendants have been executed. A morphism \((t,J)\to(t/K,J')\) is the selected contraction set \(K\), with \(J'\) an ideal of the quotient, subject to \[ \pi_K(J)\subseteq J'. \tag{C.47.1} \] Thus execution may be added before contracting. For \(K=\varnothing\) the morphism is precisely an inclusion of execution ideals. Distinct edge sets remain distinct arrows, even when the source and target shapes agree.

Theorem C.47.1.1. These data form a finite category. Composition uses the lifted union of original edge sets from C.44.1 and the final target ideal. Its only endomorphisms are identities. The completed \(n\)-corolla is terminal. The height \[ h(t,J)=2(L-V(t))+|J| \tag{C.47.2} \] has range \(0\le h\le2L-1\), strictly increases along nonidentity arrows and bounds their chain length by \(2L-1\). This bound is sharp for every \(n\), including zero.

Proof. Contracting a selected operation edge identifies its two vertices; the connected clusters give the quotient operation vertices. The map \(\pi_K\) preserves operation ancestry, allowing equality. Consequently the inverse image \(I=\pi_K^{-1}(J')\) of an ideal is an ideal. The arrow condition is equivalently \(J\subseteq I\). It makes every arrow factor as executing the additional vertices to reach \((t,I)\), followed by the contraction from this cluster-saturated state to \((t/K,J')\).

For a second contraction \(K'\) of the quotient, each surviving edge lifts uniquely to the original tree. The composite quotient is contraction of \(K\cup\widetilde K'\), and its vertex projection is exactly \(\pi_{K'}\pi_K\). If \(\pi_K(J)\subseteq J'\) and \(\pi_{K'}(J')\subseteq J''\), their composite sends \(J\) into \(J''\). It is therefore a permitted arrow. The lifted-union associativity proof of C.44.1 gives associativity here, with the final ideal unchanged. Empty contraction and unchanged ideal give the identity. Finiteness follows from the finite formal-tree set, finite internal edge subsets and finite ideal sets. No quotient by parallel contraction labels is taken.

Put \(k=|K|\). A cluster with \(a\) vertices contracts exactly \(a-1\) internal edges. Let \(k_{\rm ex}\) count the contracted edges in the clusters belonging to \(J'\). Since \(I\) contains every vertex of exactly those clusters, \[ |I|=|J'|+k_{\rm ex},\qquad 0\le k_{\rm ex}\le k. \tag{C.47.3} \] The height difference is consequently \[ h(t/K,J')-h(t,J) =2k+|J'|-|J| =k+(k-k_{\rm ex})+(|I|-|J|). \tag{C.47.4} \] It is at least \(k\). If \(k>0\) it is positive. If \(k=0\), it is \(|J'|-|J|\), positive unless the arrow is the identity. Thus there are no nonidentity endomorphisms. Since \(|J|\le V\), \(h\le2L-V\le2L-1\); the lower bound is immediate. Strictly increasing integer height gives the chain bound.

To reach the completed corolla one must contract all \(V(t)-1\) internal edges; it is the unique edge set with a one-vertex quotient. Its completed target ideal contains every image of \(J\), so it gives the unique arrow. This proves terminality. For sharpness put an \(n\)-corolla at the bottom of a chain of \(L-1\) unary vertices. Execute its \(L\) vertices from bottom to top, one at a time, and then contract the \(L-1\) edges one at a time in completed states. All these arrows have height increase one, giving \(2L-1\) arrows. At \(n=0\) the bottom vertex is genuinely nullary, so the same chain proves that case too.

The normalized nerve contraction obtained by appending the unique terminal arrow is exactly C.44.1's full contraction, retaining parallel arrows and their compositions. Thus the finite projective resolution proof of C.31.2 applies to this category with its new height bound. ∎

C.47.2. The actual typed enhanced diagram

The frontier of \((t,J)\) is the ordered list obtained by stopping at each executed operation output and otherwise descending to external inputs; unexecuted nullary vertices contribute no input. C.44.3 proves its arity \[ m_J=n+\sum_{v\in J}(1-r(v)),\qquad 0\le m_J\le n+L. \tag{C.47.5} \] Its generator category is the finite additive envelope of the actual rational IC input category \(\mathcal G_{\mathbf Q}^{\otimes m_J}\), and its perfect enhancement when needed. The zero-frontier category is the coefficient category. Executing a nullary vertex selects the actual \(IC_0\) object in the arity-one output; its full endomorphisms are retained.

Theorem C.47.2.1. For the joint arrow \(f=(K,J'):(t,J)\to(t/K,J')\), put \(I_f=\pi_K^{-1}(J')\). The actual partial forest \(F^t_{I_f,J}\), followed by its canonical frontier relabelling, gives a functor from the source frontier category to the target frontier category. The rational finite-frame tensor, proper and unit maps give its coherent enhanced identity and composition comparisons, including all higher cells. They retain the selected original contraction labels. The complete comparison of C.29 carries this finite native diagram after extension to \(E\).

Proof. First the frontier at a cluster-saturated ideal \(I\) has a canonical ordered bijection with the frontier at \(\pi_K(I)\) in the quotient. A completed maximal cluster output is represented by the original top vertex of that cluster. All vertices below a completed cluster are also completed, by the ideal condition. A cluster not completed has no vertices in \(I\), so one descends to exactly the same surviving boundary inputs and their same order. External input labels are unchanged by contraction. This constructs the bijection directly, including nullary clusters. Numerically a cluster has boundary arity \(r_{\rm cl}\) satisfying \[ 1-r_{\rm cl}=\sum_{v\in\mathrm{cluster}}(1-r(v)), \tag{C.47.6} \] since its internal edges number one less than its vertices. Summing over completed clusters gives \(m_I=m_{\pi_K(I)}\). Thus the relabelling is between categories with the same number of factors; it deletes no arbitrary factor.

The arrow condition gives \(J\subseteq I_f\), so the partial forest of C.44.3 is defined on the source's actual arbitrary frontier factors. Those already completed at \(J\) are its variables. Every newly executed vertex acts by its ordered convolution, by the identity in arity one, or by the actual unit functor in arity zero. The canonical frontier bijection identifies its output with the target's frontier, proving the type assertion.

For composable arrows \(f=(K,J')\) and \(g=(K',J'')\), let \(I=\pi_K^{-1}(J')\) and \(P=(\pi_{K'}\pi_K)^{-1}(J'')\). These are nested ideals of the original tree with \(J\subseteq I\subseteq P\); both \(I,P\) are saturated under \(K\). The second arrow's quotient partial forest has a canonical native comparison with \(F^t_{P,I}\). Indeed each \(K\)-cluster is either already a completed input variable at \(I\), or has no executed vertex there. If newly completed at \(P\), its whole original operation tree is executed. Comparing that complete operation tree with its collapsed corolla is exactly C.44.3's native unit/associativity contraction on this fixed input profile. The completed-variable case is the identity. The comparison therefore works on arbitrary frontier inputs, not only on inputs that came from an earlier convolution.

Literal substitution of the two original partial forests gives the same typed forest, with the original enhanced comparison \(F^t_{P,I}F^t_{I,J}\simeq F^t_{P,J}\), as proved by the typed forest calculation in C.44.3. The latter is the functor of the composite contraction and final ideal. This proves the composition comparison. Empty contraction and unchanged state have the identity forest, so give the identity comparison.

For any longer string of joint arrows, pull all its intermediate ideals back to the first tree. They are nested and each required contraction is saturated at the profiles where it is used. Both ways of grouping its comparisons execute the same partial forests and contract the same selected clusters. The expanded finite chain proof of C.44.3 retains the original proper composition, tensor interchange and identity-unit higher diagrams on these forests. Its actual higher cells thus supply the entire longer-string comparison, with the same ordered edge and state labels. This invokes that proved full native diagram; it does not use an objectwise negative-Hom vanishing assertion or identify parallel arrows.

Coefficient extension commutes with those same enhanced finite-frame tensor, proper and unit maps by C.33.1. The full strong comparison of C.29.3 carries their ordered composites and all their higher unit/associativity cells. It therefore carries the entire finite joint native diagram. This is the actual enhanced diagram comparison, not yet a simultaneous point in a chosen common-core polynomial coordinate group.

Finally a finite selected generator pool can be closed under the actual forward images at this stage. Process its finitely many objects by increasing height, adding the finite IC summands of each outgoing forest image to its target pool. Every edge goes strictly forward, so this finite process terminates. These functors are perverse exact and send each finite selected IC tuple to a finite additive IC sum by the earlier Satake heart results. Their represented cross mapping cohomology is therefore nonnegative, even and degreewise finite by C.33.1. This supplies the bounded finite-corner data for the native diagram without demanding an infinite tensor-closed pool. ∎

C.47.3. The exact compatible grafting domain

Take an outer tree \(t_0\) with \(m\) external leaves and cap \(L_0\), and inner trees \(t_i\) of arity \(n_i\) and cap \(L_i\), one at each outer leaf. Keep all their operation vertices and graft seams as in C.44.2. For ideals \(J_0,J_i\), form the disjoint union of their embedded operation sets in the grafted tree. Call the tuple compatible when this union is an ideal. Equivalently, every inner tree attached below an executed outer vertex has been completed in its entirety; other inner ideals can be arbitrary.

Theorem C.47.3.1. The full subcategory of compatible objects in the product of the joint categories admits the actual grafting functor into \(\mathcal E_{\sum_i n_i,\sum_{i=0}^mL_i}\). It retains every contraction-set label and is noncollapsing on arrows. Its height is the exact sum of the factor heights. Nested grafts associate on their common compatibility domain. If the outer ideals are empty at both ends of an arrow, the native functor is exactly the external product of the inner partial-forest functors. General compatible graft comparisons retain the original enhanced unit, tensor and proper maps. All statements include \(m=0,n_i=0\).

Proof. The union is an ideal precisely under the stated condition: an executed outer operation has each attached inner operation among its operation descendants, and the original ideals already include its outer descendants. An executed inner operation has no new operation descendant outside its own tree. This proves both directions, with no condition to add at an empty outer leaf set.

For a factor arrow embed its chosen original contracted edges in the grafted tree. None is a new seam. The old factor edge sets are disjoint, and their union has quotient exactly the graft of the factor quotients, by C.44.2. Its vertex projection restricts to the original factor vertex projections. Each executed source vertex consequently maps into the embedded executed target union, by the factor arrow condition. The compatible target union is an ideal. This proves the joint-arrow condition. Composition is the same disjoint embedded lifted-edge union in both orders. Identities are retained, so this is a functor on that full subcategory.

All operation vertices remain distinct in the object graft. Hence \(V_{\rm graft}=\sum_{i=0}^mV_i\) and \(|J_{\rm graft}|=\sum_{i=0}^m|J_i|\). Using the stated sum of caps, \[ h_{\rm graft} =2\left(\sum_iL_i-\sum_iV_i\right)+\sum_i|J_i| =\sum_i h_i. \tag{C.47.7} \] If a factor contracts an edge, its embedded union is nonempty and strictly reduces grafted vertex count. If no factor contracts an edge but a state increases properly, the disjoint executed union increases properly. Thus no nonidentity factor arrow becomes an identity under grafting. The same disjoint embeddings retain parallel contraction labels.

Nested substitution keeps exactly the same operation vertices, leaf order and executed union in either grouping. Its compatibility condition is exactly that this final union be an ideal of that one grafted tree. Thus the common domain and result agree, proving associativity with no suppressed seams.

For empty outer ideals, the source and target frontiers are the concatenations of their inner frontiers. In the saturation preimage for a grafted arrow no outer vertex is executed: the factor contraction clusters do not cross a seam. Its partial forest therefore consists exactly of the disjoint inner partial forests, in their original order. This proves the external-product assertion on its actual variable factor categories. An inner nullary functor can create the actual unit in its own ordered position; the empty product is the coefficient category. Neither case discards a unit endomorphism complex.

For general compatible ideals the partial forest is literal substitution of these inner forests and the newly executed outer forests. C.44.3's expanded chain maps compare their two groupings by the actual tensor, proper and unit maps. The identical operation vertices and selected contractions retain every higher diagram, just as in C.47.2. This proves the native graft comparison on the stated exact domain. At \(m=0\) there are no inner factors and grafting is the outer identity. Zero inner external arities keep all their nullary vertices and satisfy the same ideal criterion. ∎

C.47.4. Solved exercises

Exercise C.47.4.1 (intermediate). For \(L=3,n=0\), put a nullary unit under two unary vertices. Give a chain of five nonidentity joint arrows and compute every height and frontier arity. Explain why no longer chain exists, and why nullary inputs cannot be omitted from this example.

Solution. Let the operation vertices from bottom to top be \(u,i_1,i_2\). Start with no executed vertex, execute them in that order, and then contract the two unary edges one at a time, keeping every remaining vertex executed. The vertex counts, executed counts, heights and frontier arities are \[ \begin{array}{c|rrrrrr} \text{stage}&0&1&2&3&4&5\\ V&3&3&3&3&2&1\\ |J|&0&1&2&3&2&1\\ h=2(3-V)+|J|&0&1&2&3&4&5\\ m&0&1&1&1&1&1. \end{array} \tag{C.47.EX1} \] Every arrow raises height by one. Theorem C.47.1.1 bounds it by \(2L-1=5\), proving maximality. The first operation is the actual unit functor from the coefficient category to the arity-one IC category. Its output has the full mapping complex of \(IC_0\). Treating the bottom nullary operation as an external input would change the initial frontier from zero to one and would describe a different diagram.

Exercise C.47.4.2 (advanced). With cap \(L=3\), take \(t=\mu(u_\ell,u_r)\) and the state in which just \(u_\ell\) is executed. Compare the smallest allowed target states after contracting the left unit edge and after contracting the right unit edge. Compute the height jumps and the actual functors on the old one-factor frontier. Also decide whether an executed binary outer vertex may be grafted to two inner unit trees when only the left one is completed.

Solution. The old state has \(V=3,|J|=1,h=1,m=1\); its factor is an arbitrary variable \(X\), not a fixed unit input. Contracting the left edge puts the already executed left unit in the root cluster. The quotient root must consequently be executed. Its descendant right unit must then be executed too. Thus the smallest target is the complete two-vertex quotient, with \(V'=2,|J'|=2,h'=4,m'=1\). The saturation \(I\) is all three original vertices. Its native functor is \(F_2(X,IC_0)\), with its original right-unit comparison to \(X\). Here \(k=1,k_{\rm ex}=1,|I|-|J|=2\), so the exact height jump is \(1+0+2=3\).

Contracting the right edge instead leaves the executed left unit as the quotient's bottom vertex. The smallest target ideal consists of just that vertex; its root cluster is unexecuted. Thus \(V'=2,|J'|=1,h'=3,m'=1\), with jump two. Its saturation is the original \(J\); its partial forest is the identity on \(X\). Here \(k=1,k_{\rm ex}=0,|I|-|J|=0\), giving \(1+1+0=2\). The two contractions have the same quotient shape but different forced states and functors.

For the graft, the executed outer root has both inner unit vertices as operation descendants. Leaving the right one unexecuted violates the ideal condition, so that tuple is outside the compatibility domain of Theorem C.47.3.1. Completing both inner units makes it compatible. Keeping the outer ideal empty allows arbitrary inner ideals and gives the exact ordered external product sector proved there.

Theorem C.47.1.1 proves the joint category, terminal corolla and sharp height bound. Theorem C.47.2.1 gives its actual enhanced partial-forest diagram on arbitrary frontier inputs. Theorem C.47.3.1 proves grafting on its exact compatible ideal domain. Exercises C.47.4.1–C.47.4.2 compute the nullary sharp chain and the two different unit contractions shown here. The native maps and input profiles were proved in C.44.1.1–C.44.3.1. Editable SVG source.

C.48. Calibrated native cells in fixed state models

C.48.1. Fix the rational cohomological target

Let \(\mathcal G_{\mathbf Q}\) be the actual rational IC generator category, with its finite additive envelope. Define \(H_{\mathbf Q}\) to have those generator labels, mapping spaces \[ H_{\mathbf Q}(P,Q) =\bigoplus_a H^a\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal G_{\mathbf Q}}(P,Q) \tag{C.48.1} \] with their original cohomological grading, zero differential and the actual Yoneda composition. Units are the original scalar identities. In positive degree this is a genuinely rational graded space; no basis of an extension-field vector space has been descended.

For every selected finite convolution tuple choose its actual finite semisimple IC decomposition over \(\mathbf Q\), including the degree-zero isomorphism and its inverse. Such a decomposition exists by the proved rational Satake heart. Carry those choices into every larger selected corner. The actual convolution maps on mapping cohomology then define graded dg functors \[ F_r^H:H_{\mathbf Q}^{\otimes r}\longrightarrow \operatorname{Add}(H_{\mathbf Q}),\qquad r\ge0. \tag{C.48.2} \] They use the fixed decompositions on objects and conjugate the original mapping-cohomology action by those exact object isomorphisms. At arity zero the object is \(IC_0\), with its full mapping spaces. The zero-input source is the coefficient field. At arity one the chosen model can be the identity. For arbitrary outputs retain finite additive matrices rather than treating an IC sum as a new simple object.

Theorem C.48.1.1. The rational graded category \(H_{\mathbf Q}\), with these ordered tensor operations, their actual cohomological associators and unit maps, is a graded monoidal dg category. The full enhanced comparison of C.29 has a representative with target \(\operatorname{Perf}(H_{\mathbf Q}\otimes E)\), whose first map on every generator mapping cohomology is the identity. It carries the entire finite native enhanced diagram of C.47, rather than just its edge functors. Its induced minimal core comparison \[ g:B\mathcal M_E\longrightarrow B(H_{\mathbf Q}\otimes E) \tag{C.48.3} \] is an actual chain coalgebra isomorphism with identity primitive component. Thus the induced pure state maps can be taken to be the literal powers \((\Omega g)^{\otimes m}\), including \(m=0\), and the canonical common input squares of C.43 and C.46 strictly commute.

Proof. Yoneda composition in mapping cohomology is associative and unital because the original enhanced composition is associative with its coherent homotopies: applying cohomology to the given homotopies gives the two required equalities. Tensor Künneth over the field identifies the cohomology of a tensor of generator mapping complexes with the tensor of their cohomologies; the split contraction proof is C.33.1. Therefore the cohomology action of each actual multilinear convolution is the displayed graded dg functor, with its graded tensor interchange signs.

The actual native associators and unit comparisons give degree-zero closed components between the chosen output objects. Their enhanced naturality gives strict graded naturality on the mapping cohomology. The pentagon and triangle are equalities on this graded category, because their original specified enhanced homotopies become equalities after passing to cohomology. Conjugating by the fixed decomposition isomorphisms retains these equalities: every intermediate isomorphism is followed by its inverse. This proves the graded monoidal dg assertion. We are constructing this graded target; we have not asserted that the original rational enhanced category is formal, or that its arbitrary natural transformation spaces have no higher homotopy.

Let \(\Phi\) be the actual full comparison of C.29.3, restricted first to IC generators and their finite additive sums. Its spectral target generator category \(S_E\) has mappings \(\operatorname{Hom}_{A,H}(A\otimes V_\lambda,A\otimes V_\mu)\), with zero differential, for \(A=\operatorname{Sym}_E(\mathfrak h[-2])\). These are the actual graded mapping spaces identified in C.21–C.22. The induced graded functor \[ L:H_{\mathbf Q}\otimes E\longrightarrow S_E \tag{C.48.4} \] is an isomorphism on mappings and identifies the chosen object labels with their corresponding spectral generators and sums. Its tensor and unit comparisons are the cohomological components of the full \(\Phi\). By the first part of the proof they are graded natural isomorphisms satisfying the strict graded pentagon and triangle. They thus make \(L\) a genuine strong monoidal dg equivalence between these zero-differential generator categories.

Relabel \(S_E\)'s selected objects by these generator labels and sums. Define \(J\) on each mapping by the inverse of \(L\)'s mapping isomorphism. It preserves composition and identities exactly because \(L\) does. For its tensor comparison take the unique preimage under the same mapping isomorphism of the inverse tensor comparison of \(L\), with the appropriate relabelled source and target. Applying the faithful \(L\) to each naturality, associativity and unit equation for \(J\) gives the already proved inverse equation for \(L\); it therefore holds before applying \(L\). This constructs the entire strong monoidal dg inverse. Both \(JL\) and \(LJ\) have their specified coherent monoidal identity comparisons. Extending through finite cones and coherent retracts gives their perfect-envelope inverses by the complete enhanced-envelope argument of A.4.

Now \(J\Phi\) is a full enhanced strong monoidal comparison into the specified rational-cohomology target extended to \(E\). Its first mapping cohomology map is \(L^{-1}L=1\). It carries every selected native operation, unit, regrouping and all the given higher cells, because it is a composite of the actual full enhanced comparison and a genuine monoidal dg functor. This is how the entire C.47 diagram is retained. No separate choice of the comparison for each edge is made. Although \(J\) is defined over \(E\), the target category and its displayed tensor operations were fixed over \(\mathbf Q\) at the start; we do not claim that \(J\)'s individual coefficients descend.

Use the fixed minimal model \(\mathcal M_E\) of the rational generator category and the zero-differential target \(H_{\mathbf Q}\otimes E\). Transport \(J\Phi\)'s whole generator functor through the actual normalized mapping contractions, exactly as in A.3.1.1 and C.38.1. Its bar map is normalized and has primitive component the identity, by the preceding calibration. It is augmented: a Taylor component on \(r\) reduced ordinary inputs, each of degree at least two, has output degree at least \(2r+1-r=r+1>0\). It cannot have a scalar output. Its consecutive-partition bar formula is a chain coalgebra map. At a fixed word its nonleading terms strictly lower primitive length, so the finite triangular inverse exists. The inverse preserves coproduct and commutes with the differential by the original identities. This is the asserted actual isomorphism \(g\).

Applying \(\Omega\) gives the strict dg isomorphism \(q=\Omega g\) of positive core replacements. Transport the given full comparison along the canonical bar-cobar equivalences, retaining their units, rather than making an unrelated choice of its power at each state. On a tensor-product state its pure map is exactly \(q^{\otimes m}\). C.43.1 proves that the actual canonical unit and shuffle maps commute strictly with this power and the input \(g^{\otimes m}\); C.46.3 proves the corresponding rectified state equations. The zero-fold map is the coefficient identity. Thus this step calibrates the full enhanced extension-field datum and its canonical pure cores. It does not yet identify that datum with a chain coalgebra point in the complete native marked raw presentation. ∎

C.48.2. Simultaneous face-compatible strict cells

Put \(U_m=U^{\otimes m}\), \(Q_m=\Omega B U_m\), and retain the canonical counit \(\epsilon_m:Q_m\to U_m\) of C.46.3. For a finite linearly ordered parameter category \([p]\), put \[ R_{n,[p]}=\Omega B(U_n\otimes k[p]). \tag{C.48.5} \] The relative coefficient category keeps the distinct parameter vertices, even when a native comparison maps two of them to the same output object. An increasing injection of parameter vertices induces the actual full-face embedding on these free cobar categories. Parallel native cells are assigned different cell labels, even when their parameter shape is the same.

Here is the precise parameter data used. For each fixed source and target frontier arity \(n,m\), take the actual finite native family of functors and enhanced comparisons in C.47 with that input and output type. Record a chosen resolved \(p\)-simplex of this family by its normalized full unital components on \(U_n\otimes k[p]\), with values in \(\operatorname{Add}(U_m)\). A mixed input is a string of actual source arrows with a nondecreasing parameter-vertex string. The component assigned to that mixed input is the corresponding component of the given native enhanced cell, transported through the one fixed input and output mapping models as in C.33.2 and C.43.2. It is not an arbitrarily selected map on that string.

To spell out why this is a unital functor, expand the native family on each such mixed string. Its boundary terms apply a source differential, compose two adjacent source arrows, compose the adjacent parameter arrows, or apply one target composition to two consecutive output blocks. These are exactly the terms in the normalized unital functor equation C.43.6. Every term keeps the same ordered source labels and parameter vertices. A parameter face simply restricts the allowed vertex labels, so applying the fixed model transport commutes with that restriction. An ordinary source identity is handled by normalization. A nonidentity parameter arrow is retained as a reduced input even when its output is a scalar identity. Thus C.43.2 gives an actual strict dg functor \[ F_\alpha^\sharp:R_{n,[p]}\longrightarrow \operatorname{Add}(U_m) \tag{C.48.6} \] for the entire supplied cell, strictly compatible with its face functors. This recording uses the complete enhanced cells provided by C.47.2 and C.29.3. It does not infer any new higher cell from individual edge data.

Theorem C.48.2.1. The native \(F_\alpha^\sharp\)'s admit dg lifts \[ \widetilde F_\alpha:R_{n,[p]}\longrightarrow \operatorname{Add}(Q_m),\qquad \epsilon_m\widetilde F_\alpha=F_\alpha^\sharp, \tag{C.48.7} \] with all face restrictions retained exactly. Given compatible previously chosen lifts on a collection of faces, one can retain those same lifts. The construction uses one \(Q_m\) at each state arity, includes zero inputs and scalar outputs, and needs no iterated strictification of its own target. It is compatible along a chosen countable increasing family of finite corners, retaining all earlier assigned generator images.

Proof. The counit \(\epsilon_m\) is surjective and a quasi-isomorphism on mappings by C.46.3. Its mapping kernels have split contractions, as in C.45.1. The source \(R_{n,[p]}\) is a free cobar. Filter its free generator complex by the number of original bar letters. The length-preserving part is the original unary differential. Binary source composition reduces that length, and a proper coproduct splits it into products of generators at smaller individual lengths. These are precisely the nonminimal hypotheses of C.46.2. The parameter arrows have degree zero before suspension; this does not invalidate the original-length induction. The finite parameter height bounds their number on a composable input.

At parameter dimension zero apply C.46.2 to choose the lift. Suppose all proper faces of a cell have already been lifted. Each face is the free subcategory generated by the bar words whose parameter vertices lie in that face. Its generator subcomplex is differential-stable: the unary differential retains the vertices; merging adjacent input arrows can only remove vertices; each proper coproduct piece has vertices from the original string. Thus the union of these face generator subcomplexes is differential-stable too. Their given lifts agree on overlaps by the preceding dimension induction. They therefore prescribe one well-defined lift on the free subcategory generated by their union. There can be products mixing generators from different faces; those products are assigned multiplicatively in this free subcategory, so no extra compatibility is assumed for them.

Apply the relative form of C.46.2 on each remaining generator complex. Its defect vanishes on the prescribed subcomplex and is a closed map out of the quotient generator complex into the contracted mapping kernel. The postcomposition kernel homotopy corrects it while staying zero on that subcomplex. This gives the lift of the whole cell with all prescribed faces unchanged. Induction on cell dimension proves the assertion for the entire finite family. On a countable increasing family, choose the same source generator lifts once as they first occur, include their finitely many target images in later target corners, and extend relatively. Every finite input receives its value at a finite stage.

At \(n=0\) the source still retains its parameter category; at \(m=0\) the counit is the identity of the coefficient category, so there is nothing to lift. A functor creating a unit has \(m=1\), and its target has the full \(IC_0\) mappings. Source scalar identities and any explicitly prescribed constant-cell generator images are kept in the relative subcomplex. There is no assumption that a nonidentity index arrow maps to a reduced target arrow. In particular the scalar outputs discussed in C.43.2 are retained in this free unital dg lift. This proves all the asserted cases. ∎

C.48.3. Retain both endpoint systems in the full prisms

Over \(E\), identify the target positive cores using C.48.1's actual strict isomorphism \(q_m=(\Omega g)^{\otimes m}\). Its canonical state isomorphism is \(\widehat q_m=\Omega B(q_m)\). The counit square \(\epsilon'_m\widehat q_m=q_m\epsilon_m\) is strict by C.46.3. The corresponding parameter-input square is strict under \(\Omega B(q_n\otimes1_{k[p]})\), by the canonical bar construction.

The calibrated enhanced comparison supplies a full comparison prism for every native cell and its faces, with the chosen \(q_n,q_m\) on the pure input and output models. To record a prism one may use the ordered product \([p]\times[1]\). Its chains are its finite standard simplex subdivision. On each such simplex use the actual enhanced comparison components, with their original face restrictions; this is the mixed-input construction of C.48.2 applied to the supplied full comparison. Its two ends are the original two native cell functors, after the displayed strict core identifications. The comparison prism includes its higher components; it is not formed from unrelated one-cross maps.

Theorem C.48.3.1. Given the two rational systems of native cell lifts chosen in C.48.2, their extension-field comparison prisms have lifts to the canonical \(Q_m\) state targets which retain both endpoint systems and every common prism face exactly. Each lifted prism projects under \(\epsilon_m\) to its supplied actual comparison. This realizes the calibrated comparison as one face-compatible family in fixed canonical state models.

Proof. Identify the target model at one prism end with the other by \(\widehat q_m\), and the source by the displayed canonical input map. The strict counit square shows that the prescribed endpoint lifts project to the correct endpoint functors. At dimension zero a prism has its two endpoint subcategories already specified. The mixed-input graph uses the full target mapping space, so its connecting parameter arrow can have the actual unit or other scalar output. Apply the relative lifting proof of C.48.2 to extend the endpoint lifts across that prism.

For higher-dimensional native cells, prescribe the two endpoint cells and the already lifted lower-dimensional comparison faces. They agree on intersections: endpoint intersections were fixed by C.48.2, and the remaining intersections are lower-dimensional prism faces already assigned in this induction. In the standard chain subdivision of \([p]\times[1]\), add its top simplices one at a time. Their overlaps and the already assigned boundary are unions of full faces, hence are differential-stable free generator subcomplexes by the explicit argument in C.48.2. The same relative generator-complex lift extends over each new simplex. Its kernel homotopy is zero on the prescribed overlap. This proves compatibility without changing either endpoint system.

Induction over parameter dimension and the finite simplex subdivision constructs the whole prism family. For countably many selected cells, choose the same nested finite-stage construction as before. No averaging over independently selected cells is used, and every lift still projects exactly to its supplied entire prism. The canonical input squares then pull this family to the literal common cores \(C^{\otimes n}\) and their actual index factors, with the single core coordinate \(g\). This proves the statement. It does not by itself prove that the family is a point satisfying all tensor-product and grafting equations in a chosen finite coordinate group; those marked operations and their full domains are still to be given. ∎

C.48.4. Solved exercises

Exercise C.48.4.1 (intermediate). Take the graded rational algebra \(H=\mathbf Q[x]/(x^3)\), with \(|x|=2\), and \(E=\mathbf Q(\sqrt2)\). A graded comparison to an \(E\)-algebra model acts by \(x\mapsto\sqrt2x\). Calibrate it against the original rational target, check the tensor multiplication map, and identify exactly which data have been defined over \(\mathbf Q\).

Solution. On the ordered basis \(1,x,x^2\), its matrix and inverse are \[ L=\operatorname{diag}(1,\sqrt2,2),\qquad J=\operatorname{diag}(1,1/\sqrt2,1/2). \tag{C.48.EX1} \] If \(\mu:H\otimes H\to H\) is multiplication, then \(L\mu=\mu(L\otimes L)\): on \(x^a\otimes x^b\) with \(a+b<3\), both sides give \((\sqrt2)^{a+b}x^{a+b}\), and for \(a+b\ge3\) both are zero. Thus \(J\mu(L\otimes L)=\mu\) and \(JL=1\). The category of rational graded mappings, its product and unit were fixed over \(\mathbf Q\) before this calibration. The matrices \(J,L\) here have coefficients in \(E\), and their individual entries have not been descended to \(\mathbf Q\). The calibrated first cohomology map is exactly the identity on the already rational target. This is the distinction used in Theorem C.48.1.1.

Exercise C.48.4.2 (advanced). Let a source generator complex have elements \(w_0,u\) in degree two and \(w_1,v\) in degree three, with \(dw_0=w_1\), \(du=w_1+v\), and all other differentials zero. The subcomplex spanned by \(w_0,w_1\) is an already fixed face. The target surjection has these quotient generators and a square-zero kernel \(x,y\) in degrees two and three, with \(dx=y\). Let a provisional lift agree with the quotient generator names except that \(u\) is sent to \(u+x\). Correct it while keeping the fixed face, and explain how this applies to two adjacent simplices in a comparison prism.

Solution. The provisional lift has defect zero on \(w_0,w_1,v\), while on \(u\) it is \[ o(u)=d(u+x)-(w_1+v)=y. \tag{C.48.EX2} \] This defect vanishes on the face, belongs to the kernel and is closed in the Hom complex with the whole source differential. With \(h(y)=x\), subtracting \(h o\) sends \(u\) back to \(u\) and retains the other images. The corrected lift is a chain map and has the same quotient projection. It leaves the whole face unchanged even though the incoming unary differential \(du\) meets that face through \(w_1\).

In \([1]\times[1]\), the two standard maximal simplices are \[ (0,0)<(1,0)<(1,1),\qquad (0,0)<(0,1)<(1,1). \tag{C.48.EX3} \] Their intersection is the full diagonal face \((0,0)<(1,1)\). On either simplex the bar generators belonging to that face form a differential-stable subcomplex, since differentials and adjacent merges cannot add a new parameter vertex. Lift the first simplex with its prescribed boundary. Lift the second relative to its boundary and that same diagonal face. The relative correction is zero on this overlap, just as in the generator calculation, so the two functors agree there exactly. Arbitrary independent lifts on both triangles would not establish that agreement. Neither construction forces additional tensor/grafting equations unless those actual marked operations are also supplied.

Theorem C.48.1.1 proves the calibrated identity leading map and canonical pure state powers. Theorem C.48.2.1 lifts the full supplied native cells, keeping their faces. Theorem C.48.3.1 lifts their entire comparison prisms while retaining both endpoint systems. Exercises C.48.4.1–C.48.4.2 compute the nonrational calibration and the unary correction on a shared face. The input and kernel constructions were proved in C.43.2.1, C.45.2.1 and C.46.2.1–C.46.3.1. Editable SVG source.

C.49. Native indexed prisms and invariant marked domains

C.49.1. Nonnegative mapping-degree windows

Take a finite selected directed path system. Its unindexed pure cores are literal tensor powers of \(C=B\mathcal M\), whose reduced letters have strictly positive suspended degree. Parameter cores are relative bars \(D_I=B(kI)\) of finite directed index categories. A nonidentity parameter letter has suspended degree minus one. Only finitely many strictly directed index steps can occur on a path in this selected system. Distinct parallel index arrows retain their separate labels. Each cross central complex is nonnegative and degreewise finite at the retained finite label corner; in the minimal model it is actual represented mapping cohomology, including its degree-zero maps. The number of cross letters on a path is bounded by its finite directed level range.

For a homogeneous labelled path term \(w\), let \(p(w)\) be its number of parameter-bar letters and \(r(w)\) its number of cross letters. Define \[ P(w)=\sum_{\text{positive core factors }c}|c| +\sum_{\text{central factors }m}|m| =|w|+p(w)+r(w). \tag{C.49.1} \] Here a cross letter is \(sm\) of degree \(|m|-1\). The positive core factor degree is already its bar degree. Thus \(P\) is nonnegative, even though the total cochain degree \(|w|\) need not be. Parameter heights serve only to bound the number \(p\); they are not included in this filtration and need not be renumbered under a face inclusion.

Theorem C.49.1.1. On a selected finite system, the subspace \(P\le D\) is finite-dimensional and preserved by every degree-zero common-core path coalgebra coordinate which retains the endpoint and string labels, is over \(g^{\otimes n}\otimes1_{D_I}\) on each indexed pure core, and has identity bare central leading maps. Such coordinates and their inverses never increase \(P\). Their full differential intertwining equations on \(P\le D-1\) use outputs only through \(P\le D\). Full parameter faces preserve \(P\) exactly, including faces that skip an intermediate vertex.

Proof. The number of positive core letters is at most \(D\), and each central degree is at most \(D\). Their fixed-degree spaces are finite on the finite retained label pools. The cross count has a finite directed bound \(R\). Each of the at most \(R+1\) surrounding core runs has a finite index-height bound, so the total parameter count is bounded, for example by \((R+1)H\) when every selected index height is at most \(H\). There are finitely many index strings and coefficient labels at this stage. Hence only finitely many basis terms satisfy \(P\le D\).

Use the full consecutive-cut reconstruction of C.40.1 for a path coordinate. A term in its output partitions the input cross string into consecutive nonempty blocks. Each block produces one cross central output. Consequently the output cross count \(r'\) is at most the input count \(r\). Outside and intermediate indexed core runs are obtained by cutting the input runs and applying their prescribed pure-core maps. Those maps apply the common \(g\) to the positive factors and the identity to each \(D_I\). They create no parameter letters. A central Taylor operation consumes its entire selected block of surrounding input runs and emits a bare central letter, hence emits no new parameter run. Thus \(p'\le p\) too. These assertions include a cut immediately beside an empty run: its coaugmentation has no parameter letters.

Every such output term has total degree \(|w|\). Therefore \[ P(w')=|w|+p'+r'\le |w|+p+r=P(w). \tag{C.49.2} \] No sign affects this degree equation. A pure core coordinate likewise retains its positive bar degree and exactly retains its parameter letters. This proves preservation of the whole window, with its complete outside coactions.

The finite triangular inverse retains the same prescribed pure cores and bare central leading maps, by C.40.3 and C.42.3. Its central nonleading terms also partition crosses and consume surrounding runs, so the same two count inequalities prove it never increases \(P\). This does not assume invertibility of an arbitrary chain projection from transfer.

The actual path differential has its full core differentials, one-cross module terms and operations merging several crosses. A core \(C\) differential has degree one and no parameter or cross count change. A pure index bar differential composes two adjacent index arrows, reducing \(p\) by one. A module or several-cross Taylor operation consumes its selected parameter inputs, outputs one bare cross, and retains all outside runs. It therefore never increases \(p\) or \(r\). Every output term has total degree \(|w|+1\), giving \[ P(dw\text{ term})\le P(w)+1. \tag{C.49.3} \] Thus applying a coordinate before or after a differential to an input in \(P\le D-1\) uses only the retained top window \(P\le D\). It is unnecessary to impose a truncated top-row differential equation whose output has been discarded.

A full face embedding includes a subset of parameter vertices and sends each nonidentity source arrow to that same nonidentity ambient arrow. It retains its number of bar letters, even when a face skips a vertex: a direct arrow over the skipped vertex is still one indexed bar letter. It leaves the positive factors and central mapping degree unchanged, so preserves \(P\) exactly. Fixed cell representatives restrict to those faces by C.48.2, and their assigned cohomology contractions can be chosen once on their identical central mapping blocks. The module perturbation sums in C.45.2 then restrict to those same faces, since every Taylor term retains its index labels. Thus these are the actual face restrictions on the finite windows. ∎

C.49.2. Exact tensor and grafting equation domains

Theorem C.49.2.1. In the shifted product module of C.41.2, \(P\) is the sum of the factor \(P\)'s. The actual core shuffle, noncollapsing native index graft, face restrictions and coefficient coaugmentation insertions do not increase that sum. A central path operation merging \(r\ge2\) crosses and consuming \(q\) parameter letters has output \(P\) equal to input \(P+2-r-q\), hence never larger than the input. This supplies finite operation domains for these actual maps on the compatible native grafting domains of C.47.3.

Proof. Undo each cross suspension by \(K(Z)=Z[-1]\), take the ordinary tensor of the modules, and restore one total cross suspension, as in C.41.4–C.41.6. The unsuspended central output is the tensor of the unsuspended central factors, with degree their sum. Positive surrounding core degrees add too. Parameter shuffle interleavings retain the total number of parameter letters. It follows directly from the definition that \(P_{\rm product}=\sum P_i\), with no correction depending on the number of tensor factors.

The positive core shuffle preserves total cochain degree, and the index shuffle preserves the number of its suspended index letters. The graft functors of C.47.3 are noncollapsing on their actual compatible full subcategory, so their bar maps retain every nonidentity index letter. Neither map creates a new central degree. Their outputs thus lie in the sum window. A coaugmentation insertion has degree zero and creates no bar letter or cross mapping degree, so it contributes zero to \(P\). Faces were checked in C.49.1.

For a merging path Taylor operation, the total bar degree increases by one, the cross count changes from \(r\) to one, and the selected \(q\) parameter inputs disappear into its bare central output. Its outside core runs retain their counts. Therefore \[ P_{\rm out}-P_{\rm in} =1+(1-r)-q=2-r-q\le0. \tag{C.49.4} \] This applies to the full higher operation, not only to binary represented evaluation. It does not erase the actual Taylor coefficients: they must still be supplied by the native cell/path construction. It proves their finite domain bound when those coefficients are present.

For a product mark impose its equation on every tuple of factor windows \(P_i\le D_i\) with \(\sum_iD_i\le D\), retaining the full tensor domain and the target sum window. Bilinearity and decomposition into homogeneous \(P\)-pieces show that the union of these domain pieces spans every tensor input of sum at most \(D\). For a graft mark, restrict this domain to C.47.3's compatible index tuples before applying the actual noncollapsing bar graft. A differential comparison uses the same domain with sum at most \(D-1\), since its output can raise \(P\) by one. These are complete domains of the stated maps; no incompatible outer/inner unit state is inserted and no output above the retained top window is silently deleted. ∎

C.49.3. The actual finite marked coordinate groups

Theorem C.49.3.1. For a finite selected face/path/product system whose full actual operation maps have been provided, impose common-core coalgebra and bicomodule equations, fixed leading entries, all face restrictions and covariance of its provided product/graft maps on the domains of C.49.1–C.49.2. These equations define a reduced closed subgroup of the finite unipotent coordinate group. Composition, inverse and smaller full-window restrictions are the actual coordinate operations. Given two sets of full differentials and actual marked maps on those frames, their nonempty simultaneous intertwining scheme is a torsor under the target stabilizer. Nonemptiness is an additional assertion to be proved using the whole calibrated native comparison, not an assumption supplied by this proposition.

Proof. Order each finite cofree-path basis by total primitive length, retaining the endpoint, string, parameter and mapping labels. C.40.3's iterated-cut injection proves that a coordinate with identity primitive and bare cross leading maps is unitriangular. C.49.1 proves its action and its finite inverse stay inside \(P\le D\). On every pure state the prescribed coordinate is the true tensor power \(g^{\otimes n}\), and on a parameter factor it is the identity. These restrictions are preserved by composition and inverse, since \(h^{\otimes n}g^{\otimes n}=(hg)^{\otimes n}\).

The coalgebra equations, prescribed leading entries and face restrictions are finite polynomial matrix equations. Each provided degree-zero operation map has its complete finite domain from C.49.2, so its covariance equation is a finite polynomial as well. Applying first one coordinate and then another preserves that domain and their tensor sum window by C.49.1. Substitution therefore proves covariance for their product. Substitution by their inverses, which preserve the same domains, proves it for the inverse. The face equations have the same substitution argument. The equations thus cut out a closed subgroup of the finite unitriangular matrix group; taking its reduced structure over characteristic zero is the convention used in C.30.3. This proves the group assertion without defining a product by maps that would insert an extra transferred \(IP\).

For differential equations use only inputs through \(D-1\), with outputs through \(D\), as proved in C.49.1. A quotient of two simultaneous solutions retains all coordinate restrictions and commutes with the target differentials and target marks on exactly those full domains, by substitution with their finite inverses. Conversely the target stabilizer sends a solution to a solution on those same domains. With a chosen solution these two constructions are inverse morphisms of the reduced affine schemes; their formulas are matrix product and finite unitriangular inverse. This is the torsor assertion.

Smaller windows are preserved by C.49.1; smaller full endpoint/string corners use only the original cuts and intermediate labels. A smaller full face family uses the identical parameter letters and central mapping blocks, as checked there. The operations themselves restrict with their whole domains by C.49.2. Hence composition, inverse and the defining equations all restrict to the actual smaller system. The conclusion remains conditional on the supplied entire native operation presentation and its simultaneous point; no family of independent edge comparisons is substituted for either of them. ∎

C.49.4. Actual face-compatible comparison coordinates

Write \(C=B\mathcal M\), \(A_m=C^{\otimes m}\), \(U_m=(\Omega C)^{\otimes m}\), \(Q_m=\Omega B U_m\). The actual native cell representatives of C.48 are \[ \widetilde F_\alpha:R_{n,I}\longrightarrow \operatorname{Add}(Q_m),\qquad R_{n,I}=\Omega B(U_n\otimes kI), \tag{C.49.5} \] with the finite directed parameter category \(I\) retained. For a simplex one may take \(I=[p]\); the full prism uses its standard subdivided \([p]\times[1]\) parameter. Its cell and face labels are never erased.

The canonical target and input coalgebra maps are \[ \ell_m=\eta_{B U_m}\psi_m:A_m\longrightarrow BQ_m, \qquad a_{n,I}=\eta_{B(U_n\otimes kI)}\psi_{n,I}: A_n\otimes D_I\longrightarrow BR_{n,I}. \tag{C.49.6} \] These are exactly the maps of C.43.1 and C.46.3; both strictly commute with the indicated tensor powers of one core map. For a represented cell graph put \[ M_\alpha(y,x,i)= \operatorname{Hom}_{Q_m}(\widetilde F_{\alpha,i}x,y), \qquad Z_\alpha=A_m\otimes sM_\alpha\otimes(A_n\otimes D_I), \tag{C.49.7} \] with its full pulled-back graph differential, not merely its central cohomology. The full graph construction is C.43.2, with target \(Q_m\). The target is augmented and positive, as required there. The maps \(a,\ell\) retain the genuine scalar outputs of the cell functor in its right module actions. A parameter face is a genuine embedding of these cofree modules.

For a fixed target object and source parameter vertex, the central complex \(M_\alpha\) depends only on the actual vertex functor and its fixed object image. It is the identical central complex wherever that vertex appears as a face of a larger cell. Its mappings are nonnegative and degreewise finite at a finite corner, since \(Q_m\) is a positive core and its images are finite perverse IC sums. Its cohomology is the original nonnegative even represented IC mapping cohomology, by C.33.1 and graph recovery. Choose its coefficient-linear central contraction once on each such actual block, retaining it at every occurrence.

The full supplied inverse prism gives the following canonical comparison.

Let the calibrated core map over \(E\) be \(g:C_E\to C'_E\), as in C.48.1. Its target state map is \(\widehat q_m=\Omega B((\Omega g)^{\otimes m})\); its parameter input map is \(\Omega B((\Omega g)^{\otimes n}\otimes1_{kI})\). The full comparison prism of C.48.3 gives the enhanced comparison of the native functor families along precisely these maps. Use its supplied coherent inverse, with direction \[ \beta_\alpha: \widetilde F'_\alpha\,\Omega B((\Omega g)^{\otimes n}\otimes1) \ \Longrightarrow\ \widehat q_m\,\widetilde F_\alpha. \tag{C.49.8} \] The inverse exists as part of C.29's actual enhanced equivalence and its coherent inverse, transported and lifted as in C.48. It is not obtained by formally reversing the interval coalgebra of C.36.

Theorem C.49.4.1. There are actual chain bicomodule comparison maps \[ T_\alpha^{\rm raw}:Z_{\alpha,E}\longrightarrow Z'_{\alpha,E} \tag{C.49.9} \] over \(g^{\otimes m}\) on the left and \(g^{\otimes n}\otimes1_{D_I}\) on the right, simultaneously compatible with all parameter faces. Transfer the full modules using the fixed central contractions and C.45.2's consumed-letter perturbation. Their minimal-central comparisons \(T_\alpha=P'_\alpha T_\alpha^{\rm raw}I_\alpha\) are actual bicomodule isomorphisms with identity bare central component. Together with the single \(g\), they give an actual extension-field point of every finite face/module/differential coordinate system of this family.

Proof. On a bare represented mapping \(m:\widetilde F_{\alpha,i}x\to y\), the map is the actual composition \[ m\longmapsto \widehat q_m(m)\,\beta_{\alpha,x,i}. \tag{C.49.10} \] This has the required type \(\widetilde F'_{\alpha,i}(q_nx)\to\widehat q_m y\). For the higher input Taylor maps use the complete source-bar components of the given natural transformation \(\beta_\alpha\), followed by that same represented target composition. More explicitly, in the ordinary unsuspended cofree module the central Taylor map on a source bar word is obtained by applying that component of \(\beta\) and composing it after the transformed represented arrow. Expand any functor component on the source word into its consecutive nonempty blocks. Apply the target composition to those outputs, the transformation component and the represented arrow. These are the consecutive-partition evaluation formulas of C.33.2, with their tensor signs fixed by moving the homogeneous component maps past their preceding suspended inputs. The strict state functor \(\widehat q_m\) handles the target core action. Restore the one cross suspension by the exact identification C.41.6.

Reconstruct the entire bicomodule map from this central Taylor map by C.39.5's outside coactions, using \(g^{\otimes m}\) and \(g^{\otimes n}\otimes1\) in the two outside slots. The strict natural squares of \(\ell_m,a_{n,I}\) show that these are exactly its input and output core maps, without choosing a naturality property for a contraction inclusion. Coassociativity gives both coaction equations.

The chain equation can be checked at its central Taylor projection. The terms applying a source differential or source composition, or splitting a source word into consecutive functor/transformation blocks, are the normalized natural-transformation equation of the supplied whole prism. Its remaining target-composition terms cancel with the represented left and right module actions. A target unary term is the differential of the displayed composed represented map; its Leibniz signs are exactly the two adjacent unary terms. These exhaust the central terms. Thus that projection is zero. The two coaction equations reconstruct every other term, giving the full chain equation. This is the natural-transformation part of the complete graph proof C.33.2, used on the actual supplied \(\beta\) rather than on separately invented homotopies.

The native comparison prisms and their inverse families agree on all faces by C.48.3, and the evaluation formulas use only their original ordered labels and the two canonical core maps. Their restrictions therefore give the identical \(T^{\rm raw}\) on every face. This proves the simultaneous raw assertion.

Now extend each previously fixed central contraction to the two cofree cores and perform the full module perturbation of C.41.2 and C.45.2. Its correction terms consume a nonempty surrounding core word, so all sums are finite wordwise even with the finite negative-degree index bars. On a full face the central contraction is the same chosen contraction, and the actual module action is the restriction of the larger cell's action. Every term of the perturbation therefore restricts to that same face term. The full inclusions \(I_\alpha\), projections \(P_\alpha\) and transferred module differentials are consequently face-compatible. Their composite \(P'_\alpha T^{\rm raw}_\alpha I_\alpha\) is a chain bicomodule map with the stated core maps.

Its bare central component is the cohomology map of the displayed represented composition. C.48.1 calibrates the full strong comparison against its actual rational cohomological tensor diagram. Hence this cohomology map, including its object/tensor comparison, is the identity in the fixed represented cohomology frames. This uses that calibrated whole diagram, not just an isomorphism of dimensions. Thus the bare central component of \(T_\alpha\) is exactly the identity.

Factor out its specified invertible core maps. Every nonleading central component consumes at least one surrounding original bar letter. The difference from the identity consequently lowers surrounding word length; the finite recursive inverse of C.41.2 exists on every word. It preserves both coactions, the chain equation and all face restrictions by the original identities. No transferred projection is declared to be an inverse. This proves the actual isomorphism assertion.

Finally use the nonnegative \(P\)-windows in C.49.1–C.49.3. Every coordinate and its inverse preserves these windows. The full chain equation is imposed on inputs through \(D-1\), retaining outputs through \(D\); faces preserve \(P\) exactly. All these equations hold for the actual just-constructed maps before truncation, so their finite restrictions are simultaneous extension-field points. This proves the claimed nonemptiness for the face/module/differential system. The additional whole nested-path, tensor and grafting marks have not been imposed in this proposition, and its point must not be substituted for their simultaneous marked point. ∎

C.49.5. Keep the parameter tag in the target

Let \(I\) be a finite directed parameter category, with no nonidentity endomorphisms and finitely many arrows. Its relative coefficient category has the distinct object identities. A native resolved cell has a normalized unital enhanced functor family with fixed input type \(U_n\), output type \(U_m\), and parameter \(I\), as recorded in C.48. Its full mixed-input components define a normalized unital \(A_\infty\) functor \(F:U_n\otimes kI\to\operatorname{Add}(U_m)\).

Retain the parameter vertex in each output object. On a mixed composable word with parameter arrows \(a_1:i_0\to i_1,\ldots,a_r:i_{r-1}\to i_r\), tag its component by their actual composite: \[ F_I(\text{mixed word}) =F(\text{mixed word})\otimes(a_r\cdots a_1). \tag{C.49.11} \] For parallel arrows the composite is that of the actual ordered arrows, not a replacement determined only by endpoints. This formula is extended linearly on each specified labelled source-word block.

Theorem C.49.5.1. The tagged components give a normalized unital \(A_\infty\) functor \[ F_I:U_n\otimes kI\longrightarrow \operatorname{Add}(U_m\otimes kI) \tag{C.49.12} \] over the identity on parameter objects and arrows. It preserves the relative augmentation. Consequently its genuine bar map and canonical strict representative are \[ \begin{aligned} B F_I &:B(U_n\otimes kI)\longrightarrow B(U_m\otimes kI),\\ \Omega B F_I &:Q_{n,I}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Add}(Q_{m,I}),\\ Q_{r,I}&=\Omega B(U_r\otimes kI). \end{aligned} \tag{C.49.13} \] They retain the entire cell, its faces and all actual scalar outputs. They compose strictly when the underlying tagged functors are composed, and need no independent lift through a target counit.

Proof. In the full functor equation on a mixed word, every term has the same total ordered parameter composite. Applying a source composition replaces two adjacent arrows by that composite, leaving the total unchanged. Composing two target blocks multiplies their two tags to that same arrow. The parameter category is concentrated in degree zero, so adding a tag introduces no new Koszul sign. The original entire mixed-input functor equation from C.48 thus proves the tagged equation term by term. Ordinary identity normalization and the object-unit maps are retained as well. This proves the normalized unital functor assertion, including every higher component, rather than just a strict functor on its first components.

Consider a reduced input word. If one of its parameter arrows is nonidentity, its total parameter composite is nonidentity: height strictly increases at that step and never decreases thereafter. Its output, even with ordinary component a scalar identity, is therefore in the reduced mapping space of the tagged target. If every parameter arrow is an identity, every reduced ordinary input has degree at least two. On \(r\ge1\) such inputs the functor component has ordinary output degree at least \(2r+1-r=r+1>0\). It cannot have a scalar output. These two cases exhaust the reduced inputs, proving preservation of the relative augmentation. Finite additive multiplicity matrices use the full relative matrix coefficient category of C.38.1 and the same degree argument.

The consecutive-partition bar formula is now a legitimate reduced bar map: every component just proved reduced can be used as a target bar letter. Its coproduct equation follows by cutting a consecutive partition; its chain equation is exactly the tagged full functor equation. Thus \(BF_I\) is an actual chain coalgebra map, with no scalar component thrown away. The cobar formula of C.38.1 sends its free generator \(tc\) to \(t(BF_I(c))\), extended multiplicatively. The chain and coproduct equations prove the two terms of the dg equation, respectively. This gives the displayed canonical strict representative.

Composition of the bar maps is the original full functor composition by the same consecutive-block formula. Applying \(\Omega\) makes that composition strictly equal on free generators and hence on all morphisms. Face inclusions restrict the original parameter-word labels and commute with their actual compositions, so restrict these same formulas. A nonidentity index arrow with ordinary output one is retained as the reduced letter \(1\otimes a\), rather than sent to zero. This is exactly why the tagged target avoids the loss of unit data exhibited in C.42.4 and repaired for a collapsed target in C.43.2. ∎

The phrase “over the identity on parameter arrows” means the tag of each component is the specified input composite. It does not assert that its ordinary target mapping component is one, or that the pure input \(D_I\) maps to a tensor-unit copy of \(D_I\). Actual parameter comparison matrices between different output objects remain present.

C.49.6. The whole nested common-core parameter graph

Fix a finite directed family of native execution steps, and a common finite parameter category \(I\) for a cell or subdivided comparison prism. At each state of frontier arity \(n\), use \(Q_{n,I}\). For each step use the strict tagged representative of C.49.5. Keep every composable string of steps as its own label and use their literal strict composite as its functor. For a string \(\sigma:i\to j\), put \[ M_\sigma(y,x)=\operatorname{Hom}_{Q_{n_j,I}}(F_\sigma x,y). \tag{C.49.14} \] For composable strings \(\sigma:i\to j\), \(\tau:j\to k\), the cross product is \[ M_\tau(z,y)\otimes M_\sigma(y,x)\longrightarrow M_{\tau\sigma}(z,x),\qquad m\otimes v\longmapsto m\,F_\tau(v). \tag{C.49.15} \] All source, intermediate, target and parameter labels are retained.

Theorem C.49.6.1. These data give one actual directed dg graph for the whole nested parameter family. They include all several-cross evaluation products and their dg identities, are strictly compatible with the parameter faces, and retain the original native enhanced functors and their literal composites under the canonical bar-cobar equivalences. Thus a supplied entire native comparison prism gives its entire nested graph, rather than a set of independent one-cross graphs. The canonical common-core pullback has pure cores \(C^{\otimes n}\otimes D_I\), retains the entire graph differential and restricts to the same parameter faces. Its cross central cohomology is nonnegative, even and degreewise finite at finite corners.

Proof. The edge representatives are strict dg functors by C.49.5. The two possible products of three cross mappings are consequently \[ (mF_\tau(v))F_{\tau\sigma}(w) =mF_\tau(vF_\sigma(w)), \tag{C.49.16} \] after inserting the appropriate three consecutive string labels and their strict composite. Both sides are target composition of the same three transformed maps. The equality follows from strict functoriality and target associativity. Inserting an intermediate pure-core arrow is checked by the same equality; pure-core compositions are the original dg ones. These are every possible composable triple. Units act by the represented identities. The dg Leibniz rule is target Leibniz and the strict dg equation for the applied functor. This proves the entire dg graph, with its genuine two-cross and longer products, as in the full proof C.38.1.

The canonical comparison from an augmented unital category to its bar-cobar replacement has the full consecutive-block formula. By its generator formula it commutes with the augmented tagged functor maps. Its finite-height quasi-equivalence and recovery proof is C.42.2 together with C.43.2; all parameter arrows remain directed and their possible bar length is bounded. Thus each edge functor represents the given entire native parameter cell. Naturality and strict composition of the canonical representatives recover each literal nested composite and the displayed represented evaluation product. No separate formality of a string corner has been assumed.

Every parameter face restricts the original tagged functor and its canonical strictification. It therefore restricts each string functor, its represented mapping complex and its evaluation product exactly. Applying this to the full prism rather than merely to its boundary gives one nested dg graph whose two endpoints are the corresponding nested endpoint graphs and whose other faces are their actual comparison faces. This is an actual graph construction over the supplied prism.

For the asserted common-core model take the full relative bar of this actual dg graph. On the pure state core use the actual map \[ f_{n,I}=\eta_{B(U_n\otimes kI)}\psi_{n,I}: C^{\otimes n}\otimes D_I\longrightarrow BQ_{n,I} \tag{C.49.17} \] from C.43.1. Change every pure run simultaneously by C.40.1's explicit consecutive-cut formula. In detail, on a path retain each original central cross letter and apply \(f_{n,I}\) in every intervening core slot before its original central graph operation. Reconstruct the result by splitting the boundary core runs. Its pure differentials are the given common-core differentials. The resulting whole-path coderivation is a coderivation by that same cut formula. The comparison to the original graph bar commutes with differentials at its central projection; coderivation uniqueness proves the full equation. Its square has zero pure part and zero central projection by the original square-zero identity, and is therefore zero too. This is the full proof of C.40.1, valid with the retained central unary differential and finite index cores as in C.43.2. It does not assume the comparison map is injective. Every several-cross evaluation and higher transferred native cell action is retained in this construction.

There are no backward parameter mappings in \(Q_{n,I}\), by its endpoint labels. Its counit is a quasi-isomorphism to \(U_n\otimes kI\) by C.42.2. At a selected pair of parameter objects, its mapping cohomology is therefore the mapping cohomology in \(U_n\) tensored with the finite space of the corresponding actual index arrows. For an actual step image, the ordinary object is a finite perverse IC sum. Consequently every central cross mapping cohomology is nonnegative, even and degreewise finite by C.33.1; finite additive matrices preserve these properties. First transfer each actual cofree one-cross module using its chosen central contraction, and then transfer the several-cross terms by C.43.3. Core input words and cross counts make the respective perturbation sums finite. The resulting whole-path model retains those exact one-cross choices and has the stated central cohomology. Its canonical common-core pullback uses the same consecutive-cut formula and preserves those central spaces.

The tagged target's face mapping complexes are actual subcomplexes, so compatible central contractions need a construction. For a fixed pair of parameter endpoints use the canonical counit on mappings \(\epsilon_{n,I}:Q_{n,I}\to U_n\otimes kI\). We construct a normalized contraction with exactly this projection, compatible with every full parameter face.

Write a cobar word as nonempty blocks of original reduced \(U_n\otimes kI\)-letters, and let \(r\) be their total number. First retain the original unary differential and the differential inserting block cuts, but omit internal binary bar compositions. At \(r\ge2\) the cut contraction of C.46.3 removes the first boundary when it is present, with coefficient \((-1)^{|u_1|}\), merging the first one-letter block with its next block; it is zero when that boundary is absent. At \(r=0,1\) it is zero. Call it \(H_0\). Its cut identity and unary sign cancellation give a normalized contraction onto the scalar and one-letter complex, which is the original mapping complex of \(U_n\otimes kI\). Its inclusion \(I_0\) sends a reduced mapping to its single-letter block.

Now restore the internal binary bar-composition term \(\delta\). It strictly lowers \(r\), while \(H_0\) preserves \(r\). Thus C.35.1's perturbation formulas are finite on each word and give \[ H_\epsilon=H_0(1+\delta H_0)^{-1},\qquad I_\epsilon=I_0. \tag{C.49.18} \] The inclusion is unchanged because \(\delta I_0=0\). Every nonzero output of \(H_0\) contains a block with at least two original letters. The canonical counit kills a word containing such a block, so \(\epsilon_{n,I}H_\epsilon=0\). Also \(\epsilon_{n,I}I_0=1\). Applying the counit to the perturbed homotopy identity shows that its perturbed projection is exactly \(\epsilon_{n,I}\), not an independently selected projection. Therefore \[ dH_\epsilon+H_\epsilon d=1-I_0\epsilon_{n,I},\qquad H_\epsilon^2=H_\epsilon I_0=\epsilon_{n,I}H_\epsilon=0. \tag{C.49.19} \] This proof retains the complete original unary differential and every internal composition. It uses decreasing original length, so also applies to the degree-zero nonidentity index arrows and their negative bar degrees.

The cut homotopy keeps every original parameter vertex and arrow label; internal composition only removes intermediate vertices. Consequently \(H_0,\delta,I_0,\epsilon\) and their displayed finite formulas commute with every full parameter face inclusion. On the target \(U_n\otimes kI\), the mapping block is the original \(U_n\) mapping complex tensored with the finite space of actual index arrows. A full face retains that same arrow space between its retained endpoints. Choose its mapping-cohomology contractions once on these ordinary blocks, with the fixed finite multiplicity matrices, and tensor them with those arrow spaces. Compose them with the counit contraction by C.45.3's explicit normalized SDR composition formula. This gives the required central contractions on the actual tagged mapping complexes, compatible with all faces, although the face complexes themselves can be proper subcomplexes.

The whole one-cross perturbation and the subsequent several-cross transfer now use these actual compatible contractions. Their formulas consume only the original words and retain the parameter, endpoint and string labels. They therefore restrict to the same face maps, proving the common-core family assertion. The cross block of a literal composite at the end of a native flattening cell can also be shared with that same string block in its nested path graph: canonical bar strictification commutes exactly with that composite by C.49.5, and the just-constructed target contractions are the same on its actual common face. No independent minimal model is substituted at their intersection.

Extracting its endpoint coordinate isomorphism with prescribed product projections remains a separate transfer step, not an assertion that its individual edge maps suffice. ∎

C.49.7. Solved exercises

Exercise C.49.7.1 (advanced). Let the positive left core have one degree-one primitive letter \(c\), and let the right index bar have the degree-minus-one arrow \(a:0\to1\). The central letters \(u_i\) have unsuspended degree zero at parameter vertex \(i\). Define a central coordinate correction that consumes one \(c\) and the arrow \(a\), sending their crossed input to \(su_0\). Write its entire cofree extension on \(c^k\otimes su_1\otimes a\), find its inverse, and calculate the total degree and \(P\) before and after its nonleading term.

Solution. With deconcatenation on the left core, the full correction is \[ S(c^k\otimes su_1\otimes a) =c^{k-1}\otimes su_0\otimes1_0\quad(k\ge1), \tag{C.49.EX1} \] and it is zero on inputs with no \(a\), no \(c\), or other index endpoints. Cutting any remaining left prefix gives the same formula on the suffix, proving its left coaction equation. The right coaction of its output is that output tensored with \(1_0\); on its input, the only nonzero corrected term is the part whose whole \(a\) stays in the module. This proves its right coaction equation too. Its output has no index arrow, so \(S^2=0\), and the coordinate \(1+S\) has actual inverse \(1-S\).
