The input's total degree is \(k-2\), from \(k\) positive core letters, one cross suspension and one index suspension. The nonleading output has degree \((k-1)-1=k-2\) too. Its \(P\) changes from \(k\) to \(k-1\). Thus a genuine degree-zero invertible cofree coordinate can strictly lower \(P\); it need not preserve its homogeneous pieces. Both it and its inverse nevertheless preserve each full window \(P\le D\), as required in Theorem C.49.1.1.

Exercise C.49.7.2 (intermediate). In the category \(0<1<2\), let \(a:0\to1,b:1\to2,c:0\to2\), with \(ba=c\). The collapsed ordinary functor sends each arrow to the scalar one. Describe the tagged version and check its two-arrow cobar equation. Explain why its finite negative-degree index words do not spoil the \(P\)-windows.

Solution. The tagged arrow images are \(1\otimes a,1\otimes b,1\otimes c\). Each is a nonidentity arrow between distinct parameter vertices, even though its ordinary component is one. Hence each belongs to the reduced relative target. The actual reduced bar map retains \(sa,sb,sc\) and the two-letter word \(sb|sa\); it is not the map that projects those outputs to zero.

For the generator \(w=t(sb|sa)\), the sign convention C.39.15 gives \[ d w=-t(sc)+t(sb)t(sa). \tag{C.49.EX2} \] Its tagged counit image is \(-1\otimes c+(1\otimes b)(1\otimes a)=0\), exactly the actual relation \(ba=c\). The one-letter generators have degree zero, while \(w\) has degree minus one. An index-bar word \(v\) of length \(p\) has total degree \(-p\), so its \(P=|v|+p\) is zero before adding any cross. These degree-zero \(P\)-terms remain finite because the directed index category allows at most two nonidentity arrows on a string. A full face that skips vertex1 retains the direct arrow \(c\) as one arrow, and therefore retains \(P\) exactly. This is the independent finite index bound used in Theorem C.49.1.1.

Theorems C.49.1.1–C.49.3.1 prove the invariant finite windows, complete operation domains and coordinate-group laws. Theorem C.49.4.1 constructs the actual face-compatible cell coordinates. Theorems C.49.5.1–C.49.6.1 retain the unit tags and construct the whole nested prism graph and common-core pullback. Exercises C.49.7.1–C.49.7.2 compute the strict filtration drop and tagged cobar relation. The canonical inputs and full native prism data were proved in C.43.1.1–C.43.2.1 and C.48.1.1–C.48.3.1. Editable SVG source.

C.50. Whole prism endpoint recovery with exact core powers

C.50.1. Recover every represented action together

Let \(A,B\) be unital dg categories over a field, with \(A\) augmented over its specified split coefficient identities as in the actual directed graph. Let \(M(y,x)\) be an actual \((B,A)\)-bimodule, covariant in \(y\in B\) and contravariant in \(x\in A\). All its higher actions are retained. For each selected \(x\), suppose the left \(B\)-module \(M_x\) is quasi-isomorphic to the represented module \(R_x=B(b_x,-)\). No assumption is made that an arbitrary natural transformation space is contractible. The selected representing objects here have the split nonzero coefficient-identity cycles of C.30.1, as do the actual finite IC sums.

Theorem C.50.1.1. Such data recover a unital enhanced functor \(F:A\to B\), with objects \(F(x)=b_x\), whose represented bimodule is equivalent to the original whole \(M\). The construction uses its entire right action; it does not infer a functor from independently chosen maps on the individual generator arrows.

Proof. Work in the dg category of unital \(A_\infty\) left \(B\)-modules and their normalized bar module maps. The entire right \(A\)-action of \(M\), expanded on consecutive source blocks, is a unital enhanced functor from \(A^{\rm op}\) to that module category. The coefficient of its source word is precisely the right action Taylor map on that word; the bimodule equation is exactly its functor equation. This is the same action/evaluation correspondence proved in C.33.2.

A module quasi-isomorphism can be inverted in this actual dg category. Here are the chain and bar details needed, rather than an assertion about inverses of arbitrary functors. Replace a given central quasi-isomorphism \(r:R\to N\) by the mapping-cylinder factorization \[ R\xrightarrow{i}L=R\oplus\operatorname{Cone}(1_N)[-1] \xrightarrow{p}N, \tag{C.50.1} \] where in degree \(q\) write an element as \((v,a,b)\in R^q\oplus N^{q-1}\oplus N^q\), and set \[ d_L(v,a,b)=(dv,-da-b,db),\quad i(v)=(v,0,0),\quad p(v,a,b)=r(v)+b. \tag{C.50.2} \] These are chain maps and \(p\) is graded-surjective. The retraction \(q(v,a,b)=v\) has contractible kernel: on its last two summands \(h(a,b)=(0,-a)\) gives \(dh+hd=1\) and \(h^2=0\). Both \(i\) and \(p\) are quasi-isomorphisms, so the kernel of the surjection \(p\) is acyclic and has a split contraction by C.30.1's explicit decomposition. The mapping cylinder is formed in the module category with the usual shifted action signs; its two actions and these maps are genuine module actions/maps.

On the cofree bar modules extend a central kernel homotopy by the identity on surrounding cores. Separate off the core and unary differential. Every remaining action term consumes at least one surrounding input letter. The finite-on-each-word perturbation formula of C.45.2 contracts the full cofree kernel, with all actions retained. Its fixed-projection section and homotopy therefore give inverse module maps and their actual module homotopies for the surjective factor \(p\). The explicit cylinder contraction gives them for \(i\). Their composite inverts \(r\). When the original quasi-isomorphism is already a bar module map with higher components, apply the same construction to its cofree mapping cylinder; the leading surjective factor has that same central kernel and all higher terms still consume surrounding letters. The identical perturbation proof then applies. Thus each stipulated module equivalence is an actual homotopy equivalence in this dg module category.

Transport the entire right \(A\)-action along those objectwise module homotopy equivalences. Write \(r_x:R_x\to M_x\), \(s_x:M_x\to R_x\), and retain the module homotopy \(1-r_xs_x=d h_x+h_xd\). For a reduced source word partition it into nonempty consecutive blocks. Apply the original whole right-action component to each block, insert \(h\) between consecutive outputs, and compose with \(r\) on the incoming end and \(s\) on the outgoing end. Sum over these partitions with the suspended tensor evaluation signs. This is the consecutive-word transfer formula of A.3.1.1 and C.35.1 in the dg module category. It has the correct component degree: a term with \(v\) action blocks has their total degree plus \(v-1\) homotopies of degree minus one. At each fixed source word the sum is finite. Commuting the differential through it replaces an internal \(h\) by \(1-rs\). The \(1\) terms cancel the adjacent source-action terms, and the \(rs\) terms are exactly the two target functor-composition blocks. The remaining terms are the original action functor equation. This is the full bar telescope and proves the functor equation into the existing dg category of the represented modules.

On the coefficient identities set the first component to \(1_{R_x}\) and every higher component with an identity input to zero. The source is augmented, so operations on reduced source words never produce a coefficient identity. This assignment changes none of the just-proved reduced-word equations. In a word containing an identity, its adjacent source composition cancels the corresponding target composition with the assigned true identity, and every other term is zero or the shorter-word equation. Thus the result is actually unital even when an initially chosen \(s_xr_x\) was only homotopic to one. The same partition construction gives its action equivalence to the original \(M\)-action. Here normalization at the ordinary object identities is part of the contraction choice. For clarity, the elementary Hom contraction associated with an object retract \(iq=E\) need not annihilate the identity: its inclusion sends \(1_R\) to \(E\), rather than to \(1_L\). Keep its projection fixed. Choose its chain inclusion to send the specified unit to \(1_L\), using the split coefficient-identity summand, and correct its kernel homotopy by \(H^{u}=H(1-I^{u}P)\). On the kernel of \(P\), the old \(H\) already contracts to zero and squares to zero. Hence \(dH^u+H^u d=1-I^uP\), \((H^u)^2=PH^u=H^uI^u=0\), and \(H^u(1_L)=0\). This is the fixed-projection construction proved in C.45.2. Thus the transfer really is normalized at the units. In computing it, full unital output components are retained; no reduced augmentation of the dg category of module maps is assumed. The consecutive formulas can be computed on unreduced words and then normalized, with each fixed input word using finitely many terms, as in C.43.2.

Finally this represented module subcategory recovers \(B\), not a larger category of unrelated transformations. Its mapping complex from \(R_y\) to \(R_x\) is quasi-isomorphic to \(B(b_x,b_y)\) by evaluation at the identity of \(b_y\). Yoneda precomposition is its section. The full normalized bar contraction is insertion of that identity in the incoming represented-module argument, with its graded insertion sign. Its differential pairs all other adjacent bar terms; the two unpaired terms are the original module map and Yoneda applied to its identity evaluation. This is the complete evaluation/contraction proof C.33.2, or equivalently the represented instance of the explicit normalized bar contraction in C.39.3. It retains every source word, not just the bare central map. Taking the opposite module subcategory changes this contravariant represented-module direction into the required forward direction \(x\to y\) in \(B\).

Choose its normalized contraction so that the homotopy vanishes on the Yoneda section. Transfer through it. The transferred binary operation is the original composition in \(B\), because the Yoneda section preserves composition exactly. Every higher transferred tree on pure Yoneda inputs contains a homotopy applied to such a composed section value and vanishes. Thus the recovered target is exactly the given dg \(B\). Composing the transported entire action with this actual Yoneda inverse gives \(F\). Its represented action is the given \(M\) up to the constructed module equivalence. This proves the whole-functor assertion. ∎

C.50.2. The actual whole prism endpoint comparison

Let \(\mathcal H\) be C.49.6's actual entire nested dg graph for a calibrated comparison prism. The ordinary comparison parameter is \(0<1\); other native cell parameters are retained separately. Let \(A,B\) be its complete endpoint graphs. Let \(M(y,x)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal H}(x_0,y_1)\), retaining every string grade and every several-cross action. This is an actual bimodule between those whole endpoint categories.

At each object \(x\) the parameter arrow supplies a closed degree-zero map \(e_x:x_0\to (q x)_1\). In the raw state core it is the canonical one-letter lift of the actual identity-valued parameter arrow, tagged by \(0\to1\); in finite additive images it has the corresponding fixed matrix identity. Composing with it gives \[ B(qx,y)\longrightarrow M(y,x). \tag{C.50.3} \]

Theorem C.50.2.1. These maps are quasi-isomorphisms of left \(B\)-modules. Consequently the complete calibrated native prism recovers an enhanced equivalence of its whole endpoint graphs, with the actual leading graded graph comparison. Every several-cross functor component is included. This statement does not yet assert an exactly prescribed common-core bar coordinate or exact product projection normalization. The objectwise kernel and action-transfer choices can be made compatibly with the actual finite full parameter faces and shared string corners.

Proof. On a fixed string summand the target complex is a represented mapping complex in the final indexed state. The source is its endpoint1 version. Composition with \(e_x\) uses that string's actual strict functor action on the canonical parameter arrow. Under the canonical counits to \(U_n\otimes k[1]\), and the original represented-module equivalences, it is exactly precomposition by the entire string's supplied enhanced comparison. The latter is an equivalence: it is the original full comparison of C.29, calibrated in C.48, and all nested strings use its actual composite. Precomposition by an equivalence is a quasi-isomorphism of mapping complexes. Concretely compose with the supplied coherent inverse; its unit and counit homotopies give the two chain homotopies of the mapping composites to the identity. The canonical counits and graph recovery are quasi-equivalences by C.42.2 and C.49.6, so the raw composition map is a quasi-isomorphism too.

The arrow \(e_x\) is an actual arrow in the whole dg graph. Thus postcomposition by any target graph morphism commutes with its precomposition exactly. This proves the full left-module equation, including all allowed target string summands. Its right source actions are the actual graph products of \(\mathcal H\), with their whole dg and bar identities. C.50.1.1 therefore applies to this actual whole bimodule and recovers a functor from \(A\) to \(B\). Its first cohomology map is the original calibrated graph comparison because the representing map on each summand was just identified with that comparison. This first map is an isomorphism on every endpoint/string block and is essentially surjective on the stipulated generator objects, so graph and perfect-envelope recovery give the enhanced equivalence.

Here is the compatibility argument for the choices, including the case of proper face subcomplexes. The corrected canonical counit contraction in C.49.6 commutes with all full parameter faces. The cylinder kernel for a fixed central comparison map is graded-isomorphic to the direct sum of its source and shifted target: in \(p(v,a,b)=r(v)+b=0\), eliminate \(b\) as \(-r(v)\). Each face keeps exactly the corresponding original word labels in \(v,a\). Thus face kernel intersections are the kernels of the common faces, and their graded subspace sums have the distributive word-support intersection property. All these kernel complexes are acyclic, since the comparison map on every face is the same proved quasi-isomorphism for that face.

The sum of the previously assigned proper-face kernel complexes is acyclic as well. To prove this explicitly, for two subcomplexes use \((K_1+K_2)/K_1=K_2/(K_1\cap K_2)\). A quotient of two acyclic complexes is acyclic: lift a quotient cycle, lift a primitive of its differential in the subcomplex, subtract it, and then lift a primitive of the resulting ambient cycle. Induction, using the word-support distributivity and the acyclicity of all finite intersections, proves the claim for a finite sum. The quotient of the full kernel by this sum is therefore acyclic and split contractible over the field.

Existing compatible normalized kernel contractions agree on intersections and preserve each face, so define one contraction on this sum. Extend it to the full kernel using an actual chain splitting of its contractible quotient. For completeness a graded section \(s\) with defect \(a=ds-sd\) is corrected to the chain section \(s+a h_Q\), where \(h_Q\) contracts the quotient: the Hom differential of \(a h_Q\) is \(-a\). In the resulting direct-sum decomposition extend the old contraction by the quotient contraction. The square-zero side condition and all restrictions then hold on each summand. This constructs compatible central kernel homotopies by induction over the face vertex sets, without calling different tagged face mapping complexes identical.

The cofree module perturbation and the subsequent entire-action transfer consume only the input words and retain their endpoint/string and parameter labels. The compatible central choices therefore give the same full module maps on each face. The Yoneda identity-insertion homotopy has that same restriction property. Thus the recovered whole endpoint functors and their original action equivalences can be chosen face-compatible. A nested corner exhaustion retains the assigned words and extends these same choices rather than reconstructing each finite graph independently.

The recovery never replaced the right \(A\)-action by a set of individual edge maps: that entire action was the source of the higher transferred functor components. In particular the construction includes all several-cross components required by the full endpoint functor equation. Its exact restrictions to a chosen prescribed core coordinate and prescribed product comparison are extra relative requirements, addressed in the next step rather than inferred from its invertible first cohomology map. ∎

C.50.3. Relative replacement by the exact core maps

For a dg category \(B\), define its dg path category as follows. An object is a closed degree-zero homotopy equivalence \(u:b_0\to b_1\). A degree-\(r\) map from \(u\) to \(v:c_0\to c_1\) is a triple \[ \begin{aligned} (a,b,h)\in{}&B(b_0,c_0)^r\\ &\oplus B(b_1,c_1)^r\\ &\oplus B(b_0,c_1)^{r-1}. \end{aligned} \tag{C.50.4} \] Set \[ \begin{aligned} D(a,b,h)={}&(\delta a,\delta b,\\ &-\delta h+va-bu), \end{aligned} \tag{C.50.5} \] For composable maps \((a_1,b_1,h_1)\) of degree \(r\) and \((a_2,b_2,h_2)\) of degree \(s\), set \[ \begin{aligned} &(a_2,b_2,h_2)(a_1,b_1,h_1)\\ &\quad=(a_2a_1,b_2b_1,\\ &\qquad h_2a_1+(-1)^s b_2h_1). \end{aligned} \tag{C.50.6} \] Here \(\delta\) denotes the original mapping differential. Identities are \((1,1,0)\). Both endpoint projections \(\pi_0,\pi_1\) are strict dg functors.

Theorem C.50.3.1. Let \(A\) be the actual augmented whole dg path graph and \(A_i\) its pure state subcategories. Suppose an actual enhanced endpoint comparison \(F:A\to B\) is given, together with its supplied coherent equivalences on \(A_i\) to the desired actual pure core functors \(q_i\). There is an enhanced comparison \(\widehat F:A\to B\) equivalent to \(F\), restricting exactly to every \(q_i\). The construction retains a previously assigned compatible replacement on any full face/path subfamily whose bar generator collection is differential-stable. It therefore applies successively to the native face family and its pure maps \(q_i=\Omega B((\Omega g)^{\otimes n_i}\otimes1_{kI})\). After the actual common-core pullback and module-first graph transfer, the calibrated native comparison consequently gives a face-compatible whole-path chain coalgebra isomorphism over the exact core powers \(g^{\otimes n_i}\otimes1_{D_I}\), with identity bare central maps.

Proof. The path formulas define a dg category. In the square of \(D\), the mixed terms in the third slot are \(-\delta(va-bu)+v\delta a-(\delta b)u=0\), since \(\delta u=\delta v=0\). Its composition is associative: the third slot of either threefold composition is the sum of its last homotopy times the first two maps, its middle homotopy with the sign of the final degree, and its first homotopy with the sign of the two final degrees. The two degrees add in the same order. For Leibniz, expanding the third slot gives \[ \begin{aligned} &(-\delta h_2+wa_2-b_2v)a_1\\ &\quad+(-1)^s h_2\delta a_1\\ &\quad+(-1)^{s+1}(\delta b_2)h_1\\ &\quad+b_2(-\delta h_1+va_1-b_1u), \end{aligned} \tag{C.50.7} \] where \(w\) is the third object's equivalence. These are precisely the third slots of \(D(a_2,b_2,h_2)(a_1,b_1,h_1)+(-1)^s(a_2,b_2,h_2)D(a_1,b_1,h_1)\). The first two slots are ordinary dg composition. This proves every dg identity and both endpoint functor assertions.

For any fixed choices of path objects, \(\pi_0\) is surjective on graded mapping complexes. Its kernel is the shifted cone of \[ B(b_1,c_1)\longrightarrow B(b_0,c_1),\qquad b\longmapsto bu, \tag{C.50.8} \] with the harmless displayed minus sign in the differential. This map is a homotopy equivalence: precomposition by the chosen homotopy inverse of \(u\), and precomposition by its two homotopies, give its inverse and chain homotopies. Its cone is contractible. One may also split that acyclic cone over the field by C.30.1. Thus \(\pi_0\) is a surjective quasi-isomorphism on each fixed mapping complex, with an actual split kernel contraction.

Choose for each source object the supplied closed homotopy equivalence \(u_x:F(x)\to q_i(x)\). It is part of the original enhanced comparison on its state. That entire supplied natural equivalence records a dg functor from \(\Omega B A_i\) into the path category with first projection \(F^\sharp|_{\Omega BA_i}\) and second projection \(q_i^\sharp\). Explicitly its first and second components on a free generator are the two prescribed functor values; its third component is the natural-equivalence component on that source bar word. The third-slot dg equation just displayed is the full natural-transformation equation, including its two endpoint-composition terms. This proves the recording on every word; it is not an inference from the object components alone.

The source \(\Omega BA\) is a free relative cobar. Its generator filtration has the length-preserving unary complex and smaller-length composition/splitting terms required in C.46.2. The prescribed pure-state generator union is differential-stable: its differentials, compositions and coproduct pieces keep their state and parameter labels. Apply that theorem's relative lifting proof to \(\pi_0:\operatorname{Path}(B)\to B\), the strict source functor \(F^\sharp\), the chosen object paths, and the already assigned pure state lift. The acyclic mapping kernels just proved are exactly its needed kernels. It extends to a full dg functor \(H:\Omega BA\to\operatorname{Path}(B)\) without changing those prescribed generator images.

Take the second projection of \(H\) and precompose with the canonical unital comparison \(A\to\Omega BA\). Its restriction to each \(A_i\) is exactly \(q_i\), since C.43.2 proves that this composite recovers all the prescribed normalized unital components, not just their first map. The path functor \(H\) supplies the enhanced equivalence to \(F\). A union of already assigned full faces or string corners is another differential-stable generator collection, by the same original label argument. The relative lifting correction vanishes there. Thus one can keep all earlier choices on overlaps and extend along the finite face family, then along a countable increasing family.

For the native comparison, the coherent pure-state equivalences used here are the actual restrictions of the whole prism recovery and its represented action equivalence. C.48 identifies their desired endpoint state functors with the displayed canonical \(q_i\). The actual canonical common-core maps from C43 strictly commute with them. Pulling the full comparison to the common cores therefore has precisely \(g^{\otimes n_i}\otimes1_{D_I}\) on every state. Its remaining cross components come from the whole \(H\), including all several-cross generator values. This proves exact pure-core replacement without asserting anything about arbitrary natural-transformation spaces.

We give the common-core graph argument explicitly. Write \(Q_A:L_C\to BA\), \(Q_B:L_D\to BB\) for the actual whole graph pullbacks of C.40.1 and corrected C.49.6. Let \(T=B\widehat F\). This bar map is augmented: a crossed input retains its different graph levels and cannot have scalar output; on a pure state its functor is exactly the prescribed augmented \(q_i\). Define \(G:L_C\to L_D\) by its pure maps \(g_i\) and by central cross Taylor map equal to the central projection of \(TQ_A\), and reconstruct it by the full consecutive-cut formula. Strict naturality of the canonical pure input maps gives identical pure maps in \[ Q_B G=TQ_A. \tag{C.50.9} \] Their central projections also agree by construction, so the full cofree path reconstruction proves this equality, including every several-cross component. The chain defect of \(G\) is a coderivation along \(G\). Its image under \(Q_B\) is zero by that equality and the chain equations for \(T,Q_A,Q_B\). The central projection of \(Q_B\) is the identity on each bare cross block. Hence the chain defect has zero central projection; its pure part is zero since all \(g_i\) are chain maps. C.40.1's coderivation uniqueness proves the full chain equation. No injectivity of \(Q_B\) has been assumed.

Use corrected C.49.6's face-compatible central contractions and C.43.3's module-first entire graph transfer on both sides. The transferred map is \(P_D^\infty G I_C^\infty\). It remains a full chain coalgebra map with those exact pure core maps. Its bare central term is the calibrated mapping-cohomology comparison, hence the identity by C.48.1. Its core map has identity primitive term. The iterated-cut argument of C.40.3 therefore makes it unitriangular by total primitive length; its finite recursive inverse preserves coproduct and differential, and C.49.1 retains its finite \(P\)-windows. All pullback and transfer terms keep the existing labels and the compatible face contractions, so the maps and inverses restrict to the same faces and shared corners. This gives the asserted actual whole-path/face/differential extension-field coordinate. Product and grafting covariance have not been inferred from this argument. ∎

C.50.4. Solved exercises

Exercise C.50.4.1 (advanced). Let \(L=ke\oplus kx\oplus ky\), with \(e,x\) in degree zero, \(y\) in degree one, and \(dx=y\). Let \(E\) project onto \(ke\), and let \(h(y)=x\), with \(h(e)=h(x)=0\). On the graded endomorphism complex put \[ P(f)=f_{ee},\qquad H(f)=hf+(-1)^{|f|}Efh. \tag{C.50.EX1} \] Explain why the ordinary Hom contraction is not normalized at the identity, and give a contraction with the same projection and inclusion \(I^u(\lambda)=\lambda1_L\).

Solution. Since \(hE=Eh=0\), one has \(H(1_L)=h\ne0\), whereas the original inclusion of the scalar identity was \(E\). The Hom differential is \(Df=df-(-1)^{|f|}fd\). Its direct telescope gives \(DH+HD=1-I^0P\), with \(I^0(\lambda)=\lambda E\), and \(H^2=PH=0\). On \(\ker P\) this is a normalized contraction to zero. Set \[ H^u(f)=H\bigl(f-P(f)1_L\bigr). \tag{C.50.EX2} \] Then \(PI^u=1\), and the chain projection \(1-I^uP\) has range in \(\ker P\), giving \(DH^u+H^uD=1-I^uP\). Since \(H\) preserves this kernel and squares to zero, \((H^u)^2=PH^u=H^uI^u=0\). In particular \(H^u(1_L)=0\). These are contractions of mapping complexes; the projection \(P\) has not been asserted multiplicative. The higher comparison uses the entire transferred action, as in C.50.1.1.

Exercise C.50.4.2 (intermediate). In the dg path category use a graded target algebra \(k[\theta]/(\theta^2)\), with \(|\theta|=1\) and zero differential, and take all three object paths to be the identity. Let \(x=(1,0,0)\) have degree zero and \(y=(0,\theta,0)\) have degree one. Check the signed Leibniz rule, explain why the factor \((-1)^s\) in the third composition slot is needed, and contract the kernel of the first projection when the object path is the identity.

Solution. The path differential gives \(Dx=(0,0,1)\) and \(Dy=(0,0,-\theta)\), while \(yx=0\). With the sign in C.50.3.1, \[ (Dy)x=(0,0,-\theta),\qquad y(Dx)=(0,0,-\theta), \tag{C.50.EX3} \] so \(D(yx)=(Dy)x-y(Dx)=0\). Omitting \((-1)^s\) would make the second term \((0,0,\theta)\), leaving the nonzero defect \((0,0,-2\theta)\) over the characteristic-zero coefficient field.

An element of the first-projection kernel is \((0,b,h)\), with differential \((0,\delta b,-\delta h-b)\). Define \[ K(0,b,h)=(0,-h,0). \tag{C.50.EX4} \] Then \(DK+KD=(0,b,h)\) and \(K^2=0\), directly retaining the original mapping differential \(\delta\). For a strictly invertible object path \(u\), replace \(-h\) by \(-hu^{-1}\). For a general homotopy equivalence, its actual inverse and two homotopies give an acyclic cone as proved in C.50.3.1. This kernel, rather than an arbitrary transformation space, is what makes the relative exact-core lift possible.

Theorem C.50.1.1 proves recovery from the entire represented action. Theorem C.50.2.1 applies it to the actual whole tagged native prism with compatible faces. Theorem C.50.3.1 proves the graded path-category formulas,relative exact-core replacement and actual whole common-core path coordinate. Exercises C.50.4.1–C.50.4.2 compute the unit correction and essential Koszul sign. The full prism and corrected compatible counit contractions are proved in C.49.6.1;the relative generator and module constructions are C.46.2.1 and C.45.2.1. Editable SVG source.

C.51. Correct product coordinates inside the whole graph

An exact product comparison must retain the whole graph differential, including operations on several successive transitions. This section proves how actual product-square homotopies give such corrections. Work over a characteristic-zero field. The hypotheses concern actual maps and homotopies over the fixed pure core powers; agreement on cohomology alone is weaker. All contractions use the full cofree module differential.

C.51.1. The homotopy after changing contraction choices

All complexes below are full cofree one-cross bicomodules over their stated pure cores. Maps and homotopies satisfy both outside coaction equations. Source-to-target maps are over the same fixed core powers. Thus all their composites have the displayed types; the Hom differential is \(\partial f=d f-(-1)^{|f|}f d\).

Use normalized contraction data \[ (i,p,h):Z\rightleftarrows N,\qquad (i',p',h'):Z'\rightleftarrows N', \] and product contraction data \[ (j,q,k):W\rightleftarrows P,\qquad (j',q',k'):W'\rightleftarrows P'. \] Here \(pi=1\), \(\partial h=1-ip\), and the corresponding identities hold for the other three contractions. Each projection followed by its homotopy, and each homotopy followed by its inclusion, is zero.

Let \(\phi:Z\to W\), \(\phi':Z'\to W'\) be the actual fixed-core product projections, and let \(t:Z\to Z'\), \(u:W\to W'\) be chain comparisons. Suppose the raw square has a specified degree-minus-one homotopy \[ R:Z\longrightarrow W',\qquad \partial R=\phi't-u\phi. \] Set \[ T=p'ti,\quad U=q'uj,\quad J=q\phi i,\quad J'=q'\phi'i'. \] In the application \(J,J'\) are the actual identity-core isomorphisms between two minimal product models: C41 and C45 construct them, and their identity leading central maps make them invertible by the finite cofree word recursion. In a general contraction diagram their invertibility is an additional hypothesis, not a consequence of the symbols above.

Theorem C.51.1.1. If \(J'\) is invertible, the desired block comparison is \(T^{\mathrm{prod}}=(J')^{-1}U J\). There is an explicit full bicomodule homotopy \[ \partial K=T^{\mathrm{prod}}-T, \] given by \[ \begin{aligned} L={}&q'R i-q'\phi'h'ti+q'u k\phi i,\\ K={}&-(J')^{-1}L. \end{aligned} \] The formula preserves any face or sector on which all its stated raw maps, homotopies and contractions have compatible restrictions. In particular it retains the actual raw homotopy \(R\).

Proof. All chain maps in the formula have degree zero. The Hom Leibniz rule therefore gives \[ \begin{aligned} J'T &=q'\phi'i'p'ti\\ &=q'\phi'ti-\partial(q'\phi'h'ti),\\ UJ &=q'ujq\phi i\\ &=q'u\phi i-\partial(q'u k\phi i). \end{aligned} \] Subtract. The difference of the two first terms is \(q'(\phi't-u\phi)i=\partial(q'R i)\). Hence \(J'T-UJ=\partial L\). Since \(J'\) and its inverse are chain maps, \[ \partial K=-(J')^{-1}(J'T-UJ) =(J')^{-1}UJ-T. \] Every summand is a composite of actual bicomodule maps of the indicated degree and over the same pure core maps. It is therefore an actual bicomodule homotopy, including all consumed-core Taylor components. The identities were in the full mapping complexes and did not discard any unary or higher action term.

Restriction commutes with each composite. If \(J'\) restricts to the same isomorphism on a face, its inverse restricts to its inverse there: restrict the two inverse identities and use uniqueness of an inverse. This proves the compatibility assertion. The same wordwise reasoning applies to an increasing compatible family of finite corners. No choice of new primitives on separate faces has been made. \(\square\)

If the block contractions are the C45 product-normalized ones, then \(\phi i=j\), \(q'\phi'h'=0\), \(k\phi i=kj=0\), and \(J=J'=1\). For an exactly commuting raw square, \(R=0\), the displayed formula is zero and \(T=U\) exactly. This recovers the exact C45 square as a special case. With other contraction choices its two homotopy terms must be retained.

C.51.2. Ordered tensor homotopies and the cross suspension

First work in the unsuspended modules \(K(Z_i)=Z_i[-1]\) of C41. For each ordered factor suppose chain maps \(t_i,t_i'\), over the same pure core powers, have a specified bicomodule homotopy \[ \partial a_i=t_i'-t_i. \] The graded tensor convention evaluates a tensor of homogeneous maps with the sign obtained by moving each map past its preceding input factors. In particular a degree-minus-one map in slot \(i\) contributes \((-1)^{\sum_{j<i}|x_j|}\) on homogeneous inputs.

Theorem C.51.2.1. Put \[ \begin{aligned} a_\Pi=\sum_{i=1}^m t'_1\otimes\cdots\otimes t'_{i-1} \otimes a_i\otimes t_{i+1}\otimes\cdots\otimes t_m. \end{aligned} \] Then \[ \partial a_\Pi=\bigotimes_i t_i'-\bigotimes_i t_i. \] This full bicomodule homotopy regroups strictly along every ordered partition. Its homotopy on the once-suspended product module \((\bigotimes_i K(Z_i))[1]\) is the underlying map \(-a_\Pi\), transported by C41's actual graded regrouping. Empty products have the coefficient identity map and zero homotopy; a genuine arity-zero block is retained as its actual factor rather than deleted.

Proof. The Hom tensor differential is a derivation. All the factors except \(a_i\) are closed and have degree zero, so differentiating the \(i\)-th term gives \[ t'_1\otimes\cdots\otimes t'_{i-1} \otimes(t_i'-t_i)\otimes t_{i+1}\otimes\cdots\otimes t_m. \] The negative term at \(i+1\) cancels the positive term at \(i\), with its full graded evaluation sign, since these are the same tensor of degree-zero maps. The two uncancelled end terms are exactly the asserted difference. For one factor it is the original homotopy equation; for no factors the difference and homotopy are both zero.

For two consecutive groups \(A,B\), the formula is \(a_A\otimes t_B+t_A'\otimes a_B\). Expanding the two group homotopies lists once, in the original factor order, the term whose homotopy occurs in each individual slot. The evaluation sign of that slot is the sum of all preceding input degrees in either grouping. Thus this is literally the displayed flat formula. Repeating this argument proves equality for every parenthesization and ordered partition. No new chain homotopy between different regroupings is needed.

Both outside coactions of each factor commute with its maps and homotopy with the same graded convention. Tensoring those equations and applying C41's graded regrouping proves the two product coaction equations. The formula is therefore a bicomodule homotopy for the entire product actions, not just a homotopy of its bare central complexes.

On a cochain shift \([1]\), both differentials are negated. For the underlying degree-minus-one map \(a\), its new Hom differential is \(-da-ad=-\partial a\). Hence the required shifted homotopy is \(-a\), whose new differential is the original difference of the two degree-zero comparison maps. This proves the displayed shift sign and, after the actual C41 one-cross regrouping, the claimed once-suspended formula. Source arity does not enter any calculation. In particular a factor with zero inputs still has its specified target-unit mappings and is present in the same formula. \(\square\)

C.51.3. Extend the correction through every transition

Let \((L,D)\) be a finite directed common-core minimal-central path coalgebra as in C43 and C49. Pure cores are tensor powers of the minimal IC bar \(C\), with the retained finite directed index bars. All unsuspended central mapping spaces are nonnegative and even; their unary differential is zero. The whole differential includes every module and several-cross operation. Count all original primitive core/index letters and cross letters to obtain its conilpotent length filtration.

Let \(G:L_0\to L\) be an actual whole chain coalgebra isomorphism over the fixed core powers, such as the C50 comparison. On each selected one-cross module let \(T_e\) be its restriction. Suppose desired replacements \(T'_e\), over the same cores and with identity bare central component, are given as chain bicomodule isomorphisms, together with actual degree-minus-one bicomodule homotopies \[ dK_e+K_e d=T'_e-T_e. \] All these data retain their endpoint/string labels and agree on every prescribed face or shared sector. On unmodified modules take \(T'_e=T_e,K_e=0\). The hypothesis is a supplied coherent homotopy of these actual module maps; equality of their cohomology dimensions is insufficient.

Theorem C.51.3.1. There is a full chain coalgebra automorphism \(A\) of the target \(L\), fixing all pure cores, such that \(AG\) has exactly the prescribed \(T'_e\) on every one-cross sector. It retains every several-cross operation and comparison component through the full chain equation. The construction is finite on each word, preserves the finite \(P\)-windows of C49, and restricts to all the supplied compatible faces. Thus it corrects the one-cross products inside an already constructed whole graph comparison rather than discarding its higher components.

Proof. Put \[ V_e=T'_eT_e^{-1},\quad N_e=V_e-1,\quad H_e=K_eT_e^{-1}. \] These are over the identity target cores. The map \(V_e\) is a chain isomorphism, and on the module mapping complex \(\partial H_e=N_e\), with \(\partial N_e=0\). Every nonleading central component of \(N_e\) consumes at least one surrounding original bar letter, by the cofree reconstruction in equation (C.39.5). Hence \(N_e\) is locally nilpotent. Define the finite-on-each-word maps \[ \ell_e=\log(1+N_e),\qquad s_e=\sum_{r\ge0}\frac{(-1)^r}{r+1}H_eN_e^r. \] They are bicomodule maps of degrees zero and minus one, respectively. The mapping-complex Leibniz rule gives \(\partial s_e=\sum_{r\ge0}(-1)^rN_e^{r+1}/(r+1)=\ell_e\). This calculation retains the complete module differential, not just its bare central part. The bare component of every degree-minus-one module map is zero: it maps an even central degree to an odd central degree. Therefore \(H_e\), and hence \(s_e\), consume at least one surrounding primitive letter.

Extend these full one-cross maps to a degree-minus-one path coderivation \(h\), zero on pure cores. On a cotensor path it is the graded sum of applying \(s_e\) in each one-cross factor and identities in all the other factors. The bicomodule equations make every summand a map on the cotensor equalizer. At a path cut a homotopy position is either before or after the cut; its two contributions are precisely \[ \Delta h=(h\otimes1+1\otimes h)\Delta. \] For a cut inside a boundary core run this is the same left or right coaction equation. These exhaust all cuts, proving the full coderivation identity with its graded evaluation signs. It is the ordered tensor calculation of Theorem C.43.3.1 with all intervening degree-zero retractions equal to the identity. In particular \(h\) preserves cross count and lowers total primitive length by at least one.

Let \[ v=[D,h]=Dh+hD. \] The commutator of the two displayed coderivation equations proves that \(v\) is a degree-zero coderivation. Also \(Dv-vD=D^2h-hD^2=0\). Its pure-core restriction is zero. On a one-cross sector its restriction is exactly \(d s_e+s_e d=\ell_e\).

The full minimal-central \(D\) lowers primitive length by at least one. On a pure \(C\)-factor this is minimality of the IC bar: no unary operation remains. An index differential merges adjacent index arrows. A one-cross module term with no consumed core input would be the zero central unary differential; all others consume at least one core input. A several-cross term merges at least two crosses. These are every type of term. Thus \(v\) lowers primitive length by at least two and is locally nilpotent. Its actual finite exponential is \[ A=\exp(v)=\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{v^j}{j!},\qquad A^{-1}=\exp(-v). \] For a degree-zero coderivation the operators \(v\otimes1\) and \(1\otimes v\) commute. Its coproduct equation therefore gives \(\Delta A=(A\otimes A)\Delta\) by the finite binomial expansion on every word. The same computation gives its coalgebra inverse. Since \(Dv=vD\), it commutes with \(D\); since \(v\) is zero on pure cores, \(A\) fixes them exactly.

On a one-cross sector, \(A_e=\exp(\ell_e)=V_e\), using the finite formal power-series identities for the nilpotent \(N_e\). Hence \((AG)_e=V_eT_e=T'_e\) exactly. On higher-cross paths the commutator contains all merging terms of \(D\); none was projected away. Its exponential supplies their required higher correction components, and the full chain equation \(DAG=AGD_0\) retains their compatibility.

All operations are on the original endpoint and concatenated-string blocks. If the given homotopies agree on a face, the logarithm, cotensor sum, commutator and exponential restrict to those same formulas there. C.49.1 applies to this actual normalized degree-zero coordinate and its inverse: their pure core maps are the identity and their nonleading terms consume surrounding inputs and merge crosses. They preserve \(P\le D\). Thus the correction uses the complete finite domains already proved, while retaining all supplied face restrictions. This proves the theorem. \(\square\)

C.51.4. Solved examples

Exercise C.51.4.1 (intermediate). Let the dg category on \(0<1<2\) have \(R=k[a]/(a^2)\), \(|a|=2\), in each mapping space, zero ordinary differential, and composition given by multiplication in \(R\). The reduced pure loops are \(a_i\). Write their suspensions as \(\alpha_i=sa_i\), and write \(u_{ji}=s1_{ji}\), \(v_{ji}=sa_{ji}\) on a strict transition \(i<j\). The degrees are \(1,-1,1\), respectively. On its relative graph bar let \(D\) be the full suspended multiplication differential. Define the degree-minus-one coderivation \(h\) by the only nonzero central Taylor values \(h(\alpha_j|u_{ji})=u_{ji}\). Compute \([D,h]\) and its exponential on \(u_{21}|\alpha_1|u_{10}\) and on \(\alpha_2|\alpha_2|u_{20}\). Explain the role of the two-transition operation.

Solution. For two adjacent odd suspended letters the local product sign is minus. The coderivation evaluation also uses the parity of its preceding letters. Put \(w=u_{21}|\alpha_1|u_{10}\). Then \[ \begin{aligned} h(w)&=-u_{21}|u_{10},\\ D(w)&=-v_{21}|u_{10}+u_{21}|v_{10},\\ Dh(w)&=u_{20},\qquad hD(w)=0. \end{aligned} \] Thus \([D,h](w)=u_{20}\). It vanishes on the output, so \(\exp([D,h])(w)=w+u_{20}\) exactly. The suspended degree is minus one on both terms; its \(P\)-weight drops from one to zero.

For \(z=\alpha_2|\alpha_2|u_{20}\), the identities \(a^2=0\) and the same signs give \[ \begin{aligned} h(z)&=-\alpha_2|u_{20},\\ D(z)&=\alpha_2|v_{20},\\ Dh(z)&=v_{20},\qquad hD(z)=0. \end{aligned} \] Consequently the exponential is \(z+v_{20}\). Both suspended terms have degree one and \(P\)-weight two. The first computation uses the actual product \(u_{21}|u_{10}\mapsto-u_{20}\). Deleting that several-transition operation would delete the required correction \(u_{20}\). Correcting only the one-transition sectors therefore does not give this full chain gauge.

Exercise C.51.4.2 (intermediate). Let \(e,x\) have degree zero, let \(y,z\) have degree one, and let \(dx=y\), all other differentials zero. Take \(t=1\), let \(t'=E\) project onto \(e,z\), and put \(a(y)=-x\), with all other values zero. Compute the ordered product homotopy on \(z\otimes y\), and check its equation and its once-suspended sign. Compare the two groupings on three factors.

Solution. The original equation is \(\partial a=E-1\): on \(x\) its value is \(a(dx)=-x\), on \(y\) it is \(d a(y)=-y\), and on \(e,z\) it is zero. For two factors the homotopy is \(a\otimes1+E\otimes a\). Its first summand vanishes on \(z\otimes y\). The second has the graded evaluation sign \((-1)^{(-1)|z|}=-1\), so its value is \(+z\otimes x\). Its tensor differential is \(-z\otimes y\), while the input \(z\otimes y\) is closed. This equals \((E\otimes E-1)(z\otimes y)\). Omitting that evaluation sign would give the opposite answer.

After one total shift the differential is negated, so the homotopy's underlying value must be negated too, giving \(-z\otimes x\). Its shifted Hom differential is again \(-z\otimes y\). For three factors either grouping gives literally \[ \begin{aligned} a\otimes1\otimes1 &+E\otimes a\otimes1\\ &+E\otimes E\otimes a. \end{aligned} \] Each slot has exactly the sign of the sum of the preceding input degrees. This verifies both the shift and the ordered regrouping on an example with a nonzero odd-prefix sign.

Theorems C.51.1.1–C.51.3.1 give the transferred square homotopy,the ordered tensor and shift signs,and the full chain gauge. Exercise C.51.4.1 computes the nonzero two-transition correction;Exercise C.51.4.2 checks the odd-prefix sign. The actual graph and bounds are Theorems C.40.1.1,C.43.3.1 and C.49.1.1. Editable SVG source.

C.52. Indexed product models and their actual shuffle domains

Parameter arrows have degree zero before suspension. Their negative bar letters must remain in the product models. We first construct the actual indexed common-cobar projections, then identify the precise product-shuffle domains and full-face restrictions. These constructions supply the raw models and homotopy components needed for the product correction of C51. Work over the same characteristic-zero coefficient field and finite full IC corners as in C49–C51. Auxiliary regrading will be reversed after each argument; the actual original degrees and signs remain part of the result.

C.52.1. Even height regrading keeps the signs

Let \(I\) be a finite directed category with a chosen integer height \(h\) strictly increasing on every nonidentity arrow. There are no nonidentity endomorphisms. Full parameter faces inherit this same height; they do not renumber it. Let \(C=B\mathcal M\) be the minimal IC bar of the earlier sections, with reduced degrees at least one. Put \[ D_I=B(kI),\quad A_{n,I}=C^{\otimes n}\otimes D_I,\quad U_n=(\Omega C)^{\otimes n}. \] All bars and tensor products retain their scalar object categories.

Proposition C.52.1.1. On a mapping or coalgebra component with parameter endpoints \(i,j\), assign auxiliary degree \[ |x|_h=|x|+2(h(j)-h(i)). \] This is a reversible regrading. It preserves the differential, composition, coproduct, every tensor evaluation sign, and every fixed-endpoint chain equation. The reduced coalgebra \(A_{n,I}\) is positive in this degree. The same assertions hold for a tensor of such factors, using the sum of their heights. Consequently the positive-cobar comparison and unit proofs of Lemma C.39.4.1 apply to these indexed coalgebras and their height-preserving comparisons. Their conclusions are quasi-isomorphisms in the original degrees as well.

Proof. The height jump is additive at a composite and at a coproduct cut. Hence both multiplication and coproduct retain degree zero; the unary differential retains its endpoints and degree one. The change in each homogeneous degree is even. Thus every sign \((-1)^{|x||y|}\), every suspended insertion sign, and each Hom differential sign is exactly its original sign. Reversing the endpoint shift recovers the original complex on each mapping block; its cycles and boundaries have merely been renumbered. Chain equations and quasi-isomorphisms are therefore equivalent in the two gradings.

An index bar word with \(q\) strict arrows has degree \(-q\) and height jump at least \(q\). A tensor of positive IC bar words with \(r\) original IC letters has degree at least \(r\). Its tensor with that index word consequently has \[ |x|_h\ge r-q+2\Delta h\ge r+q. \] Every reduced element has \(r+q\ge1\). This proves positivity. There are finitely many index words, since \(q\) is bounded by the height range. Finite IC corners are degreewise finite. The same inequality bounds their original word length at a fixed auxiliary degree, so the finite-degree filtration arguments of Lemma C.39.4.1 apply literally.

For several factors, tensor degrees and height jumps both add. In particular the source and target of every regrouping have the same auxiliary grading. A full face is a restriction of endpoint and original word labels, so retains all formulas. On the actual compatible native grafting domains C47 proves additivity of the execution height; there too the regrading is the same sum on both sides. Nothing in this argument declares an incompatible intermediate execution state admissible. \(\square\)

C.52.2. The actual indexed common-cobar projection

Retain the actual strictly natural map from C43, \[ \psi_{n,I}:A_{n,I}\longrightarrow B(U_n\otimes kI), \qquad V_{n,I}=\Omega A_{n,I}. \] Define \[ \rho_{n,I}=\epsilon_{U_n\otimes kI}\,\Omega\psi_{n,I}: V_{n,I}\longrightarrow U_n\otimes kI. \] This is the projection from the actual common cobar; its source differs from the canonical full bar-cobar \(Q_{n,I}\).

Theorem C.52.2.1. The functor \(\rho_{n,I}\) fixes the tuple/parameter objects and is graded-surjective and a quasi-isomorphism on each mapping block. Its kernel has a contraction. These contractions can be chosen compatibly with all finite full parameter faces and with an increasing compatible system of finite IC corners. The projection itself is strictly natural under every core map \(g\): \[ \rho'_{n,I}\,\Omega(g^{\otimes n}\otimes1) =((\Omega g)^{\otimes n}\otimes1)\rho_{n,I}. \] At \(n=0\) it is the genuine \(\Omega D_I\to kI\) counit; the parameter category remains present.

Proof. After Section C.52.1's even height regrading all reduced input coalgebras and all nonidentity ordinary arrows of \(U_n\otimes kI\) are positive. The unit maps for each \(C\), the identity on \(D_I=B(kI)\), and the bar shuffle give exactly \(\psi_{n,I}\). The complete unit and shuffle proofs C.39.3–C.39.4 show it is a chain coalgebra quasi-isomorphism. Lemma C.39.4.1 makes its cobar a quasi-isomorphism; the full bar-cobar cut proof makes the counit a quasi-isomorphism. Their composite is therefore one as well. Reversing the regrading proves the assertion in the original mapping degrees.

For surjectivity take any free generator \(tc\) in the \(a\)-th \(\Omega C\) target factor. The cobar generator on the same \(c\) in that single input factor, with all other factors coaugmented and with an identity index, maps to \(tc\) in that target factor. A strict index arrow \(b:i\to j\) is the image of the cobar generator on \(sb\in D_I\), with all IC factors coaugmented. These statements follow from the one-letter twisting projection of the canonical shuffle. The free words in the target factors and these index arrows span every mapping block. Products of their just-stated preimages give preimages with the actual endpoints. Finite additive matrices preserve this surjectivity and quasi-isomorphism.

There is a useful actual chain-linear section \(\sigma\). Choose the ordinary factor order. Embed each \(\Omega C\) factor by the one-factor coalgebra inclusion at the source parameter vertex, multiply the factors in that fixed order, and put the canonical one-letter index arrow after the resulting IC mapping, at its output IC object. The graded tensor mapping space has precisely these ordered factor words and actual index arrows as a basis. The embedding of each factor is a dg functor, its multiplication is a chain map with the graded tensor rule, and the index lift is closed. Thus the displayed ordered construction is a chain-linear section on mapping complexes. It is not claimed to preserve multiplication between different factors. Directly \(\rho\sigma=1\), and \(\sigma\) retains every full face: it uses only the two original parameter endpoints.

The kernel is acyclic because \(\rho\) is a quasi-isomorphism, so it is split contractible over the coefficient field by C.30.1. Here is why compatible contractions exist even for proper face subcomplexes. Fix the parameter endpoints. Every nonzero full face contains both endpoints and therefore the identical target mapping block. The chain section \(\sigma\) lies in their common endpoint face. Thus each face source decomposes into that same section image and its own kernel. The source face subspaces have the distributive original-word support lattice. Passing to the quotient by the common section image preserves their intersections, sums and distributivity, so the same is true of the face kernels. Every finite intersection is the kernel for its common full face and is acyclic by the already proved face assertion.

The acyclic-face-union argument in Theorem C.50.2.1 now applies: add faces one at a time, using the quotient of one acyclic complex by its acyclic intersection. The sum of previously assigned face kernels and its quotient in the full kernel are acyclic. Extend the existing contraction using a chain splitting of that quotient. Explicitly a graded section with defect \(a=ds-sd\) is corrected to \(s+a h_Q\), since \(\partial(a h_Q)=-a\). Extend the contraction by that of the quotient. This retains its square-zero condition and every earlier restriction. It proves the finite face claim without equating different face source complexes.

For increasing full IC corners use the same factor-word section, and the analogous relative kernel quotient splitting on each new finite collection of blocks. Every original word appears at a finite stage; its choice is retained thereafter. Naturality of \(\rho\) itself does not depend on these choices: the canonical \(\psi\) is strictly natural by C.43.1 and the counit is natural on its free generators. Their two squares give the stated exact equality. At \(n=0\) these same formulas leave precisely the index bar and its counit. In particular it is not replaced by a scalar category when \(I\) has arrows. \(\square\)

C.52.3. Native product blocks and their full kernel projection

For ordered block factors put \[ A_i=C^{\otimes n_i}\otimes D_{I_i},\qquad B_i=C\otimes D_{I_i},\qquad A=\bigotimes_i A_i,\quad B=\bigotimes_i B_i. \] The \(n_i\) may be zero. Let actual strict block representatives \(F_i:\Omega A_i\to\operatorname{Add}(\Omega B_i)\) be given. Write \[ \mu:\Omega A\longrightarrow\bigotimes_i\Omega A_i, \qquad \nu:\Omega B\longrightarrow\bigotimes_i\Omega B_i \] for C41's canonical one-factor twisting projections. Set \(P=(\bigotimes_i F_i)\mu\).

Theorem C.52.3.1. The maps \(\mu,\nu\) are actual graded-surjective dg quasi-equivalences. They regroup strictly and have all their original graded permutation signs. There is a lift \(\widetilde P:\Omega A\to\operatorname{Add}(\Omega B)\) with \(\nu\widetilde P=P\). Its represented common-core module has a graded-surjective quasi-isomorphism \[ \begin{aligned} \phi:B\otimes s\operatorname{Hom}_{\Omega B} (\widetilde P x,y)\otimes A \longrightarrow B\otimes s\operatorname{Hom}_{\bigotimes_i\Omega B_i} (Px,\nu y)\otimes A. \end{aligned} \] The target is exactly \((\bigotimes_i K(Z_i))[1]\), with all index cores retained. The full kernel contraction and fixed-projection SDR of C45 apply, including every higher module action. Compatible full factor faces can be retained in the lifts and SDRs. The actual native strict block representatives \(F_i\) can themselves be chosen in these stated common-cobar sources and targets, including their full parameter faces.

Proof. Give the product endpoints the sum of the heights of their \(I_i\)'s. Section C.52.1 makes every reduced \(A_i,B_i\) positive, without changing a sign. C.41.1 therefore proves both quasi-equivalences, their strict regrouping and their graded permutations. Their generator formula proves graded surjectivity: each free generator in an individual target factor is the image of its pure one-factor input generator. Their kernels are acyclic. The source \(\Omega A\) is free on its reduced coalgebra generators. Its unary generator complex is retained, and its remaining differential uses smaller original primitive length. The relative generator lifting proof C.46.2, applied to \(\nu\), gives the stated actual lift of \(P\).

To obtain the actual native \(F_i\)'s, start with the complete tagged native functor of C49. Its canonical strict representative, followed by the target counit, maps \(Q_{n_i,I_i}\) to \(\operatorname{Add}(U_1\otimes kI_i)\). Precompose it with \(\Omega\psi_{n_i,I_i}:V_{n_i,I_i}\to Q_{n_i,I_i}\). Now lift this actual dg functor through the surjective quasi-isomorphism \(\rho_{1,I_i}:\Omega B_i\to U_1\otimes kI_i\) of Section C.52.2. C.46.2 applies to its free common-cobar source and to the just-constructed mapping-kernel contractions. A full face is generated by original words whose parameter vertices lie in that face. The union of prescribed face generator subcomplexes is differential-stable. The relative lift therefore keeps those earlier face images, proving the asserted simultaneous native block choice. This constructs representatives of the supplied entire native functors, not only their leading cohomology maps.

Postcomposition by \(\nu\) on its target mappings is a surjective quasi-isomorphism, since \(\nu\) has exactly that property on every fixed mapping block. Its square with the source action is strict by \(\nu\widetilde P=P\). Pull back the two represented graph modules along the canonical units of \(A,B\). Their two coactions are the same outside cores. The canonical identity \(B\nu\,\eta_B=\operatorname{sh}(\bigotimes_i\eta_{B_i})\), proved in C.41.2, makes the displayed full bicomodule map exactly the identity on those outside cores and the target mapping projection in its central slot. It has the strict full module equation.

The product target's mapping complex is literally \(\bigotimes_i\operatorname{Hom}_{\Omega B_i}(F_i x_i,y_i)\). The complete differential, coaction and one-total-cross-suspension calculation of C.41.2 applies word for word after the even regrading. It proves the asserted product identification, not only its equality on cohomology. The source arities never enter that calculation; a genuine zero-input block still contributes its target mapping factor.

Now apply the fixed-projection proof C.45.2: choose a contraction of the central mapping kernel, extend it by the outside coactions, and perturb by the terms consuming surrounding original core letters. Their geometric series terminate on each word. This contracts the full cofree kernel and constructs the section and normalized homotopy with precisely projection \(\phi\). Thus no several-cross comparison can be inferred merely from this projection; the projection and its complete homotopies are the actual input for the later C51 correction.

For the face choices one can see the needed kernel lattice explicitly. The graded target of \(\nu\) has its ordered tensor-factor cobar word basis. Its chain-linear section multiplies their one-factor inclusions in that order. In the free source basis, a word containing a genuinely mixed-factor generator is killed by \(\nu\). Every other word is a pure-factor interleaving and maps, with its actual Koszul sign, to its ordered factor-word basis element. Its difference from that signed canonical section element is a kernel basis element. These elements, together with the killed mixed words, form a basis of the kernel: subtract the unique canonical word for each target basis element. A full factor face retains exactly a subset of this basis, because reordering the factors keeps each factor's original parameter vertices. Hence these face kernel subspaces have the distributive support lattice. Their finite intersections are the same kernels for common full factor faces and are acyclic. The relative quotient contraction argument of Section C.52.2 gives compatible contractions.

The source subcategory generated by the union of prescribed full factor faces is differential-stable. Relative C46 lifting thus keeps those earlier images in \(\widetilde P\). The fixed-projection cofree perturbation then restricts term by term to the compatible face SDRs. All sums remain finite on original words in the original grading. This proves the asserted face compatibility. \(\square\)

C.52.4. The shuffle domain and its full-face intersections

Let \(I_1,\ldots,I_m\) be finite directed categories as in Section C.52.1. Fix their actual arrow bases and relative bars. There is the original bar shuffle \[ j:\bigotimes_i D_{I_i}\longrightarrow D_{\prod_i I_i}. \] Every nonempty factor bar letter changes exactly its own parameter coordinate. All signs are the actual suspended Koszul signs.

Theorem C.52.4.1. The shuffle is an injective chain coalgebra map. If \(J\) is any full subcategory on a subset of the product vertices, its image intersects \(D_J\) in precisely the span of the images of those factor-word tuples whose Cartesian product of vertex sets lies in \(J\). Distinct factor-word tuples have disjoint shuffle supports. The intersection statement retains actual parallel-arrow labels. The induced map on free cobars is injective on its generator complexes and on its underlying free graded categories.

Proof. The chain and coproduct equations are the full bar-shuffle identities proved in C.34.2 and C.39.3. They apply here with the original negative index bar degrees: alternatively Proposition C.52.1.1 makes them positive without changing any sign.

For injectivity inspect an output bar word in a shuffle. Each of its arrows changes exactly one coordinate, since that step is the given nonidentity factor arrow tensored with the other identity arrows. Thus its coordinate label is uniquely recoverable. Reading the arrows of each coordinate in their original order recovers that entire factor word, including every actual parallel-arrow label. The output therefore occurs in the shuffle of only that one factor-word tuple. Different interleavings of the same tuple also give different output words: their sequences of changed coordinates differ. Every coefficient is plus or minus one. This proves both disjointness and injectivity over the coefficient field.

For a fixed tuple of factor words, every prefix in every factor can be reached simultaneously by an interleaving: perform the chosen prefixes in their factor orders, then finish the remaining arrows. Consequently the union of all vertices visited by its shuffled words is exactly the Cartesian product of its individual vertex sets. A full face bar retains a word if and only if every one of that word's vertices lies in the face. Thus all shuffle terms lie in \(D_J\) exactly under the stated rectangle condition. Disjoint support prevents cancellation of a bad shuffle term against a different tuple. The same criterion therefore holds for arbitrary linear combinations. This proves the intersection assertion.

Choose the interleaving which orders the coordinate blocks once and for all. Sending that word to its factor-word tuple with the inverse of its shuffle sign, and all other output words to zero, is a graded linear left inverse. It is not being used as a coalgebra map. The injection on reduced coalgebra generator complexes induces one on their shifts. A tensor algebra on an injective map of vector spaces is injective: choose a vector-space complement, or apply its linear left inverse on each tensor power. The identical argument on composable object blocks proves the relative free-category assertion for \(\Omega j\). \(\square\)

Pairwise intersections with faces do not determine intersection with a sum of faces. Here is a concrete distinction. Take two copies of \([1]\) with arrows \(a,b\), and let \(x=sa\otimes sb\). In the square product, let \(p_a\) be the two-arrow bar word along \(00\to10\to11\), and \(p_b\) that along \(00\to01\to11\). In the target-to-source word convention, \[ j(x)=p_b-p_a. \] The minus sign is \((-1)^{|sa||sb|}=-1\). Let \(J_a,J_b\) be the respective full three-vertex faces. The degree-minus-two shuffle line meets neither face separately, but is contained in their sum: \[ \begin{aligned} \langle j(x)\rangle\cap D_{J_a}^{-2}&=0,\\ \langle j(x)\rangle\cap D_{J_b}^{-2}&=0,\\ \langle j(x)\rangle\cap(D_{J_a}^{-2}+D_{J_b}^{-2}) &=\langle j(x)\rangle. \end{aligned} \] Indeed the two distinct bar words are independent basis vectors and each belongs to its own face. The direct diagonal arrow is also present in both full faces, but has degree minus one and does not change this degree-minus-two computation. Thus independently fixed face-generator images must satisfy the actual signed shuffle relation before a product image can be prescribed on their union.

C.52.5. Extend a central homotopy with every face retained

In the transferred indexed native graph, a bare central cohomology block at fixed parameter endpoints is the same in every full face containing those endpoints. It is the actual IC mapping cohomology tensored with the space of actual arrows between those endpoints, as proved in corrected C.49.6. It carries no extra hidden intermediate parameter vertices. The outside cores still retain their full original index words.

Theorem C.52.5.1. Fix one cofree one-cross module and its endpoint/string grading, over identity outside core maps. Suppose a homogeneous central Taylor map has been specified on a graded subspace of its inputs, retaining those endpoint/string labels. It has a graded linear extension to the whole central input space. The cofree extension is a full bicomodule map, and it preserves every full parameter face. In particular this applies to a degree-minus-one homotopy on one actual product-shuffle submodel. For several prescribed submodels, the same assertion holds when the prescriptions already define a linear map on their actual sum.

Proof. Choose a homogeneous basis of the prescribed subspace in each fixed label and input/output degree block, and extend it to a basis of that whole block. Assign zero on the added basis vectors. The resulting linear map retains its homogeneous degree and the required labels. This is an ordinary vector-space extension; no chain equation is asserted for the homotopy at this step.

Complete it by the cofree outside-coaction formula (C.39.5), with the graded evaluation sign of its homogeneous degree. Explicitly the degree-\(r\) central map is moved past the retained left outside piece, contributing \((-1)^{r|c_{(1)}|}\). Coassociativity and the two counits give the two bicomodule equations by the same proof as C.39.2. On a prescribed subbicomodule the formula recovers its original map, since its cuts are cuts of that submodel.

Now take an input belonging to a full face. Every outside piece in its coproduct still lies in that face. The central output has the endpoints of the consumed middle piece, so those endpoints lie in the original face. By the stated bare-central identification that entire output block is present in the face. Every reconstructed output therefore remains in it. No assumption that an arbitrary basis complement was itself a face complement has been used.

The construction chooses one global map and restricts it to all faces, so the restrictions agree on their intersections automatically. It does not retain arbitrary previously fixed values on all those faces. If such values must be retained, they are additional prescribed subspaces and all linear relations in their sum must hold, including the signed square relation in Section C.52.4. For a family of product submodels the same linear extension argument applies to their sum precisely when its prescriptions are a well-defined linear map there. Pairwise agreement alone is not substituted for that condition. \(\square\)

This theorem is useful for C51's gauge construction: the extended homotopy need not itself be closed. Its commutator with the full graph differential is closed, and its finite exponential gives the chain correction. Compatibility of the prescribed product values on their actual sum remains necessary.

C.52.6. The actual resolved-square homotopy component

Transport the two outside target cores through the fixed isomorphisms \(g^{\otimes n}\), so that the full module comparisons may be read in the dg category \(\mathcal E\) of cofree bicomodules over the same cores. Its mapping differential is the full Hom differential; its compositions are actual module-map compositions. This transport is only a re-expression of the supplied extension-field core isomorphism.

Proposition C.52.6.1. Suppose an actual strict dg functor \(\Omega Bk[2]\to\mathcal E\) is given, whose three objects are \(Z,W,W'\), and whose three degree-zero arrow images are \[ a=\phi:Z\to W,\qquad b=u:W\to W',\qquad c=\phi't:Z\to W'. \] Then minus the image of the two-arrow free generator is an actual degree-minus-one bicomodule map \(R\) with \(\partial R=\phi't-u\phi\). Conversely that exact homotopy and the three closed maps give this entire resolved two-simplex. Every face restriction of a supplied family restricts this same formula.

Proof. The relative bar of \(k[2]\) has the three suspended strict arrows of degree minus one, and its unique two-arrow word \(s e_{12}|s e_{01}\) of degree minus two. Its binary differential is \(-s e_{02}\). Its only reduced coproduct is \(s e_{12}\otimes s e_{01}\). Therefore the exact cobar formula (C.39.15) gives \[ d\,t(s e_{12}|s e_{01}) =-t(s e_{02})+t(s e_{12})t(s e_{01}). \] The generator has degree minus one. Its image \(H\) satisfies \(\partial H=ba-c\), so \(R=-H\) has precisely the asserted sign and type. There are no longer reduced index words and no other free generators. Assigning these four generator images and the object identities consequently defines the dg functor if and only if the displayed equation and the three closed-arrow equations hold. Extension to all products follows by the dg Leibniz rule. Full cofree module maps and their Hom differential include all source/target action components, so this is not merely a bare-central homotopy. A restriction of the dg functor restricts these generator values, proving the last assertion. \(\square\)

C.52.7. Solved examples

Exercise C.52.7.1 (intermediate). Take zero IC inputs and the full parameter category \([2]=\{0<1<2\}\), with height \(h(i)=i\). Describe the \(0\to2\) mapping complex of \(V_{0,[2]}=\Omega D_{[2]}\), its projection to \(k[2]\), and the kernel contraction. Compute all its auxiliary degrees. Explain why zero inputs do not make this source a scalar category.

Solution. Write \(a,b,c\) for the degree-zero cobar generators on the strict arrows \(0\to1\), \(1\to2\), \(0\to2\). There is one further generator \(H=t(s e_{12}|s e_{01})\), of degree minus one. Formula (C.39.15), or Proposition C.52.6.1, gives \[ dH=ba-c. \] There are no other composable reduced words from zero to two. Thus this mapping complex has basis \(H\) in degree minus one and \(ba,c\) in degree zero. Its projection sends both \(ba,c\) to the actual arrow \(e_{02}\), and sends \(H\) to zero. The kernel has basis \(H,ba-c\), with \(dH=ba-c\). The contraction sends \(ba-c\) to \(H\) and sends \(H\) to zero. Its square is zero and its two contraction identities hold on those two basis vectors.

The section of the projection sends \(e_{02}\) to \(c\). The full normalized homotopy is consequently \(k(ba)=H\), \(k(c)=k(H)=0\); on each basis vector \(dk+kd=1-\sigma\rho\). The generators \(a,b\) have height jump one and auxiliary degree two; \(c\) and \(ba\) have height jump two and auxiliary degree four; \(H\) has auxiliary degree three. Its differential retains auxiliary degree one, since \(3+1=4\). The parameter objects, arrows and this nontrivial negative-degree resolution are still present when the number of IC factors is zero.

Exercise C.52.7.2 (advanced). Let \(a_1,a_2,a_3\) be the strict arrows in three copies of \([1]\). Consider the signed six-term shuffle of \(sa_1\otimes sa_2\otimes sa_3\) in the bar of the cube \([1]^3\). Let \(J\) be the full subcategory obtained by omitting vertex \(110\). Delete just the shuffle terms visiting that vertex. Is the resulting four-term element closed? Use \([v_0,\ldots,v_q]\) for the bar word on the forward vertex path, retaining the original suspended signs.

Solution. The full shuffle is closed, since its three one-letter factor words are closed and the shuffle is a chain map. The deleted terms are exactly \[ \begin{aligned} &-[000,100,110,111]\\ &\quad+[000,010,110,111]. \end{aligned} \] Their signs are minus and plus: reversing the three distinct odd suspended letters has three inversions, and interchanging the first two factor steps changes that sign once. For a three-arrow forward path, merging at its first intermediate vertex has sign plus and merging at its second has sign minus. Thus the boundary of the deleted pair is \[ [000,100,111]-[000,010,111]. \] The intermediate path \([000,110,111]\) cancels between its two contributions. Since the full six-term boundary is zero, the four retained terms have boundary \[ -[000,100,111]+[000,010,111]\ne0. \] Both displayed words lie in \(D_J\) and are distinct basis words. Merely deleting the inadmissible shuffle states therefore breaks the chain equation. The valid product domain is the rectangle subspace of Theorem C.52.4.1, with the actual restriction of the shuffle, rather than a clipped shuffle on an inadmissible full product word.

Proposition C.52.1.1 proves the reversible even height grading. Theorems C.52.2.1–C.52.3.1 construct the actual indexed projections and product modules. Theorems C.52.4.1–C.52.5.1 identify the full-face shuffle domains and central homotopy extensions. Proposition C.52.6.1 gives the exact resolved-square sign. Exercises C.52.7.1–C.52.7.2 retain zero-input parameter data and compute a nonzero boundary from clipped shuffle terms. Editable SVG source.

C.53. Native module coherence with the whole parameter family

The product comparison uses maps and homotopies in the full dg category of represented cofree modules. A change of module model changes the coherent cells as well as their edge maps. This section records their homogeneous signs, the triangle correction and a construction transporting the entire resolved parameter family while retaining its chosen edge representatives. The raw native product squares are on the actual indexed product models of C52. A module-valued coherent family and a whole nested-path coordinate are different objects; all several-transition and product/grafting restrictions must still be retained when using these constructions for tensor descent.

C.53.1. Signed full represented evaluation

Use the normalized full natural-transformation and graph-module models of C.33.2. The target category is a dg category \(B\); the source may have all its normalized unital higher operations. A full homogeneous natural-transformation component has its total degree in that bar model, including its dependence on the source bar word. It is not merely its object component. Keep finite additive represented objects throughout.

Lemma C.53.1.1. Represented evaluation is a dg functor from the opposite of the full natural-transformation category to the dg category of the represented cofree modules. On a bare homogeneous target map its degree-\(r\) action is \[ m\longmapsto(-1)^{r|m|}m\beta. \] On a full source bar word use the same formula on its homogeneous full transformation component, with the tensor evaluation signs, and reconstruct by the outside coactions. It retains all source actions and is compatible with parameter faces. After one total cochain shift, a degree-\(r\) map has the additional factor \((-1)^r\).

Proof. First take ordinary homogeneous target maps. For the displayed operator \(R_\beta\), the ordinary Hom differential gives \[ \begin{aligned} \partial R_\beta(m) &=(-1)^{r|m|}\bigl(dm\,\beta+(-1)^{|m|}m\,d\beta\bigr)\\ &\quad-(-1)^r(-1)^{r(|m|+1)}dm\,\beta\\ &=(-1)^{(r+1)|m|}m\,d\beta =R_{d\beta}(m). \end{aligned} \] The two terms containing \(dm\) cancel. For \(|\gamma|=s\), two successive evaluations have coefficient \((-1)^{r|m|+s(|m|+r)}\). Hence \(R_\gamma R_\beta=(-1)^{rs}R_{\beta\gamma}\), exactly the graded opposite composition sign. Identity evaluation is the identity. Thus this is an actual dg functor on represented mappings, with its correct contravariant direction.

For the full source action, apply that evaluation to each consecutive source block in the C.33.2 bar formula. Terms differentiating or merging the source inputs give exactly the same terms in the full transformation differential. Terms composing two adjacent source-image blocks are exactly the two twisted endpoint actions of that differential. Target unary terms are the calculation just given, with the degree of the entire homogeneous bar component. The remaining target-composition terms cancel by the dg Leibniz and associativity identities. These are all terms in the full module Hom differential, because a represented graph word crosses only once. Consequently evaluation commutes with the full differential.

For composition, cutting the source word into the two transformation blocks gives the same two consecutive evaluations. Moving their homogeneous component maps past the preceding suspended inputs gives exactly the tensor evaluation signs on both sides. The graded opposite sign already calculated is the only additional interchange. The outside coaction formula reconstructs the remaining components uniquely, proving both coaction equations and the full composition identity. This is the complete transformation part of C.33.2 with the homogeneous signs displayed.

On a cochain shift \([1]\) the source and target differentials are negated. The dg shift functor sends a degree-\(r\) map to \((-1)^r\) times its underlying map: substitution into the Hom differential gives the required degree-\(r+1\) shift sign. This also retains composition. It is the precise additional sign when restoring C41's one total cross suspension. Every formula uses only the original source word and its cuts, so restricts to every parameter face. \(\square\)

C.53.2. Transport the triangle and its three boundaries

Let \(\mathcal E\) be a dg category of actual full cofree module complexes over fixed cores. If needed, transport the target cores back through the already fixed \(g\), so that these are identity-core module maps. Suppose \[ a:X_0\to X_1,\quad b:X_1\to X_2,\quad c:X_0\to X_2 \] are closed degree-zero maps and \(H:X_0\to X_2\) has degree minus one with \(\partial H=ba-c\). At each vertex retain chain maps \(i_j:\widehat X_j\to X_j\), \(p_j:X_j\to\widehat X_j\) and an actual module homotopy \(\partial h_j=1-i_jp_j\).

Lemma C.53.2.1. The transported edges are \[ \widehat a=p_1ai_0,\qquad \widehat b=p_2bi_1,\qquad \widehat c=p_2ci_0. \] Their actual two-simplex is \[ \widehat H=p_2Hi_0-p_2b h_1a i_0, \qquad \partial\widehat H=\widehat b\widehat a-\widehat c. \] If the desired three closed edges instead satisfy \(a'=\widehat a+\partial A\), \(b'=\widehat b+\partial B\), \(c'=\widehat c+\partial C\), for specified degree-minus-one homotopies, the corrected simplex is \[ H'=\widehat H+B\widehat a+b'A-C, \qquad \partial H'=b'a'-c'. \] These formulas retain every supplied compatible face restriction.

Proof. The full Hom differential is a derivation and every displayed edge or inclusion/projection has degree zero.
