Thus \[ \begin{aligned} \partial\widehat H &=p_2(ba-c)i_0-p_2b(1-i_1p_1)a i_0\\ &=p_2b i_1p_1a i_0-p_2c i_0\\ &=\widehat b\widehat a-\widehat c. \end{aligned} \] For the replacement formula, its differential is \[ \begin{aligned} &\widehat b\widehat a-\widehat c +(b'-\widehat b)\widehat a\\ &\quad+b'(a'-\widehat a)-(c'-\widehat c) =b'a'-c'. \end{aligned} \] This retains the cross term already contained in \(b'A\); replacing it by \(\widehat b A\) would in general omit \((\partial B)A\). Each expression is a composite of actual module maps and homotopies, so the equality is in the complete module Hom complex, not only on bare central terms. By C.52.6 it is exactly the image of the free two-arrow generator in the resolved simplex. Restriction commutes with all these composites, proving the compatibility assertion. \(\square\)

In particular a change of module model does not preserve only the three edges: its middle-vertex homotopy contributes the explicit second term of \(\widehat H\). This is the two-simplex instance of the whole consecutive-word action transfer used in C50.

C.53.3. Chosen raw native product-square homotopies

Work over the extension field \(E\) of C.48.1 and retain its given entire calibrated enhanced strong monoidal comparison. Its pure core map is \(g\), and every pure state uses its specified power. Take one finite actual ordered list of native block functors with the C52 indexed models. Use its actual product-shuffle source domain; on a full execution face retain the rectangle subdomain of C.52.4.

Write \(Z,Z'\) for the two raw common-cobar block modules and \(W,W'\) for their actual once-suspended product modules. C.52.3 and C45 give fixed projections and normalized chain sections \[ \phi:Z\to W,\quad i_\phi:W\to Z,\qquad \phi':Z'\to W',\quad i'_{\phi}:W'\to Z', \quad \phi i_\phi=1,\quad\phi'i'_{\phi}=1. \] All four maps are over the identity respective cores. Let \(u:W\to W'\) be the shifted product of the individual full comparison maps, over the exact powers of \(g\). Let \(\tau:W\to W'\) be the original native block comparison interpreted on these product modules by the actual represented-module equivalences.

Theorem C.53.3.1. The original full monoidal comparison supplies an actual degree-minus-one module homotopy \[ R_0:W\to W',\qquad \partial R_0=\tau-u. \] For the chosen raw lift \[ t=i'_{\phi}\tau\phi:Z\to Z', \] an actual raw square homotopy is \[ R=R_0\phi,\qquad \partial R=\phi't-u\phi. \] The product-normalized choice \(t^{\rm prod}=i'_{\phi}u\phi\) satisfies the square exactly, and its homotopy from \(t\) is \[ K=-i'_{\phi}R_0\phi,\qquad \partial K=t^{\rm prod}-t. \] The construction retains the full factor faces of this actual supplied native product cell and has its calibrated leading cohomology map.

Proof. Before changing models, the full monoidality datum compares the native block comparison with the external product of its individual comparisons. This is the specified coherence cell of the actual enhanced strong monoidal comparison of C.48.1. Its full source-bar components are part of that datum; equality of the three cohomology maps is not substituted for them. Use the original mixed-input recording of C.48.2 on this cell, with the dg category of full represented modules as target. C.33.2's transformation construction and Section C.53.1 give all its module components, differential and composition, with the graded opposite and one-cross shift signs retained. The unital recording C.43.2 works for this dg target without assuming it has an augmentation.

Transport the actual block functors into the common-cobar models by C.52.3's represented-module equivalences. The projection \(\phi\) is precisely the represented target-mapping map induced by the canonical product projection, whose square with the source functor was proved strict in C.52.3. Its chosen chain section and homotopy are therefore actual model-equivalence data. For the product modules choose the tensor of the individual data with C41's single total suspension. Their degree-zero comparison transports as the product of the individual comparisons, so its edge is exactly \(u\). The other edge is the interpreted native comparison \(\tau\).

Section C.53.2's formula transports the complete resolved coherence cell, including the middle-vertex homotopy term. If boundary representatives were changed to these chosen projections or product representatives, its boundary-replacement formula uses exactly their supplied model-equivalence unit/counit homotopies. Thus it is a recorded two-simplex in the actual full module dg category, with the native edge \(\tau\) and product edge \(u\). Its third edge can be the identity on \(W\); equivalently use its degenerate first edge and these two parallel edges. Proposition C.52.6.1 identifies minus its two-arrow generator image as \(R_0\), proving \(\partial R_0=\tau-u\).

All these comparisons are over the same outside core powers. Indeed C.48.1 fixes those powers before recording the cells; the canonical \(\rho\) and product projections commute strictly with them by C.52.2 and C.41.1. Pulling the full represented equations to the common cores therefore leaves identity outside coactions after transport through \(g\). The resulting degree-minus-one component is an actual bicomodule homotopy over those powers. No homotopy correcting a pure state map has been silently omitted.

Now the remaining assertions are direct full-module identities: \(\phi't=\tau\phi\), so \[ \partial(R_0\phi)=(\tau-u)\phi=\phi't-u\phi. \] Also \(\phi't^{\rm prod}=u\phi\), and \[ \partial(-i'_{\phi}R_0\phi) =i'_{\phi}(u-\tau)\phi=t^{\rm prod}-t. \] The chosen lifts represent the original comparison because the sections and projections are actual module homotopy equivalences. The kernel SDRs and the original calibrated comparison induce the identity on the fixed mapping cohomology frames, proving the leading-map assertion.

The original cell and all its retained full factor faces are one supplied family. The recording uses their same original words, and C52/C45 give compatible projection data on those faces. Every transport and evaluation term consequently restricts to the same face term, including the two-simplex term. This proves the stated face claim. Restriction to a compatible execution face is the actual rectangle restriction, never the deletion of unsafe shuffle terms. \(\square\)

C.53.4. The explicit path-projection kernel contraction

Let \(\mathcal E\) be any dg category over the coefficient field; in the application its morphisms are full bicomodule maps with the full Hom differential. For a closed homotopy equivalence \(u:X\to Y\) use the path object of C.50.3. A degree-\(r\) map from \(u_i\) to \(u_j\) has components \[ \begin{aligned} f&:X_i\to X_j,\quad |f|=r,\\ g&:Y_i\to Y_j,\quad |g|=r,\\ a&:X_i\to Y_j,\quad |a|=r-1. \end{aligned} \] Its differential and composition are \[ \begin{aligned} D(f,g,a)&=(\partial f,\partial g, -\partial a+u_jf-gu_i),\\ (f_2,g_2,a_2)(f_1,g_1,a_1) &=(f_2f_1,g_2g_1, a_2f_1+(-1)^{|f_2|}g_2a_1). \end{aligned} \] The full dg identities were proved in C.50.3, with their essential last composition sign. Projection \(\pi_0\) keeps \(f\).

Lemma C.53.4.1. Suppose \(u_i=p_i:X_i\to Y_i\) has a chain section \(i_i\), with \(p_i i_i=1\), and a normalized homotopy \[ \partial h_i=1-i_i p_i,\qquad h_i^2=p_i h_i=h_i i_i=0. \] Then the kernel of \(\pi_0\) on the mapping complex from \(u_i\) to any \(u_j\) is contractible. On a homogeneous pair \((g,a)\) of total degree \(r\), its differential and contraction are \[ \begin{aligned} d_K(g,a)&=(\partial g,-\partial a-gp_i),\\ k(g,a)&=(-a i_i,(-1)^r a h_i). \end{aligned} \] They satisfy \(d_Kk+kd_K=1\), \(k^2=0\), including their full cofree module actions. These formulas retain every face on which the original retract data have compatible restrictions.

Proof. Put \(C=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal E}(Y_i,Y_j)\), \(B=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal E}(X_i,Y_j)\). The chain map \(f:C\to B\) is \(g\mapsto gp_i\), with retraction \(r:B\to C\), \(a\mapsto a i_i\). In degree \(s\), put \(H_B(a)=(-1)^s a h_i\). The Hom derivation identity gives \[ \partial H_B(a)+H_B(\partial a)=a(1-i_i p_i). \] Indeed the two terms containing \((\partial a)h_i\) have opposite signs, and the remaining term is \(a\partial h_i\). Thus \(\partial H_B+H_B\partial=1-fr\). Also \(rH_B=H_B f=H_B^2=0\), by the three normalized identities for \(h_i\). These are actual mapping-complex equations; postcomposition and precomposition retain the full coactions with their homogeneous signs.

The mapping kernel is the pair complex \(C^r\oplus B^{r-1}\), with the displayed differential. On it define \(k(g,a)=(-r a,-H_Ba)\). Direct substitution gives first component \(-r\partial a+r\partial a+rf g=g\). Its second component is \(\partial H_Ba+H_B\partial a+fr a+H_B f g=a\). Finally \(k^2=0\) since \(rH_B=H_B^2=0\). This proves the normalized contraction with its displayed homogeneous sign. Restriction commutes with every composite. \(\square\)

C.53.5. Transport the entire coherent module family

Let \(I\) be a finite directed parameter category. An actual coherent family of module objects has its full unital resolved recording \[ F:\Omega B(kI)\longrightarrow\mathcal E. \] This is the supplied entire family, not a diagram inferred from closed edge maps. Its free generators are nonempty composable strings of nonidentity arrows of \(I\). A string of length \(q\) has generator degree \(1-q\). Its differential merges adjacent arrows or splits into products of two shorter strings, with the original C.39.15 signs.

At each parameter object let \((i_i,p_i,h_i)\) be a normalized module retract from \(X_i=F(i)\) to a chosen \(Y_i\), as in Section C.53.4. For an original arrow \(\alpha:i\to j\), prescribe \[ \begin{aligned} G(\alpha)&=p_j F(\alpha)i_i,\\ A(\alpha)&=p_jF(\alpha)h_i. \end{aligned} \]

Theorem C.53.5.1. There is a unital dg functor \[ \mathscr H:\Omega B(kI)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Path}(\mathcal E) \] with object path \(p_i:X_i\to Y_i\), first projection exactly \(F\), and the displayed prescribed second and third components on every one-arrow generator. Its second projection \(G\) records an actual entire coherent family on the chosen module models. It includes all higher comparison components and an actual coherent equivalence to the original family. A previously assigned full face family can be retained whenever its path lifts agree on their actual free-generator intersections and have these same object/edge values. The construction is finite on each original generator and extends along compatible increasing finite corners without changing earlier values.

Proof. For an original degree-zero arrow put \(f=F(\alpha)\), \(g=p_j f i_i\), and \(a=p_j f h_i\). The first two are closed. The third satisfies \[ \partial a=p_j f(1-i_i p_i)=p_jf-gp_i. \] Thus \((f,g,a)\) is a closed path morphism with exactly the stated endpoints. Assign the coefficient identity to the path identity \((1,1,0)\). This defines the lift on all length-one free generators and their free products. It does not yet claim the higher coherence relations, which belong to the higher free generators.

Induct on the original string length \(q\ge2\). All terms in the generator differential \(dx\) involve shorter generators or products of them, so their lifted values are already assigned. Choose any graded preimage \(v\) of \(F(x)\) under \(\pi_0\) on the fixed mapping block; for example \((F(x),0,0)\) is a graded preimage. Set its degree-one defect \[ o=Dv-\mathscr H(dx). \] It lies in the kernel because \(\pi_0\mathscr H=F\) on shorter generators and \(F\) is a dg functor. It is closed: apply \(D\), use the already assigned chain equation on every shorter product and \(d^2x=0\). The explicit mapping-kernel contraction \(k\) of Section C.53.4 gives the corrected value \[ \mathscr H(x)=v-k o. \] Its projection remains \(F(x)\), and \(D\mathscr H(x)=\mathscr H(dx)\), since \(Dko=o\) for a closed kernel element. Extend multiplicatively. The dg Leibniz rule proves the chain equation on every product of the newly assigned generators. This completes the induction with every original sign.

There are finitely many strict-arrow strings in a finite directed category, bounded by its height range. No infinite series or limiting primitive is used. Full parameter faces are generated by the original strings whose vertices lie in that face. Merging removes vertices and splitting retains subsets, so the union of prescribed face generator complexes is differential-stable. Their agreeing path lifts give one assignment on that free subcategory. Perform the correction only on the remaining generators. This retains the full assigned faces exactly, rather than separately rechoosing a simplex on each face.

The same induction works in the actual dg category of full cofree modules: all homotopies and kernel corrections are actual module maps, and their full mapping differential is the one used throughout. Each new finite IC corner or finite family of parameter cells retains the already assigned generators and extends only the new ones. Every fixed original word receives its value at a finite stage.

Finally \(\pi_1\mathscr H\) is a dg functor because \(\pi_1\) is one by C.50.3. Its parameter edges have the prescribed compressed values, and every higher generator has the assigned coherent value. The whole path family supplies the equivalence to \(F\), with object components \(p_i\), all of which are homotopy equivalences. This is an actual resolved comparison including its higher homotopies, not an objectwise identification alone. \(\square\)

C.53.6. Solved examples

Exercise C.53.6.1 (intermediate). Let \(X\) have basis \(e,x\) in degree zero and \(y\) in degree one, with \(dx=y\). Let \(Y=ke\), let \(i:Y\to X\) be inclusion, \(p:X\to Y\) the projection, and \(h(y)=x\), all other values zero. Start with the strict triangle whose three vertex complexes are \(X\), whose three edges are identities, and whose two-simplex component is zero. Replace its middle vertex by \(Y\). Determine the transported triangle and explain why its two-simplex component is necessary.

Solution. The retraction satisfies \(pi=1\), \(dh+hd=1-ip\), and \(h^2=ph=hi=0\), by evaluation on the three displayed basis vectors. The outside vertex models have identity inclusions/projections and zero homotopies. Lemma C.53.2.1 gives \[ \widehat a=p,\qquad\widehat b=i,\qquad\widehat c=1_X, \qquad\widehat H=-h. \] Its differential is \(\partial\widehat H=ip-1_X=\widehat b\widehat a-\widehat c\). On \(x,y\) this is minus the identity and hence is nonzero. Keeping the three compressed edge maps but omitting the middle-vertex term would leave precisely this nonzero triangle defect. The transferred coherent triangle includes \(-h\) even though the original two-simplex was zero.

Exercise C.53.6.2 (intermediate). Keep \(X,Y,i,p,h\) from the previous exercise and use the path object \(u=p:X\to Y\). In the kernel of its first mapping projection, let \(x^*,y^*:X\to Y\) send \(x,y\), respectively, to \(e\) and kill the other basis vectors. Check the contraction of Lemma C.53.4.1 on \((g,a)=(0,x^*)\), of total degree one, and on \((1_Y,0)\), of total degree zero. What happens if the factor \((-1)^r\) is omitted?

Solution. The degrees of \(x^*,y^*\) are zero and minus one, and \(\partial x^*=0\), \(\partial y^*=x^*\). The corrected kernel homotopy has \[ k(0,x^*)=(0,-y^*). \] Its differential is \((0,x^*)\), while \(d_K(0,x^*)=0\). Thus \((d_Kk+kd_K)(0,x^*)=(0,x^*)\). On the degree-zero element, \(k(1_Y,0)=0\) and \(d_K(1_Y,0)=(0,-p)\). Applying \(k\) to the latter gives \((pi,ph)=(1_Y,0)\), which proves its contraction equation too. The square-zero identities follow here from \(x^*i=0\), \(y^*h=0\), \(h^2=ph=hi=0\).

Omitting the sign in the degree-one case gives \(k(0,x^*)=(0,y^*)\), whose differential is \((0,-x^*)\), the opposite of the required answer. This sign is needed in the full Hom complex before any higher parameter generator is corrected.

Lemmas C.53.1.1–C.53.2.1 prove the represented evaluation signs and triangle transport. Theorem C.53.3.1 gives the chosen raw native product-square homotopies. Lemma C.53.4.1 contracts the path-projection kernel,and Theorem C.53.5.1 transports the entire coherent parameter family. Exercises C.53.6.1–C.53.6.2 calculate the middle-vertex term and the nontrivial Hom sign. Editable SVG source.

C.54. Relative pure actions and coherent product normalization

A comparison with prescribed tensor core powers must retain the entire pure-state action. We recover the whole comparison relative to that action, then compute its homotopy to the chosen product lift. The last two results replace product edges within their entire coherent parameter family. Work with the actual cofree module and path models of C49–C53 over the fixed characteristic-zero coefficient field. The simultaneous product-shuffle prescriptions and all higher grafting equations retain their full domains.

C.54.1. Recovery relative to the full pure actions

Let \(A\) be a directed dg graph category, with pure state subcategories \(A_i\) and all its original several-transition products. There are no backwards cross arrows. Let \(B\) be the corresponding target category, and fix the actual strict pure functors \(q_i:A_i\to B_i\subset B\). Let \(M\) be the whole \((B,A)\)-bimodule of the given comparison prism.

For its restriction \(M_i\) in the source pure state put \[ R_i(y,x)=B(q_i x,y). \] Suppose an actual quasi-isomorphism between \(R_i\) and \(M_i\) is specified in the dg category of full \((B,A_i)\)-bimodules. This includes every pure-source bar component. An objectwise equivalence of left \(B\)-modules alone is not this hypothesis. All cofree modules and homotopies retain both outside pure actions and their full normalized bar components.

Theorem C.54.1.1. Under these hypotheses the recovered full enhanced functor \(F:A\to B\) can be chosen with restriction exactly \(q_i\) on every pure state. Its action equivalence to \(M\) retains the specified full pure bimodule equivalences. Its cross components are obtained by transferring the entire mixed action, with all several-transition components included. When a native coherent cell is interpreted using these same module equivalences and contractions, its restriction agrees with the restriction of this recovery; it is not an independently chosen comparison.

Proof. Work first in the dg category of full \((B,A_i)\)-bimodules, separately for each state. Invert a stipulated quasi-isomorphism there using C.50.1's mapping-cylinder construction and the full cofree kernel perturbation of C.45.2. For clarity one can arrange a strict normalized retraction to the exact prescribed model \(R_i\) after a harmless module cylinder enlargement. If \(p_i:M_i\to R_i\) is the resulting full quasi-isomorphism, use \[ L_i=M_i\oplus\operatorname{Cone}(1_{R_i})[-1], \qquad p_i'(m,a,b)=p_i(m)+b. \] This is the cofree mapping cylinder; when \(p_i\) has higher components, its projection has those same full components. Its central projection is surjective and its kernel is acyclic. The fixed-projection kernel argument gives actual full bimodule maps and homotopy \[ I_i:R_i\to L_i,\quad P_i:L_i\to R_i,\quad H_i, \qquad P_iI_i=1,\quad\partial H_i=1-I_iP_i, \] with \(H_i^2=P_iH_i=H_iI_i=0\). Every correction consumes outside bar letters, so the series is finite on each word. This is the full bimodule kernel proof, not a splitting only of the underlying vector spaces. The projection \(L_i\to M_i\) and its cylinder inclusion also have their actual normalized pure-bimodule contraction.

Extend the entire mixed \(A\)-action from \(M\) to \(L\) through that cylinder inclusion and projection. On every action involving a cross input, insert the projection on its incoming module end and the inclusion on its outgoing end. Their projection-inclusion composite is the identity on \(M_i\). Thus two adjacent mixed actions have exactly the original composite. The cylinder's own pure actions remain unchanged. The full mixed identities follow term by term from the original action identities and the fact that these are maps of both pure actions.

Now transfer only the mixed action along \((I_i,P_i,H_i)\). Absorb all pure actions and their unary differential in the underlying full \((B,A_i)\)-module structures. For a mixed source word partition its cross positions into nonempty consecutive blocks. Apply its original whole mixed-action component on each block, insert \(H\) between two successive block outputs, and apply \(I\) and \(P\) on the two ends. The outside pure bar inputs are included in these full bimodule maps, with their cofree tensor evaluation signs.

The proof of the complete action transfer in C.50.1 applies with these full pure-module complexes as its coefficient mapping complexes. Moving the differential past an inserted \(H\) gives \(1-IP\). Its identity terms cancel the adjacent original source-action terms, and its \(IP\) terms are the two transferred target-action blocks. The remaining terms are the original whole mixed-action identity. This checks every consecutive block and hence the complete action equation. The finite directed height bounds the number of cross positions; the cofree pure corrections were already finite wordwise. All sums are therefore finite on each original input.

On a pure word there is no mixed action to transfer. Its action is the already assigned \((B,A_i)\)-action on \(R_i\), which is exactly the represented action of \(q_i\). This is why no later independent pure-state replacement, with potentially different higher homotopies, is needed. Source coefficient identities act by the original true module identities; normalization retains them.

Recover the target \(B\) by the full represented Yoneda evaluation of C.50.1, with its opposite direction as stated there. Its section is strict Yoneda composition, and its normalized homotopy annihilates that section. On a pure word all the input maps are precisely the Yoneda images of \(q_i\). The first evaluation returns \(q_i\); every higher transfer tree contains a homotopy on a composed section value and is zero. Thus the recovered target is the original dg \(B\) and the pure functor is exactly \(q_i\), including all its prescribed normalized components. Mixed words retain their full transferred values.

Finally, restriction of these formulas to a chosen native cell uses the same original action components, the same module maps and the same contractions. Its consecutive partitions and their signs are the same ones. The full natural-transformation evaluation of C.53.1 is this restricted action formula. Therefore interpreting that cell through these stipulated data gives the actual restriction of the whole recovery. The entire action equivalence is the one produced by the same transfer, and its pure part is the retained bimodule equivalence. This proves the assertion without inferring relative pure compatibility from equality on objects or on cohomology. \(\square\)

C.54.2. The native exact-core comparison

Use the calibrated comparison prism of C48–C50. Its desired strict pure state functors are \[ q_i=\Omega B\bigl((\Omega g)^{\otimes n_i}\otimes1_{kI}\bigr). \] The single \(g\) and these literal powers are fixed before recovery. All target graph levels, actual parameter tags and several-transition strings are retained in \(B\).

Proposition C.54.2.1. The full pure bimodule equivalences in Section C.54.1 are supplied by this prism, so its whole endpoint recovery can be made relative to these exact \(q_i\)'s. Its canonical common-core comparison therefore has the exact powers \(g^{\otimes n_i}\otimes1_{D_I}\). A comparison of a chosen native block module, interpreted with this same recovery data, is the actual one-cross restriction of this full comparison, before any independent product projection normalization.

Proof. At a source object \(x\) the actual comparison parameter arrow gives the representing map of C.50.2. Its pure-source higher components are the original coherent state comparison, not a chosen objectwise extension. Record all those components by the full represented evaluation of C.33.2 and C.53.1. Its pure-source naturality equation is exactly the right \(A_i\)-module equation, including all source-word components. Its left \(B\)-module equation is the actual represented composition equation. Thus it is a genuine \((B,A_i)\)-bimodule map between \(R_i\) and the restriction of the entire prism module.

Its central map is the composition with the actual parameter arrow. Under the canonical counits it is precomposition by the given state equivalence, whose coherent inverse gives the two mapping-complex homotopies. C.50.2 proves the resulting central quasi-isomorphisms on every allowed target string. The cofree kernel argument then gives the full pure-bimodule equivalence, retaining all its action components. The stated hypothesis of Section C.54.1 is therefore fulfilled by actual prism data, not by an assumed contractible transformation space.

Apply the relative recovery. It retains the displayed strict pure functors, so C.43.1's strict naturality of the canonical common-input maps gives exactly the displayed common-core powers. Pull back the whole bar comparison by C.40.1's consecutive-cut construction; its chain defect vanishes at the central projection and on the pure parts, so coderivation uniqueness proves the full chain equation as in C.50.3. Every several-transition component is still included.

To interpret a native block, restrict the original full prism action and use the same pure-bimodule cylinder maps, contractions and Yoneda evaluation. The first theorem's restriction assertion makes this the literal one-cross restriction of the constructed full comparison. No unrelated core or input-corner equivalence has been introduced. This proves the claim. \(\square\)

C.54.3. The explicit homotopy to the product lift

Let \(T:Z\to Z'\) now be an actual one-cross restriction of the whole recovered comparison. Let \(\phi:Z\to W\), \(\phi':Z'\to W'\) be the C52 product projections, with sections \(i,i'\) and normalized homotopies \[ \partial h=1-i\phi,\qquad \partial h'=1-i'\phi'. \] All these equations are in the full bicomodule Hom complexes. Set \(\tau=\phi'Ti\). Interpret the original native product coherence cell using these same recovery data, and let \(\partial R_0=\tau-u\) be its actual homotopy of C53, where \(u\) is the shifted product of the individual comparisons.

Theorem C.54.3.1. The map \(T^{\rm prod}=i'u\phi\) has the exact product projection square. There is an actual full homotopy \[ \begin{aligned} K={}&-h'T-i'\phi'Th-i'R_0\phi,\\ \partial K={}&T^{\rm prod}-T. \end{aligned} \] The unnormalized whole restriction itself has raw square homotopy \[ R=\phi'Th+R_0\phi,\qquad \partial R=\phi'T-u\phi. \] These formulas retain all compatible full faces. After the actual one-cross minimal transfers, they give the homotopy required by the whole-graph gauge theorem C.51.3.1.

Proof. Every displayed map other than a homotopy is closed and of degree zero. Thus \[ \begin{aligned} \partial R &=\phi'T(1-i\phi)+(\tau-u)\phi\\ &=\phi'T-u\phi, \end{aligned} \] using \(\tau=\phi'Ti\). Similarly \[ \begin{aligned} \partial K &=-(1-i'\phi')T-i'\phi'T(1-i\phi) -i'(\tau-u)\phi\\ &=i'u\phi-T. \end{aligned} \] The three intermediate \(i'\phi'T\) and \(i'\tau\phi\) terms cancel exactly. These are complete module equations, so all pure inputs and higher action components have been retained. Also \(\phi'T^{\rm prod}=u\phi\), since \(\phi'i'=1\).

Compose \(K\) with the chosen chain inclusion and projection of the minimal one-cross models on its two ends. Its Hom differential is the corresponding difference of their two transferred comparison maps. Their bare leading cohomology maps are the calibrated identity; their finite cofree inverses therefore exist. The hypotheses of C.51.3.1 for this prescribed one-cross change are exactly met. That theorem extends its correction through every several-transition component of the minimal whole graph. It requires compatible supplied values on every simultaneous prescribed sector; this calculation does not remove that requirement.

Full face restriction commutes with every composite and with the same fixed-projection SDRs. Consequently \(K,R\), their transfers and the resulting individual-sector gauge have the claimed restrictions. \(\square\)

C.54.4. Replace edges in the whole coherent parameter family

Let \(F:\Omega B(kI)\to\mathcal E\) record the given entire coherent module family, for a finite directed parameter category \(I\). The objects \(X_i=F(i)\) and their full module differentials are fixed. For every original nonidentity arrow \(\alpha:i\to j\), suppose \(f_\alpha=F(\alpha)\) is to be replaced by a closed map \(g_\alpha:X_i\to X_j\), with a specified full degree-minus-one module homotopy \[ \partial K_\alpha=g_\alpha-f_\alpha. \] On unchanged arrows put \(K_\alpha=0\). The assignments include the actual arrow labels, including parallel arrows. On full parameter faces they are restrictions of the same assignments.

Theorem C.54.4.1. There is an entire unital dg functor \(G:\Omega B(kI)\to\mathcal E\), with the same objects and the prescribed \(g_\alpha\) on every original arrow. It comes with an actual resolved path equivalence from \(F\), whose object components are the identities. Every higher parameter generator is retained. The construction is canonical from the stated data and the fixed bar convention, is finite on each word, and commutes with full parameter-face restriction. It retains an entire previously assigned subfamily on which every \(K_\alpha\) is zero by taking the constant path lift on that subfamily.

Proof. Use the object paths \(1_{X_i}\) in \(\operatorname{Path}(\mathcal E)\). Their mapping projection kernel has differential and normalized contraction \[ d_K(g,a)=(\partial g,-\partial a-g),\qquad k(g,a)=(-a,0). \] These are Lemma C.53.4.1 with \(i=p=1\), \(h=0\), and one can also verify them directly: the first component of \(d_Kk+kd_K\) is \(-\partial a+\partial a+g=g\), the second is \(a\), and \(k^2=0\).

On the one-arrow generator set its path value to \[ \mathscr H(\alpha)=(f_\alpha,g_\alpha,-K_\alpha). \] It is closed because the third differential is \(\partial K_\alpha+f_\alpha-g_\alpha=0\). The object identity maps to \((1,1,0)\). Induct on the original length of a higher generator \(x\). The entire value of \(\mathscr H(dx)\) has already been assigned, since each merge and proper split uses shorter strings. Put \[ v=(F(x),0,0),\quad o=Dv-\mathscr H(dx),\quad \mathscr H(x)=v-ko. \] Exactly as in Theorem C.53.5.1, the defect is closed and belongs to the kernel of the first projection. Thus its corrected differential is \(\mathscr H(dx)\), and its first projection is still \(F(x)\). Free multiplicative extension gives the dg functor on every original word. Projection to the second component is the asserted entire \(G\). No new primitive is chosen in this formula: the kernel contraction is the fixed \((-a,0)\). Its third component on every generator of length at least two is zero, although its third components on products are the full signed path products and need not be zero.

Every formula uses the original labels and shorter subwords. Restricting to a full face therefore performs exactly the same recursion. More generally an assigned differential-stable union of face generators is retained by using those values and correcting only the other generators. If all its edge homotopies are zero, take its whole constant lift \((F,F,0)\). On its higher generators the displayed recursion gives that same value: its already assigned differential has third component zero, while \(Dv\)'s third component is \(F(x)\), so \(v-ko=(F(x),F(x),0)\). Thus the constant subfamily is retained.

The finite directed height bounds every original strict-arrow string. Along an increasing compatible family of finite corners the same formulas retain every earlier value. The path object components are identities, so the resulting entire path family is an enhanced equivalence. This proves the result in the actual full module Hom complexes, without any assertion that arbitrary transformation spaces are contractible. \(\square\)

For a triangle \(0<1<2\), write its original edges as \(a,b,c\) and its degree-minus-one generator image as \(H\), with \(\partial H=ba-c\). The formula gives exactly \[ H'=H+K_ba+b'K_a-K_c, \qquad \partial H'=b'a'-c'. \] This is Lemma C.53.2.1's full boundary replacement, including the term \((\partial K_b)K_a\) inside \(b'K_a\). Thus the higher-word recursion extends the actual triangle formula, with its original signs.

C.54.5. Normalize the chosen raw product squares coherently

Take the chosen raw native product models and the full supplied coherence family of C53. For a selected product-comparison edge write its current map as \(t=i'_{\phi}\tau\phi\) and its desired product map as \(t^{\rm prod}=i'_{\phi}u\phi\). Here \(u\) is the actual once-suspended tensor of the individual comparisons. Theorem C.53.3.1 constructs the actual degree-minus-one homotopy \[ K=-i'_{\phi}R_0\phi,\qquad \partial K=t^{\rm prod}-t. \]

Corollary C.54.5.1. For any finite compatible collection of these edges within the actual module-valued parameter family, the original coherent family admits a replacement whose selected edges are exactly their product maps and whose objects and outside core powers are unchanged. All its higher parameter cells are included, with the same full-face restrictions. Untouched full subfamilies may be kept exactly. The normalized product square \(\phi't^{\rm prod}=u\phi\) is an exact full module equation on every selected product domain.

Proof. Express the module category over the fixed outside cores by transporting through the one previously fixed \(g\), as in C53. The displayed \(K\)'s are actual module homotopies in that dg category. Their compatible face values are the ones provided by the same original native cell and its C52 fixed-projection data. Apply Section C.54.4 with these \(K\)'s on the selected edges and zero on unchanged edges. Its entire path construction keeps the objects and all outside core maps, changes the edge to \(t+\partial K=t^{\rm prod}\), and assigns all the higher parameter generators. Its relative statement keeps every stipulated untouched full subfamily. The exact square follows from \(\phi'i'_{\phi}=1\), giving \(\phi't^{\rm prod}=\phi'i'_{\phi}u\phi=u\phi\). These are complete module equations, including all consumed-core components. No several-transition operation of a nested path graph has been projected away or inferred from this parameter-family statement. \(\square\)

C.54.6. Solved examples

Exercise C.54.6.1 (intermediate). Let \(X\) have basis \(e,x\) in degree zero and \(y\) in degree one, with \(dx=y\). Put \(h(y)=x\), all other values zero, and let \(E=dh+hd\). Start with the identity-valued strict triangle on three copies of \(X\). Replace its first two edges by \(a'=b'=1+E\), keep its direct edge \(c'=1\), and use edge homotopies \(K_a=K_b=h\), \(K_c=0\). Compute the new two-simplex and its differential. Identify the term lost by using the old edge \(b\) in place of \(b'\) in its formula.

Solution. The operator \(E\) is the identity on \(x,y\) and zero on \(e\). Hence \(E^2=E\), \(Eh=h\), and \(E\) is closed. The new edges are chain isomorphisms: they act by one on \(e\) and by two on \(x,y\). Each edge difference is \(\partial h=E\). Theorem C.54.4.1 gives \[ H'=h+(1+E)h=3h. \] Its differential is \(3E\), which is exactly \[ b'a'-c'=(1+E)^2-1=3E. \] Using the old \(b=1\) would give \(2h\), with differential \(2E\), leaving defect \(-E\ne0\). The missing term is \((\partial K_b)K_a=Eh=h\). Thus both edge changes must be retained when computing the coherent triangle.

Exercise C.54.6.2 (advanced). Use the algebraic example \(R=k[t]/(t^2)\), with \(|t|=0\). Let \[ N=Re\oplus Rf\oplus Rx\oplus Ry, \quad |e|=|y|=0,\quad |f|=|x|=-1,\quad dx=y, \] with all other differentials zero, and put \(V=Re\oplus Rf\) with zero differential. Make three \(R\)-linear retracts from \(N\) to \(V\) as follows. The middle one has its ordinary inclusion and projection and homotopy \(h_1(y)=x\). For the first take \(I_0(e)=e+ty\), \(I_0(f)=f\), the ordinary projection \(P_0\), and \(h_0(y)=x\), \(h_0(e)=-tx\). For the last take the ordinary inclusion \(I_2\), the projection \(P_2(x)=-f\), \(P_2(e)=e\), \(P_2(f)=f\), \(P_2(y)=0\), and \(h_2(y)=x+f\). Unspecified homotopy values are zero. Check these retracts and transport the identity triangle on \(N\). What is its higher component, and what happens to the pure \(R\)-action?

Solution. The compositions \(P_iI_i\) are the identity on \(e,f\). On the first model, \((1-I_0P_0)(e)=-ty\) and \((dh_0+h_0d)(e)=-ty\); on \(x,y\) both sides are the identity and on \(f\) both are zero. On the last model, \((1-I_2P_2)(x)=x+f=h_2(dx)\), while both sides send \(y\) to \(y\) and kill \(e,f\). The middle identities are the ordinary acyclic-pair contraction. These computations also give \(h_i^2=P_ih_i=h_iI_i=0\) on each basis vector.

All three maps and homotopies are \(R\)-linear. Thus for every pure word length \(r\ge0\), \[ P_i t^r I_i=t^r,\qquad h_i t^r I_i=0. \] The entire pure action is retained exactly, and the transfer terms with an internal homotopy on a pure input are zero. All three compressed triangle edges are the identity on \(V\). Its higher component is \(H'=-P_2h_1I_0\). Directly, \[ H'(e)=-P_2h_1(e+ty)=-P_2(tx)=tf, \qquad H'(f)=0. \] It is a nonzero degree-minus-one closed map, as required by the zero triangle defect on \(V\). Its pure \(t\)-linearity is also exact. This finite algebraic module example illustrates relative recovery; it is not an identification of \(R\) with a geometric IC endomorphism algebra. Fixing the pure actions does not discard mixed higher components.

Theorems C.54.1.1–C.54.3.1 prove relative recovery,the native exact-core application and the full product homotopy. Theorem C.54.4.1 and Corollary C.54.5.1 replace edges throughout the coherent parameter family. Exercises C.54.6.1–C.54.6.2 compute the triangle cross term and a nonzero higher action with the pure algebra action retained. Editable SVG source.

C.55. Central shuffle retractions and simultaneous linear prescriptions

An extension of a central Taylor map need not be a reverse coalgebra map. We construct an ordered chain retraction of the actual relative parameter shuffle,prove its exact regrouping and interchange laws,and use it before the central projection in a cofree module. This gives an explicit way to verify all linear relations in a sum of product-shuffle domains when their prescribed values have the stated retraction form.

The shuffle and Alexander–Whitney setting is discussed in Boris Shoikhet, A bialgebra axiom and the Dold–Kan correspondence,arXiv:1109.5441v2, Sections2.1–2.2. The relative bars here omit outer endpoint faces;the proofs below establish their formulas and all signs directly. This gives a sufficient compatibility criterion for the native gauge application. The relative extension in Section C.56 permits homotopy primitives to be adjusted without imposing this original retraction form.

C.55.1. An ordered chain retraction on the relative bars

For finite directed categories \(I_1,\ldots,I_m\), set \(D_i=B_{S_i}(kI_i)\), \(D=B_S(k\prod_iI_i)\). A reduced ordinary arrow in the product has a nonempty support: the coordinates where its actual arrow is nonidentity. Its bar suspension is odd of degree minus one. Every arrow and its actual parallel-arrow label is retained. Write words in target-to-source order as before.

Define a graded map \(r_m:D\to\bigotimes_iD_i\) as follows. It kills a word containing an arrow supported in two or more coordinates. It also kills a word whose single-coordinate labels are not weakly increasing in target-to-source order. On a remaining word, group its original letters in coordinate order and return the tuple of its factor bar words, with coefficient one. Empty factor words retain their actual vertex identities. An entirely empty word maps to the tuple of those identities. There is no arbitrary deletion of a parameter vertex in this definition: each retained factor word is its actual coordinate projection.

Theorem C.55.1.1. The map \(r_m\) is an endpoint-preserving chain map and is a left inverse to the actual shuffle \(j_m:\bigotimes_iD_i\to D\). Its iterated projections regroup strictly for every ordered partition of the factors. For an ordered partition \(\pi\) into consecutive blocks, write \(j_\pi\) for the shuffle of their product-category bars. Then \[ r_m j_\pi=\bigotimes_{B\in\pi}r_B, \] with the literal ordered regrouping on the right. These are linear chain maps; \(r_m\) is generally not a coalgebra map.

Proof. There is no internal unary differential on the ordinary index arrows. The bar differential only merges adjacent actual arrows, with its original suspended sign. Nonidentity arrows form an augmentation ideal in each directed category: a nonzero composable product is again nonidentity. Thus a word with a mixed-support arrow remains mixed under every merge involving it, or gives zero. Every other merge leaves that arrow present. Its image under \(r_m\) and the image of its differential are both zero.

Next take a word containing an inversion of its coordinate labels. A same-coordinate merge leaves an inversion unless its product is zero; a distinct-coordinate merge makes a mixed-support arrow. Thus this kernel type is also preserved by the differential. Finally, on a word whose coordinate labels are ordered, merges within a factor block have exactly that factor's bar differential sign, multiplied by the parity of the preceding factor word lengths. Those are precisely the tensor differential signs on \(\bigotimes_iD_i\). Merging at a block boundary creates a mixed-support arrow and is killed. This proves the full chain equation, including every type of adjacent merge.

In a shuffle of factor words, exactly one interleaving is in increasing coordinate order. It is the original concatenation of the ordered factor words, so its Koszul sign is plus one. Every other interleaving contains an inversion and is killed. Its retained factor projections are the original factor words. Hence \(r_mj_m=1\), including all empty-word and actual object cases.

For an iterated ordered projection to be nonzero, its arrows must each lie in one final factor and its labels must be ordered between blocks and within each block. This is exactly the single global increasing-label condition. The surviving factor words and signs are identical. This proves strict regrouping. For \(r_mj_\pi\), if a block input fails its own ordered projection, every shuffle output fails the global one. Otherwise only the interleaving keeping the consecutive blocks in their original order survives, with sign one. This gives the stated formula.

For the coalgebra limitation, take two nonempty one-letter factor words \(a,b\). The canonical concatenated product bar word has image \(a\otimes b\). The coproduct of this tensor contains both middle cuts, including the one with the second-factor letter on the left and the first-factor letter on the right, with their odd interchange sign. The original concatenated word has only its one original middle cut. Its projected coproduct therefore lacks the other nonzero tensor term. The two terms have different factor/endpoint labels, so cannot cancel. This proves that \(r_m\) need not preserve the coproduct. \(\square\)

C.55.2. The exact signed four-factor interchange

For four ordered index factors use the coordinate permutation \((I,J,K,L)\mapsto(I,K,J,L)\). There are two linear chain maps from \(D_{I\times J}\otimes D_{K\times L}\) to \(D_{I\times K}\otimes D_{J\times L}\): first shuffle, permute coordinates and apply the two-block retraction; or first apply the two input retractions, interchange the middle two factors with their Koszul sign, and shuffle within the resulting two output groups.

Theorem C.55.2.1. These two maps are equal, with every actual arrow label and suspended sign retained.

Proof. If an input word contains an arrow changing both of its coordinates, the first composite always has a mixed-support arrow between its two final output groups and is killed. The second composite is killed by the corresponding input retraction. If an input word has its two coordinate labels in the wrong order, any shuffle preserves that original order. The offending second-group letter still precedes the first-group letter, so the final retraction kills it. The other composite is again zero. These cases exhaust input words killed by either input retraction.

It remains to consider ordered input words with lengths \(a,b\) in their \(I,J\) blocks and \(c,d\) in their \(K,L\) blocks. A shuffled word survives the final retraction precisely when all its \(I,K\) letters precede all its \(J,L\) letters. Its choices are exactly an \((a,c)\)-shuffle in the first output group and an \((b,d)\)-shuffle in the second. This is a bijection of terms with the two separate shuffles in the other composite, preserving each actual arrow and its endpoints.

The global shuffle sign has the signs of those two shuffles, together with the sign for moving every \(K\)-letter across every \(J\)-letter. All these letters are odd, so the latter is \((-1)^{bc}\). This is exactly the tensor Koszul sign interchanging the two middle bar words in the second composite. Thus the coefficients of each matching term agree. Empty blocks give the same argument with the relevant exponent zero. This proves the identity on every input basis word and hence linearly. It is an identity for the actual relative bars, proved without using outer simplicial faces. \(\square\)

The retraction preserves full factor faces, since its retained factor words use only the original coordinate vertices. For an arbitrary full subcategory of the product, its output need not belong to the safe rectangle domain of C.52.4. In the square, a three-vertex face can contain the canonical two-step word while omitting the other corner. Its retraction is the two-letter factor tensor, whose full shuffle visits that omitted corner as well. Thus a reverse map of entire full-face coalgebras has not been constructed.

C.55.3. A central extension respecting the whole sum of product domains

Use an actual once-suspended product one-cross module of C41/C52. Its bare central mapping block is the prescribed tensor of its individual mapping blocks; its outside IC cores already retain their ordered factor decomposition. Suppose the outside index cores are global product bars. On the underlying graded cofree module apply the ordered retraction to each outside index run, keep the central tensor identification, and perform the C41 Koszul regrouping. Call the resulting graded linear map \(\mathcal R\). The actual module shuffle embedding \(\mathcal J\) has \(\mathcal R\mathcal J=1\). No assertion that \(\mathcal R\) commutes with the full module action differential or its coactions is needed or made.

Proposition C.55.3.1. For a homogeneous central Taylor map \(c\), retaining endpoint and string labels, on the finest factor product model, \(\widetilde c=c\mathcal R\) is a homogeneous linear extension of its central values to the global indexed model. Its full cofree extension is a bicomodule map, restricts to the prescribed map on the actual product-shuffle submodel, and preserves every full parameter face through its central endpoints. For an ordered partition \(\pi\), if the prescribed coarser central values are precisely \[ c_\pi=c\Bigl(\bigotimes_{B\in\pi}\mathcal R_B\Bigr), \] then this single extension satisfies all those prescriptions at once. In particular they define a well-defined linear map on their actual sum, including any relations not detected by pairwise intersections.

Proof. The retraction identity in Section C.55.1 applied to the two outside runs, followed by the inverse fixed regrouping, proves \(\mathcal R\mathcal J=1\). Hence the central restriction of \(c\mathcal R\) is exactly \(c\). Reconstruct the full homogeneous bicomodule map by equation(C.39.5), including its degree evaluation sign. Both it and the original product map followed by the shuffle embedding have the same outside core maps and central Taylor values. The cofree uniqueness proof C.39.2 makes their restrictions equal on the entire product submodel, not only on bare central inputs.

On a full parameter face, every outside cut remains in that face and the central output has the endpoints of the consumed original input. Those endpoints lie in the face, whose bare central block is the full block at those endpoints. C.52.5 therefore proves that the reconstructed map preserves that face, even when \(\mathcal R\) itself does not take it into a safe rectangle. The retraction was used only before the central projection; no forbidden outside word is reconstructed.

For each ordered partition, Section C.55.1's exact identity \(r_mj_\pi=\bigotimes r_B\), on both outside runs, gives the corresponding identity for \(\mathcal R\) and that partition's module shuffle. Consequently \(\widetilde c\) restricts to exactly the stated \(c_\pi\). As all these values are restrictions of one linear map, every relation in the sum of the prescribed input subspaces is automatically respected. This supplies the asserted actual-sum certificate. Section C.55.2 gives its additional exact interchange identity when two ordered groups of factor cores are exchanged and shuffled. \(\square\)

C.55.4. Solved examples

Exercise C.55.4.1 (intermediate). In the product of two copies of \([1]\),let \(A_{\rm top}:01\to11\), \(A_{\rm bottom}:00\to10\), \(B_{\rm left}:00\to01\), \(B_{\rm right}:10\to11\). Put \(w=sA_{\rm top}|sB_{\rm left}\). Compute its ordered retraction and the defect of its coproduct equation. Let \(J\) be the full face on \(00,01,11\). Does the retracted tensor have a full shuffle in \(D_J\)?

Solution. Let \(a,b\) be the one-letter factor bars. Both have degree minus one,and the word has its factor labels in the prescribed order. Thus \(r_2(w)=a\otimes b\). In addition to its two outer cuts,the tensor coproduct has middle terms \[ \begin{aligned} &(a\otimes1_1)\otimes(1_0\otimes b)\\ &\quad-(1_1\otimes b)\otimes(a\otimes1_0). \end{aligned} \] The original word has only its middle cut \(sA_{\rm top}\otimes sB_{\rm left}\),whose retracted image is the first displayed term. Consequently \[ \begin{aligned} \Delta r_2(w)&-(r_2\otimes r_2)\Delta w\\ & =-(1_1\otimes b)\otimes(a\otimes1_0)\ne0. \end{aligned} \] The tensor endpoints identify its factors with the missing cut \(-sB_{\rm right}\otimes sA_{\rm bottom}\). The minus sign is the interchange of the two odd bar letters. Hence the ordered retraction is not a coalgebra map.

The shuffle of \(a\otimes b\) is \(sA_{\rm top}|sB_{\rm left}-sB_{\rm right}|sA_{\rm bottom}\). Its second word visits \(10\),which is absent from \(J\). Thus \(w\in D_J\) does not imply that its retracted tensor belongs to the safe rectangle domain of Theorem C.52.4.1. This is why the retraction is used at the central Taylor map before the outside coactions are reconstructed.

Exercise C.55.4.2 (intermediate). Take three one-letter odd factor bars \(a,b,c\) from three copies of \([1]\),and use target-to-source word order. Let a homogeneous central coordinate have value \(\lambda\) on \(a\otimes b\otimes c\). Extend it by the ordered retraction. Compute its values on the six interleavings. Check that the two ordered regroupings \((ab)|c\) and \(a|(bc)\) give the same value on the full three-factor shuffle.

Solution. Write \(ABC\) for the word in that coordinate order, with the actual coordinate arrows at the uniquely determined intermediate vertices;use the analogous notation for its other interleavings. Only \(ABC\) survives \(r_3\). Thus the extended central map has value \(\lambda\) there and zero on the other five words. The full signed shuffle is \[ \begin{aligned} &ABC-ACB-BAC\\ &\quad+BCA+CAB-CBA. \end{aligned} \] Its value is therefore \(\lambda\). To check the actual regrouping relation,let \(AB,BA\) be the two words in the first product bar. Their shuffles with \(C\) are \[ \begin{aligned} (AB)\mathbin{\mathrm{sh}}C&=ABC-ACB+CAB,\\ (BA)\mathbin{\mathrm{sh}}C&=BAC-BCA+CBA. \end{aligned} \] Their difference is the displayed full shuffle,and their central values are \(\lambda,0\). For the other grouping, \[ \begin{aligned} A\mathbin{\mathrm{sh}}(BC)&=ABC-BAC+BCA,\\ A\mathbin{\mathrm{sh}}(CB)&=ACB-CAB+CBA. \end{aligned} \] Again their difference is the same full shuffle,and their values are \(\lambda,0\). Thus the two product-domain expressions satisfy the same actual signed linear relation after extension. Each sign is the parity of the permutation of the original three odd letters. This is a concrete instance of the whole-sum certificate in Proposition C.55.3.1.

Theorems C.55.1.1–C.55.2.1 prove the ordered retraction,regrouping and full signed interchange. Proposition C.55.3.1 extends compatible central prescriptions on their actual sum. Exercises C.55.4.1–C.55.4.2 compute the missing coproduct cut and the common three-factor shuffle relation. The retraction is used before the central projection;it is not a reverse coalgebra map. Editable SVG source.

C.56. Commuting shuffle cuts and full relative extension

Ordered product domains admit simultaneous linear extension because their actual cut projections commute. Their common decomposition also supplies an acyclic relative quotient. Passing to the full cofree module requires its complete action differential; a finite perturbation contracts that relative Taylor kernel. The resulting extension theorem permits actual homotopy primitives to be adjusted and glued on product intersections. Its native application requires the specified chain submodels and compatible closed product maps.

C.56.1. The ordered cut projections commute

Let \(D=D_{I_1\times\cdots\times I_m}\), with the same finite directed index categories as C55. For a cut \(c\in\{1,\ldots,m-1\}\) write \[ P_c=j_c r_c:D\to D, \] where the two blocks are the factors before and after that cut, and the shuffle and ordered retraction are the actual C55 chain maps. For a set of cuts \(T\), let \(\pi_T\) be its ordered interval partition and put \(P_T=j_{\pi_T}r_{\pi_T}\), with \(P_\varnothing=1\).

Theorem C.56.1.1 (the exact cut-projection algebra). These are chain idempotents and satisfy \[ P_TP_U=P_{T\cup U}=P_UP_T. \] Consequently their images have the common decomposition \[ \begin{aligned} D&=\bigoplus_{E\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m-1\}}D_E,\\ D_E&=\operatorname{im}\left( \prod_{c\in E}P_c\prod_{c\notin E}(1-P_c)\right),\\ \operatorname{im}P_T&=\bigoplus_{E\supseteq T}D_E. \end{aligned} \] Their finite sums and intersections therefore form a distributive lattice of subcomplexes. In particular a sum of product-shuffle domains contains no additional unresolved linear relation once its maps agree on all their pairwise intersections.

Proof. Each \(r_cj_c=1\) by C.55.1, so \(P_c^2=P_c\). Take two cuts \(c<d\), and combine the factors into the three consecutive blocks \(A,B,C\). C.55.2 with the fourth factor the coefficient unit gives the exact identity \[ r_{A,BC}j_{AB,C} =(1_A\otimes j_{B,C})(r_{A,B}\otimes1_C). \] Both sides keep all original endpoints; the unit bar contributes only its degree-zero coaugmentation. Multiply on the left by \(j_{A,BC}\) and on the right by \(r_{AB,C}\). Strict shuffle associativity and ordered retraction regrouping then give \[ P_cP_d=j_{A,B,C}r_{A,B,C}. \] Using the other unit placement in C.55.2 gives \(P_dP_c=j_{A,B,C}r_{A,B,C}\) as well. This proves commutativity and the formula for two cuts, including their full suspended signs.

Insert the remaining cuts one at a time. The same identity splits the one current block containing the new cut; associativity and regrouping leave the other blocks unchanged. Induction gives \(P_T=\prod_{c\in T}P_c\) and hence the asserted multiplication law. These are chain maps because all the original factors are.

For commuting idempotents the displayed products selecting an eigenvalue zero or one at every cut are themselves idempotents. Two different choices have a factor \(P_c(1-P_c)=0\), so their images are disjoint. Expanding \(\prod_c(P_c+(1-P_c))=1\) gives their sum as the identity. This proves the direct-sum decomposition in the actual chain complexes. Each \(P_T\) acts by one exactly on the indicated summands. Sums and intersections are therefore unions and intersections of these common summand sets, proving distributivity.

On a common summand belonging to two prescribed images, agreement on their pairwise intersection makes their linear values identical. Assign that value on each summand included in the sum, and extend linearly. This proves the stated gluing assertion for any finite family. It is a consequence of the proved common decomposition, not an assumption about arbitrary arrangements of subspaces. \(\square\)

C.56.2. One contraction can retain every ordered product domain

Let \(C_0=\{1,\ldots,m-1\}\) be the full cut set. The finest product shuffle is \(j_{C_0}:\bigotimes_iD_{I_i}\to D\). It is a quasi-isomorphism by the actual finite-height shuffle proof C.42.1, or C.39.3 after the even height regrading of C.52.1.

Theorem C.56.2.1 (a common normalized index-bar contraction). There is a normalized contraction \[ \left(j_{C_0},r_{C_0},H\right): D\rightleftarrows\bigotimes_iD_{I_i}, \] with \[ dH+Hd=1-P_{C_0},\quad H^2=r_{C_0}H=Hj_{C_0}=0, \qquad HP_T=P_TH \] for every ordered cut set \(T\). The choices can retain a finite family of full factor faces and an increasing compatible system of finite factor corners. They are made blockwise at fixed endpoints and height jump. No preservation of an arbitrary nonrectangular full product face is asserted for this outside-bar homotopy.

Proof. Every cut shuffle is a quasi-isomorphism and has its chain left inverse, so each \(P_c\) induces the identity on \(H^\bullet D\). For a summand \(D_E\) with \(E\ne C_0\), choose a cut not in \(E\). Its summand projector contains \(1-P_c\), which induces zero on cohomology. A chain idempotent splits the complex and its cohomology; hence this summand's cohomology is zero. It is split contractible over the field by C.30.1. Choose a normalized contraction on each of those acyclic summands and take their direct sum. Put zero on \(D_{C_0}=\operatorname{im}P_{C_0}\). This gives precisely \(dH+Hd=1-P_{C_0}\) and \(H^2=0\).

It commutes with every cut projector since each projector is scalar zero or one on each summand. Its range lies in the kernel of \(P_{C_0}\), giving \(r_{C_0}H=0\), and it vanishes on the finest image, giving \(Hj_{C_0}=0\). All summands retain the original endpoint and height blocks; choose their splittings there.

A full factor face is preserved by every shuffle and ordered retraction. Thus each of its summand parts is the image of the same summand projector on that face. These parts have distributive original-word support sums and intersections: the projector preserves each face, so its image on an intersection is the intersection of its images. Every finite intersection is a common factor face. The preceding acyclicity proof applies to each nonfinest summand on that face as well. The acyclic face-union and quotient-splitting construction of C.50.2 therefore extends the chosen contraction to each next face without changing its previous values. Do this separately in each summand and then take their sum. It retains commutation with the cut projectors. The same relative construction retains all earlier blocks in an increasing finite system. This proves the asserted face and corner statement. \(\square\)

C.56.3. The whole sum of product domains and its relative Hom kernel

Take a nonempty finite collection \(\mathcal T\) of cut sets and put \(U=\sum_{T\in\mathcal T}\operatorname{im}P_T\). Define \[ Q_U=1-\prod_{T\in\mathcal T}(1-P_T). \]

Theorem C.56.3.1 (acyclic product union and linear homotopy extension). The operator \(Q_U\) is a chain projector with image exactly \(U\), and \(U\hookrightarrow D\) is a quasi-isomorphism. Its quotient is split contractible, using the contraction in Theorem C.56.2.1. For any target complex \(V\), the kernel of restriction \(\operatorname{Hom}(D,V)\to\operatorname{Hom}(U,V)\) is contractible. Pairwise compatible chain maps on the product domains extend to a chain map on \(D\). If a closed global map \(L\) of degree zero has a specified degree-minus-one primitive \(K_U\) on \(U\), then \(K_U\) extends to a global primitive of \(L\).

Proof. On the common summand \(D_E\), the operator \(Q_U\) is one if any selected \(T\) is contained in \(E\), and zero otherwise. Thus it is exactly the projector onto the sum described in Theorem C.56.1.1. Every \(P_T\) induces the identity on cohomology; each factor \(1-P_T\) induces zero. Since the collection is nonempty, \(Q_U\) induces the identity. Its split image inclusion is therefore a quasi-isomorphism. The finest summand is contained in \(U\). The common contraction \(H\) preserves every selected image and therefore \(U\), and induces a normalized contraction of \(D/U\).

Write that quotient contraction as \(h_Q\). On a homogeneous degree-\(r\) map \(f:D/U\to V\), set \(\mathsf h(f)=(-1)^r f h_Q\). The Hom derivation calculation of C.53.4 gives \(\partial\mathsf h+\mathsf h\partial=1\) and \(\mathsf h^2=0\). This is exactly the restriction kernel, because its maps factor through \(D/U\). Thus it is contractible.

The gluing statement of Theorem C.56.1.1 gives one well-defined chain map \(f_U:U\to V\) from the pairwise compatible chain maps; its extension is simply \(f_UQ_U\). For the primitive statement put \(K_0=K_UQ_U\), so the closed defect \(e=L-\partial K_0\) vanishes on \(U\). It defines a closed degree-zero quotient map, whose primitive is \(e h_Q\). Pull that map back along the quotient and add it to \(K_0\). The result has differential \(L\) and restricts to \(K_U\). This proves the full relative extension assertion in the ordinary Hom complexes. \(\square\)

The ordinary Hom complex in Theorem C.56.3.1 is the leading coefficient complex for the later cofree module Taylor problem. Extending these conclusions to the full module differential requires retaining its source and target action terms; that extension is not replaced by the chain property of the ordered index retraction alone.

C.56.4. The precise full Taylor restriction problem

Use one cofree one-cross module \(Z=L\otimes sN\otimes A\) over common pure IC tensor cores with finite directed index bars. Fix an ordered list of \(m\) root factors. Its outside IC cores are the literal ordered tensor powers of the same minimal \(C\). Its index cores are bars of the corresponding product parameter categories. At each actual endpoint/central-label block the graded central space has the fixed root tensor identification. A cut projector acts on both outside index runs and is the identity on the central block and IC factor words. Thus its image is the graded product-shuffle submodel for that cut. Empty outside words retain their scalar object identities.

Assume each selected cut submodel is an actual chain subbicomodule along its outside shuffle maps, with the stated product differential. The full source differential preserves every such submodel. All their finite intersections have the corresponding refined product model. Let \(U\) be their nonempty finite sum. These are model hypotheses, not conclusions inferred solely from the index-bar calculation.

Let \(Z'\) be the full target cofree module, and fix its outside core comparison maps \(g_L,g_R\). They are the prescribed normalized common tensor powers, tensored with the index identities. In particular they commute with each actual product shuffle. A full homogeneous bicomodule map along those core maps is determined by its central Taylor map through the cofree formula, with the degree evaluation sign. Its differential is the complete Hom differential \(\partial F=d'F-(-1)^{|F|}F d\).

Theorem C.56.4.1 (contractible full Taylor restriction kernel). Under these hypotheses, the kernel of restriction of full Taylor maps from \(Z\) to \(U\) is contractible. Its contraction is finite on each original input word and retains the fixed endpoints,root labels and core maps. This includes all source and target module-action terms in the full Hom differential. It does not require the ordered index projections to be full module chain maps.

Proof. Work first with the differential \(\partial_0\) which retains the source and target central unary differentials and the internal index-bar differentials. The minimal IC core unary differentials are zero. All remaining pure IC and module-action terms will be retained as a perturbation below.

On the pair of outside index runs the graded cut projectors are the tensor products of their two cut projectors. They commute and multiply by union of cut sets, by the commuting-cut theorem. Their maps on cohomology are the identity, since each outside shuffle is a quasi-isomorphism and tensoring preserves it over the field. They commute with the central unary differential and are the identity on the IC factor words. The common-summand proof therefore gives a normalized contraction of the leading quotient by \(U\). Choose it at fixed outside endpoints,height jumps and IC word counts,and tensor it with the central coefficient complexes with their actual Koszul signs. Every nonretained summand is acyclic by that same identity-on-cohomology argument. Call the resulting quotient contraction \(h_Q\).

A Taylor map in the restriction kernel is a linear map out of this quotient with values in the target central block. On degree-\(r\) maps set \(\mathsf H_0(f)=(-1)^r f h_Q\). The explicit Hom calculation of C.53.4 gives \[ \partial_0\mathsf H_0+\mathsf H_0\partial_0=1, \qquad\mathsf H_0^2=0. \] This is a contraction of the actual leading Taylor restriction kernel. It preserves the original IC word count and outside index height.

Now write \(\partial=\partial_0+\delta\). The kernel is stable under \(\partial\): a full cofree map with zero central restriction vanishes on each source product submodel by its coactions;its differential vanishes there because that submodel is an actual chain submodule. The same holds for \(\partial_0\),so \(\delta\) also preserves the kernel.

For an original input define \[ R=\#\{\text{original outside IC bar letters}\} +\sum_{\text{outside index runs}}\Delta h. \] It is a nonnegative integer. The leading contraction keeps it fixed. Every term of \(\delta f\),evaluated at this input,uses a value of \(f\) at smaller \(R\). An internal minimal IC operation merges at least two original letters and decreases their count. A source module operation consumes a nonempty outside piece. If it contains an IC letter its count decreases;if it contains only index arrows its positive height is consumed. For a target module operation,expand the cofree comparison formula:the central Taylor map is evaluated on the middle input left after those outside pieces were removed. The same strict decrease holds. Normalized core maps cannot turn a nonempty outside input into a scalar identity,and retain the actual index endpoints. These are every term omitted from \(\partial_0\).

Consequently \((\delta\mathsf H_0)^j f\) is zero on a fixed rank-\(R\) input for \(j>R\). The full perturbation formula is therefore the actual finite-on-each-word contraction \[ \mathsf H=\mathsf H_0(1+\delta\mathsf H_0)^{-1}. \] The complete algebraic perturbation proof C.35.1 gives \(\partial\mathsf H+\mathsf H\partial=1\) and \(\mathsf H^2=0\),with no convergence assumption. It acts inside the Taylor restriction kernel and retains every specified label. This proves the theorem with all module terms present. \(\square\)

C.56.5. Closed comparisons and their actual homotopies extend

Use the same hypotheses. The graded cut projectors need not be full module chain maps,but they do give a common direct-sum decomposition of the graded input spaces. This suffices for graded extension.

Theorem C.56.5.1 (full relative comparison and homotopy extension). A set of pairwise compatible closed full Taylor maps on the selected product submodels extends to a closed full bicomodule map on \(Z\). If a closed global map \(L\) of degree zero has compatible specified degree-minus-one primitives on those submodels,there is a global primitive retaining them. If the prescribed leading central term is the calibrated identity,the closed comparison has that exact leading term and its usual finite cofree inverse.

Proof. Graded distributivity of the cut images glues the prescriptions to a well-defined map on their sum. Extend its central Taylor map linearly on the remaining common graded summands,and reconstruct the full cofree map. This gives a graded extension \(F_0\) of the closed prescribed comparisons. Its defect \(e=\partial F_0\) is a closed degree-\(r+1\) element of the restriction kernel,where \(r\) is the common degree of the prescribed maps. The first theorem corrects it by \[ F=F_0-\mathsf H e. \] It is closed and has the same prescribed restrictions. The construction retains the fixed outside core maps because the entire kernel complex was the one for those maps.

For the primitive problem extend the prescribed Taylor homotopy to \(K_0\). The closed degree-zero defect \(e=L-\partial K_0\) vanishes on \(U\). Then \(K=K_0+\mathsf H e\) has \(\partial K=L\) and the required restrictions. Every product submodel contains the bare central block, so the correction kernel has zero bare central value. A prescribed identity leading map is thus unchanged. The cofree recursion of C.39.2 gives its inverse,finite on original surrounding words over the already invertible core powers (invertibility of these powers is required for this last assertion). Its inverse is a chain map by the original chain equation. \(\square\)

C.56.6. The primitive choices themselves can be made compatible

Suppose the desired closed comparisons already agree on the cut intersections. On each selected product submodel suppose an actual homotopy to the original global comparison is given,as in C54. These homotopies need not initially agree with one another.

Proposition C.56.6.1 (glue the homotopies without changing their differentials). They can be changed by closed full module maps so that they agree on all their intersections,and then extended to one global homotopy. The construction retains every previously chosen product submodel. Its hypotheses do not require an Alexander–Whitney form for the original native homotopies.

Proof. Order the finite list of submodels. Keep the first homotopy. For the next submodel \(S\),its intersection with the preceding sum is the sum of the refined product domains,by the common graded cut decomposition. Inside \(S\),the refined cut projectors still commute; their leading shuffles are quasi-isomorphisms,and the same full action terms lower the rank used in Theorem C.56.4.1. Thus its relative Taylor restriction kernel has the contraction just proved.

The difference between the retained homotopy and the new given homotopy on that intersection is closed:their differentials are restrictions of the same difference of the two closed comparison maps. Extend this closed degree-minus-one map from the intersection to \(S\) by Theorem C.56.5.1's closed-map extension. Adding it to the new homotopy leaves its differential unchanged and makes its restriction equal to the previous choices. Continue through the finite list. The resulting homotopies agree pairwise and hence on their entire sum. Theorem C.56.5.1's primitive extension now gives the asserted global homotopy. All corrections were made only on the new submodel,so the earlier prescriptions remain fixed. \(\square\)

For native use one must verify the stated common-root central identifications,actual chain submodel embeddings and the compatibility of the desired closed product comparisons on the refined domains. The proposition removes the extra requirement that independently given homotopy primitives already have the ordered retraction form. Full grafting covariance and the marked point still require their own verified native domains and equations.

C.56.7. Two solved extension examples

Exercise C.56.7.1 (three binary factors; intermediate). Let \(I_1=I_2=I_3=[1]\). In the relative index bar,fix the endpoints \(000\) and \(111\). Let \(S_1,S_2\) be the two ordered two-block shuffle domains and \(U=S_1+S_2\). Compute the dimensions of \(D,U,D/U\) in degrees minus one,minus two and minus three. Explain directly why \(U\to D\) is a quasi-isomorphism.

Solution. A length-\(q\) path is an ordered partition of the three changing coordinates into \(q\) nonempty steps. There is one one-step path,six two-step paths and six three-step paths. Each two-block domain has one length-two generator and two length-three generators. Theorem C.56.1.1 identifies their intersection with the finest three-factor shuffle,which has only one generator here,in degree minus three. Thus

Cohomological degree \(\dim D\) \(\dim U\) \(\dim(D/U)\)
\(-1\) 1 0 1
\(-2\) 6 2 4
\(-3\) 6 3 3

The degree-minus-two differential in \(D\) has rank one:every two-step path merges to the single one-step path with coefficient \(1\) or \(-1\). The six degree-minus-three words form the edges of a hexagon whose vertices are the six two-step words;internal merging is its signed incidence differential. Each two-step word has exactly two refinements,and the hexagon is connected. Its incidence matrix has rank five:successive edge differences span the five differences from a chosen vertex,and every column has total signed sum zero after the bar orientation is applied. The remaining top cycle is the signed three-factor shuffle of Exercise C.55.4.2.

On each \(S_i\),the top differential has rank one,as it is the two-path differential of its two-coordinate factor tensored with the remaining arrow. Their degree-minus-two images are independent:one uses the step changing coordinates \(2,3\),the other the step changing coordinates \(1,2\). Hence \(d:U^{-3}\to U^{-2}\) has rank two. Its sole cohomology class is again the common finest shuffle in degree minus three. The inclusion identifies these classes and both complexes have zero cohomology elsewhere. The quotient is therefore acyclic,also as asserted by Theorem C.56.3.1. In particular, one must use the actual sum of the two shuffle domains;counting them as disjoint would give the incorrect top dimension four.

Exercise C.56.7.2 (a necessary perturbation; intermediate). Consider the acyclic complex with \(a,c\) of degree minus one and \(b,e\) of degree zero. Put \(d_0a=b,d_0c=e\),and let \(h_0b=a,h_0e=c\),with all other values zero. Assign rank zero to \(a,b\) and rank one to \(c,e\). Add the rank-decreasing perturbation \(\delta c=b\),zero on the other basis vectors. Compute the full normalized contraction and its signed Hom contraction.

Solution. We have \(d^2=(d_0+\delta)^2=0\),since both summands land in degree zero,where the differential vanishes. The leading contraction preserves rank,but it is not a contraction for \(d\):indeed \(dh_0(e)=e+b\). Here \((\delta h_0)^2=0\),so the full finite perturbation is \[ h=h_0(1+\delta h_0)^{-1}=h_0-h_0\delta h_0, \qquad h(b)=a,\quad h(e)=c-a. \] It vanishes on \(a,c\),so \(h^2=0\). On \(b,e\), \(dh\) is the identity;on \(a,c\),\(hd\) is the identity, since \(d(c)=e+b\). Thus \(dh+hd=1\) on every basis vector.

For a target complex \(V\) and a degree-\(r\) linear map \(f\),the signed Hom contraction is \(\mathsf H(f)=(-1)^r f h\). Writing \(\partial f=d_Vf-(-1)^rfd\),direct substitution gives \[ \begin{aligned} \partial\mathsf H(f)&=(-1)^r d_Vfh+fhd,\\ \mathsf H(\partial f)&=(-1)^{r+1}d_Vfh+fdh. \end{aligned} \] Their sum is \(f\),and \(\mathsf H^2=0\). For example, take \(V=k\) in degree zero and \(f\) of degree one with \(f(a)=1,f(c)=0\). Then \(\mathsf H(f)(b)=-1\) and \(\mathsf H(f)(e)=1\);its Hom differential is exactly \(f\). This example isolates the action perturbation and the Hom sign. It is an algebraic quotient example;identifying a native geometric module still requires the hypotheses of Theorem C.56.4.1.

Theorems C.56.1.1–C.56.3.1 identify the commuting cut algebra and its acyclic quotient. Theorems C.56.4.1–C.56.5.1 and Proposition C.56.6.1 give full relative Taylor extension and primitive gluing. Exercises C.56.7.1–C.56.7.2 compute the dimensions and the necessary homotopy correction shown here. Editable SVG source.

C.57. Product module actions and the native root tensor

Compatible actions on the actual product domains extend to a full module differential. The construction kills each remaining curvature term in increasing outside rank,retaining the prescribed pure actions. Ordered output-root induction then gives product-compatible one-cross models. An actual comparison on the finest domain extends to the whole module and transports the entire path differential. The native partial forest also has the required graded central root tensor,including unit outputs and identity strands. The finest native comparison and all higher external grafting equations remain additional requirements.

C.57.1. Relative extension of the entire module action

Let \(Z=L\otimes sN\otimes A\) be one of C56's graded cofree one-cross modules. The pure cores are the prescribed minimal IC tensor cores and finite-height index bars. Their full differentials are fixed. Fix the central unary differential too. Let \(d_b\) be the resulting baseline differential on \(Z\),with no action consuming an outside piece. It squares to zero,by the tensor differential calculation.

Use the C56 graded cut images \(S_T\). They have their complete central space \(sN\) and are the cofree pullbacks along the actual outside shuffle coalgebra embeddings. Select a nonempty finite collection and put \(U=\sum S_T\). Each is stable for \(d_b\). At every central input put \[ \begin{aligned} R&=\#\{\text{original outside IC letters}\}\\ &\quad+\sum_{\text{outside index runs}}\Delta h. \end{aligned} \] The leading part \(d_{b,0}\) includes the index-bar and central unary differentials. It preserves \(R\). Every other pure minimal operation decreases \(R\) by at least one. All operations are normalized;none sends a nonempty outside core word to a scalar identity.

Theorem C.57.1.1 (relative module-structure extension). Suppose compatible degree-one full bicomodule maps \(\mu_T\) are prescribed on the selected cut domains. Suppose they have zero bare central value and \((d_b+\mu_T)^2=0\) there. Then there is a global full module differential \(D=d_b+\mu\) with those exact restrictions. It keeps the pure core differentials and central unary differential fixed. Its construction uses finitely many corrections on every original input.

Proof. A homogeneous bicomodule endomorphism over identity pure cores is determined by its central Taylor map. Let \(E\) be their graded associative algebra under ordinary composition,and let \(\partial_b f=d_bf-(-1)^{|f|}fd_b\). The bicomodule equations for \(d_b\) make this a differential on \(E\). In detail,the pure-core coderivation terms on the two sides cancel when differentiating the equation for a bicomodule map. Thus \(\partial_b f\) again satisfies that equation. The ordinary composition calculation gives \(\partial_b(fg)=(\partial_b f)g+(-1)^{|f|}f\partial_b g\) and \(\partial_b^2=0\).
