Applying the same entire horizontal associativity to a mixed operator word, first substitute \(j\) or \(q\) next to \(u\). Its image is an ordinary identity parameter mark. Every higher one-output component containing that mark vanishes, by the parameter-unit normalization proved in Theorem C.69.2.1. The cofree expansion still keeps standard identity insertions in its longer output words; they are not discarded. \(\square\)

C.70.3. One transport across all intermediate types

For each selected actual geometric fiber category \(G_a\) choose a full model bridge \(R_a\) with one resolution object per geometric object. Such a bridge comes from Theorem C.68.3.1 by choosing one of its resolutions over each required object and retaining the full subcategory on them. Its geometric projection \(q_a\) is identical on those labels, with graded-surjective quasi-isomorphic mapping complexes. Choose the full normalized sections \(j_a\) once, as above.

Theorem C.70.3.1 (the entire split horizontal transport). On the full operator categories define

\[ \begin{gathered}L_{ab}(F)=j_b Fq_a,\\ L_{ab}:\\ \operatorname{Fun}_\infty(G_a,G_b)\\ \longrightarrow\operatorname{Fun}_\infty(R_a,R_b).\end{gathered} \tag{C.70.9} \]

including every higher parameter operation, using Theorem C.69.2.1's horizontal bar composition. Then on their entire tensor bars

\[ \begin{gathered}B L_{ac}M_G\\ \quad=M_R\circ\bigl(\\ \qquad B L_{bc}\otimes B L_{ab}\bigr).\end{gathered} \tag{C.70.10} \]

It retains all original operator and parameter labels. Its identity object is \(E_a=j_aq_a\), with exact relations

\[ \begin{gathered}E_a^2=E_a,\\ E_b L_{ab}(F)\\ \quad=L_{ab}(F)\\ \quad=L_{ab}(F)E_a.\end{gathered} \tag{C.70.11} \]

The full Nat isomorphisms of Theorem C.70.2.1 compare these idempotent local units with the actual identity functors. This is a common transport across the changing intermediate fiber; it is not a separate independent choice at each original string's endpoints.

Proof. Precomposition by the dg \(q_a\) and full postcomposition by the normalized \(A_\infty\) j_b are precisely the coalgebra operations of Theorem C.69.2.1. Their composite is a normalized \(A_\infty\) functor on each complete operator category, which defines \(B L_{ab}\). Its object expression is the displayed one. On two composable operator bars expand both transported factors and associate the entire horizontal composition. The middle factors become \(q_bj_b\). They are exactly \(\operatorname{Id}_{G_b}\), with zero higher components. Thus they cancel in the entire expression, leaving j_c, the full composition of the two original operator bars, and \(q_a\). This is exactly \(B L_{ac}M_G\). This argument holds for all original parameter lengths, not just for its object or single-parameter components. All signs move the same suspended factors through the same tensor permutation, by Theorem C.69.2.1's exact associativity.

The same cancellation with one identity operator gives E_a^2=E_a and the two exact corner relations. The unit isomorphisms exist by Theorem C.70.2.1, including their two exact projection/source-image identities. These show that whiskering the unit with an image \(L_{ab}(F)\) has the identity unary comparison, and that all its higher mixed one-output components are the ordinary normalized unit ones. The longer bar words retain their identity insertions as in Theorem C.70.2.1. All maps use the original typed operator bars, so their cuts and full-face restrictions are unchanged. Iterated middle cancellation works for any finite original string, which proves the last assertion. \(\square\)

C.70.4. Two solved relative-source calculations

Use the actual 19-dimensional one-object bridge \(R\) of Exercise C.68.5.1, with \(q\) its projection to the unaugmented End(\(V\)), and \(j\) its full section. Write \(S=(1,0,0)\), \(M_{ab}=(0,E_{ab},0)\), and \(Z_{ab}=(0,0,E_{ab})\). The degree of \(M_{ab}\) is \(|a|-|b|\), while the degree of \(Z_{ab}\) is \(|a|-|b|+1\). In particular \(S\) is not the unit of \(R\): that unit is \(S+M_{ee}+M_{ff}+M_{yy}\). Keep these four summands in every ordinary-unit calculation.

Exercise C.70.4.1 (the leading differential does not preserve the relative condition; advanced). Let \(\varphi_{\rm base}\) have only \(\varphi_{\mathrm{base},1}(S)=S\) and define the entire degree-one cochain \(\varphi=\varphi_{\mathrm{base}}-\varphi_{\mathrm{base}}E\). Through original source length two its nonzero values are

\[ \begin{gathered}\varphi_1(S)=S,\\ \varphi_1(M_{ee})=-S,\\ \varphi_2(M_{ef},M_{ye})=S.\end{gathered} \tag{C.70.12} \]

with every other value in that word window zero. Show that \(\varphi\) vanishes after precomposition with \(j\) but that its leading unary differential \(d_0 \varphi\) does not. Explain why the contraction of Theorem C.70.1.1 still applies to this relative kernel.

Solution. Let \(\varphi_{\rm base}\) have only \(\varphi_{\mathrm{base},1}(S)=S\). Then on the displayed word window \(\varphi=\varphi_{\mathrm{base}}-\varphi_{\mathrm{base}}E\). Indeed the scalar component of \(j_1\) is \(\beta\), so precomposition \(E\) contributes \(S\) on input \(M_{ee}\); its nonzero second scalar value on \((M_{ef},M_{ye})\) is -1 by (C.68.10). No other scalar component of \(j\) has the degrees and basis support needed in this window. Since the functor \(E\) is unital, the two terms cancel on an ordinary unit input; higher unit inputs give zero. Thus \(\varphi\) is normalized. The entire same definition \(\varphi_{\mathrm{base}}-\varphi_{\mathrm{base}}E\), including any later word components, vanishes after \(j\) because \(Ej=j\). Thus its full differential also vanishes after \(j\), since precomposition \(j\) is a dg functor.

The failure of the leading differential already occurs at source inputs \(A=E_{ey}\) and \(B=E_{ye}\) of End(\(V\)). One has \(dA=-E_{ef}\). The linear section sends A to \(M_{ey}\) and B to \(M_{ye}-Z_{fe}\). In the source-unary part of \(d_0 \varphi\) on those two inputs, the term from \(dM_{ey}=-M_{ef}-Z_{ey}\) has coefficient -1 from the degree-one Hom differential. It therefore contributes +\(S\). The other source-unary and output-unary terms cannot meet the only nonzero two-input value of \(\varphi\) at these inputs. The one-letter \(j_2(A,B)\) has degree -1 and takes values in ker \(q\). That kernel has no degree-minus-one mapping component, so \(j_2(A,B)=0\). Consequently

\[ \begin{gathered}((d_0\varphi)j)_2(E_{ey},E_{ye})\\ \qquad=S\ne0.\end{gathered} \tag{C.70.13} \]

This is an actual failure of separate leading stability. The full \(d \varphi\) still vanishes after \(j\); its remaining action/composition terms cancel that leading restriction. Theorem C.70.1.1 requires stability only under full \(d\) and \(H_0\). Both hold here, so its finite symmetric contraction applies.

The displayed finite window proves the failure in the whole cochain too: later input components cannot contribute to an evaluation on this two-letter original input. Likewise each relative contraction equation on this window is the corresponding restriction of the full original-word formula. \(\square\)

Exercise C.70.4.2 (the second component of the actual relative unit; advanced). For \(u:\operatorname{Id}_R\to E\) constructed by Theorem C.70.2.1 using the output contraction of Exercise C.68.5.1, compute \(u_1(Z_{ee})\) and \(u_2(M_{ef},Z_{ye})\). Prove that omitting the second value breaks its closed full Nat equation.

Solution. On the mapping kernel \(q\), its contraction is

\[ \begin{gathered}k_q(f,0,a)\\ \quad=(\beta(a),0,-H_G(a)).\end{gathered} \tag{C.70.14} \]

The first Taylor value of the relative unit on that kernel is this contraction. Since \(H_G(E_{ee})=-E_{fy}\), it gives

\[ u_1(Z_{ee})=S+Z_{fy}. \tag{C.70.15} \]

Here \(DS=Z_{ee}+Z_{ff}+Z_{yy}\) and \(DZ_{fy}=-Z_{ff}-Z_{yy}\), so the differential of this value is \(Z_{ee}\), as required by the first unit equation.

The symmetric correction at the next original word gives

\[ \begin{gathered}u_2(M_{ef},Z_{ye})\\ \qquad=-S-Z_{fy}.\end{gathered} \tag{C.70.16} \]

For the two-letter source word \((M_{ef},Z_{ye})\), the contribution from the first Taylor level to \(d u\) is +\(Z_{ee}\). Indeed \(E_1(M_{ef})=M_{ef}+Z_{ey}\) and \(u_1(Z_{ye})=-Z_{fe}\). Their product is +\(Z_{ee}\) by the third-component sign in the bridge multiplication. The source unary term \(dM_{ef}=-Z_{ef}\) has no contribution at this truncated first Taylor level, and the other terms on this input vanish. The differential of \(-S-Z_{fy}\) is -\(Z_{ee}\), canceling that defect. The full second component also vanishes on \((Z_{ef},Z_{ye})\), so its source-unary contribution on this word is zero. Thus the stated second value is necessary for closure on this actual input.

The whole-word formula of Theorem C.70.2.1 supplies every later component and its exact \(q\) projection and \(Bj\) restriction. The geometric-series full inverse has both of those same identities. The finite calculation retains the ordinary source unit \(S+M_{ee}+M_{ff}+M_{yy}\) and the nonzero second Taylor component of \(j\); replacing either by a single scalar letter would change the equations just computed. \(\square\)

Theorems C.70.1.1–C.70.3.1 give the full relative contraction, exact split unit and entire changing-fiber transport. Exercises C.70.4.1–C.70.4.2 exhibit the failure of separate leading stability and the necessary second unit component. Editable SVG source.

C.71. The actual native diagram with strict formal units

The strict-height native index separates formal identities from positive arrow labels whose enhanced functors happen to be identities. Split model transport retains that distinction, all changing-frontier comparison cells and the supplied whole extension-field comparison.

C.71.1. Formal identities and the positive original-arrow bar

Let \(I\) be the actual strict-height native joint index of Sections C.47 and C.64, or a finite full forward corner. Its nonidentity arrows remain their actual selected contraction/execution labels. Write \(G_s\) for its geometric dg fiber, whose type is the actual frontier arity \(m_s\). The full native operator \(F_f\) and all its higher comparison cochains are those of Theorem C.47.2.1. In the coherent word presentation, its horizontal operations are the complete coalgebra composition \(M\) of Section C.69. Each normalized positive index component is evaluated on all original mapping inputs in its source fiber.

Choose Theorem C.70.3.1's split bridges \(q_m:R_m\to G_m\) and sections \(j_m\) once for each actual frontier type. Reuse them at all states with that type. Where an additional actual comparison endpoint changes the geometric fiber, keep that endpoint in the type label too. Do not reconstruct these choices independently on separate finite index corners.

Theorem C.71.1.1 (the actual unital native transport). There is a normalized coherent native diagram on the \(R\) fibers with the following operator objects:

\[ \begin{gathered}T_f=j_{m_t}F_fq_{m_s}\\ \quad(f:s\to t,\ f\ne1_s),\\ T_{1_s}=\operatorname{Id}_{R_{m_s}}.\end{gathered} \tag{C.71.1} \]

Every full positive native index cell is transported by Theorem C.70.3.1's entire operator-bar map \(L\). All formal identity degeneracies have their ordinary normalized values. Every original selected arrow label is retained, even if its native functor equals an identity functor. In particular a nonidentity f with \(F_f=\operatorname{Id}\) has model \(E=jq\), rather than being reassigned the formal identity's model.

The bridge projections give the exact whole comparison

\[ \begin{gathered}q_{m_t}T_f\\ \qquad=F_fq_{m_s},\end{gathered} \tag{C.71.2} \]

including every original source Taylor component and every higher native index cell. On formal identities that comparison is the actual identity. The diagram retains its full-face restrictions and all finite forward corners of the one chosen global family.

The same construction retains a supplied entire two-endpoint native comparison diagram. Thus it applies to the actual extension-field native comparison of Theorem C.48.3.1 after all its fibers have been extended to the same coefficient field. This assertion does not yet prescribe the common-core calibration and external-product/grafting coordinates of a full marked point.

Proof. A composite of nonidentity arrows in \(I\) cannot be an identity: each factor has strictly positive height jump and their sum remains positive. Consequently the original positive index words are closed under their source-composition faces. Their full bar calculations therefore retain all actual parallel-arrow labels and never turn a positive source face into a formal identity face.

On this entire positive word presentation, apply Theorem C.70.3.1's \(L\) at each pair of outer fiber types. It is a chain coalgebra map on the complete operator bars. Its exact horizontal identity

\[ \begin{gathered}B L M_G\\ \quad=M_R\circ\bigl(BL\otimes BL\bigr).\end{gathered} \tag{C.71.3} \]

carries every actual native equation to the corresponding \(R\) equation. This includes the full source unary differentials, all higher parameter cochains and every intermediate changing-frontier type. Inserting the successive fixed \(q_m\) and \(j_m\) cancels each middle \(q_mj_m\) exactly. Thus the positive diagram is a simultaneous transport of the original whole family, rather than an assignment selected from its edge classes.

Now assign \(\operatorname{Id}_R\) to each formal identity arrow. Set every higher index component with a formal identity argument to its normalized zero value; retain the usual unary identity and ordinary unit insertion values. The types of the remaining positive components do not change: an old formal identity factor \(E=jq\) next to an image \(L\)(\(F\)) acts exactly as the identity, by Theorem C.70.3.1's full corner relations. The same is true on the entire image operator bars; the higher mixed one-output unit terms are the normalized ones of Theorem C.70.2.1. Thus replacing that factor by \(\operatorname{Id}_R\) retains the source and target operator word of each such component. Check its full bar equations at such an argument. If the identity is internal, its two neighboring source-composition faces give the same remaining positive component with opposite suspended bar signs. If it is at an outer boundary, the source-composition term and the strict identity functor action give that same component with opposite signs. The higher one-output horizontal terms at an identity parameter vanish by Section C.69's normalized unit rule. These are all possible terms meeting the identity slot. With multiple identities repeat the same local cancellation at the first such slot; it either cancels the same two terms or leaves an already normalized zero higher component. Hence every formal-unit equation holds.

This unital extension concerns the original index-arrow slots. It does not replace arbitrary objects of an untagged full functor category by identity functors. Nonidentity labels whose operators happen to equal Id remain positive original letters. Their composites are still positive index labels, so every such component stays in the already transported positive diagram. In particular \(L(\operatorname{Id})=jq\) is kept on that labelled arrow. This proves the asserted distinction, including unit-output and unary execution/contraction arrows.

For a positive arrow, postcomposition by \(q_{\rm target}\) cancels \(j_{\rm target}\) in its whole formula, leaving \(F_fq_{\rm source}\) exactly. On a full operator bar the same Section C.69 associativity cancels that pair before any one-output projection. Thus every transported higher native cell projects to its original entire cell after source \(q\). On a formal identity the equation is \(q\operatorname{Id}_R=\operatorname{Id}_Gq\), with identity comparison. The normalized unit equations therefore project to the original unit equations as well. This gives the exact whole comparison, and each \(q\) fiber is an actual mapping quasi-isomorphism and object equivalence by its construction.

The \(q\) and \(j\) choices were made once by actual fiber type and object labels. The formula for a component uses its original word and no new parameter vertex. Restricting to any genuine full index face therefore restricts the same component, and intersecting two such faces gives the same literal restriction. Theorem C.47.2.1's finite forward image closure retains the finitely many needed geometric object images. At each fixed original input all Exercise C.68.5.1 section and Section C.69 evaluation sums are finite. Restriction to its finite forward corner hence gives the same actual finite calculation. No fresh independently prescribed face data are asserted to extend.

Finally, an entire two-endpoint comparison can be included as its given joint diagram on \(I\) times [1], keeping the endpoint in each fiber label. Give a comparison arrow the additional positive endpoint height jump. The summed height is again strict, with finite forward corners; its positive-arrow words have the property used in the first paragraph. Apply the identical transport to that whole supplied diagram, including its diagonal mixed arrows and cells. On its two endpoint faces the result is precisely the restriction already described. All coefficient-extended fibers are categories over the same field, so their mapping and section arguments are those of Exercise C.68.5.1/Section C.70 over that field. This retains the actual full comparison of Theorem C.48.3.1; it does not infer a coordinate calibration or prescribed external product from that comparison alone. \(\square\)

C.71.2. Solved native unit calculations

Use the actual Exercise C.68.5.1 one-object bridge \(R\) of dimension 19 and \(G=\operatorname{End}(V)\), with \(V=ke^0\oplus kf^{-1}\oplus ky^0\), \(df=y\). Let \(L(e)=y\) and \(U_t=1+tL\); its inverse is \(1-tL\) because \(L^2=0\). The strict dg functor \(F_t\) is conjugation by U_t. Its model is \(T_t=jF_tq\), retaining the full nonzero second Taylor component of \(j\).

Exercise C.71.2.1 (an identity-valued arrow retains its actual label; advanced). Use a strict-height index with two parallel arrows \(a_0,a_1:0\to1\), with native \(F_{0}\) and \(F_{1}\), and \(b:1\to2\) with native \(F_{2}\). Their distinct composites \(c_0,c_1:0\to2\) have native \(F_{2}\) and \(F_{3}\). Formal identities must model \(\operatorname{Id}_R\), while \(a_0\) retains \(E=jq\ne\operatorname{Id}_R\). Check the entire composition \(T_tT_s=T_{t+s}\), its \(q\) projection, units and full-face restrictions. Explain why passing to mapping cohomology cannot identify the two parallel labels or replace \(a_0\) by a formal identity.

Solution. The matrix \(L\) is closed and square-zero. Therefore U_t is a closed invertible degree-zero map and \(U_tU_s=U_{t+s}\). Conjugation by it is a strict unital dg functor and \(F_tF_s=F_{t+s}\). On the full \(R\) source bar the model has the exact formula

\[ B T_t=Bj\,BF_t\,Bq. \tag{C.71.4} \]

Consequently its entire composite is

\[ \begin{gathered}B T_t\,B T_s\\ \quad=Bj\,BF_t(Bq\,Bj)\\ \qquad BF_s\,Bq\\ \quad=B T_{t+s}.\end{gathered} \tag{C.71.5} \]

since \(Bq Bj\) is the identity, including all higher terms. Its full \(q\) projection is B \(F_t Bq\) by that same cancellation. A formal identity is instead the actual identity bar map, which composes as the strict unit with each B \(T_t\). All these are genuine full bar equations, with their nonminimal source unary differential and ordinary source identity letters.

For a concrete distinction, write \(S=(1,0,0)\) in \(R\). Then \((T_0)_1(S)=0\) because \(q\)(\(S\))=0, whereas \((\operatorname{Id}_R)_1(S)=S\). Thus the nonidentity \(a_0\) retains the actual model \(E=T_0\), which differs from the formal identity. Its label has source 0, target 1; a formal identity has the same source and target. A quotient by a matching underlying functor would change these actual index data.

The eight index labels are \(i_0,i_1,i_2,a_0,a_1,b,c_0,c_1\). There are 15 composable pairs, including their formal unit pairs, and 24 composable triples. The selected original rule \(ba_0=c_0,\ ba_1=c_1\) retains both parallel composites. A full object face retains all labels whose endpoints belong to it; source and target closure makes it stable under composition. In particular the face \(\{0,1\}\) retains both \(a_0\),\(a_1\), and the face \(\{0,2\}\) retains both \(c_0\),\(c_1\). Its model is the literal restriction of the whole formula above, with no new section choice.

Finally \(H(V)=ke\), so \(H(\operatorname{End}(V))=k\) by the split Hom contraction of Exercise C.68.5.1. Each U_t induces the identity there, hence each \(F_t\) does too. These identical cohomology actions do not change any selected index arrow label, nor the full bar maps just computed. The native diagram is retained by its actual operators and higher data, rather than reconstructed from those cohomology actions. \(\square\)

Exercise C.71.2.2 (a native comparison requires positive Taylor components; advanced). Use the [2] labels \(a:F_0,\ b:F_2,\ c:F_3\), with native comparison \(\beta=U_1\) from \(F_2F_0=F_2\) to \(F_{3}\). It is an actual closed dg natural isomorphism, since \(\beta F_2(g)=F_3(g)\beta\) on every matrix. Its transported full comparison is \(\alpha=j_{*,1}(\beta q):T_2\to T_3\). Compute its bare and first relevant Taylor components, give its actual full inverse, and exhibit the closedness defect of its bare truncation.

Solution. For a source word \(w\) of length \(L\) consisting of \(g\)-component \(R\) letters, the full marked formula of Section C.69 is the sum over cuts \(w=w_L|w_R\) of the following expression, where \(|w_L|\) is the suspended degree of that original source subword:

\[ \begin{gathered}(-1)^{|w_L|}j_{L+1}\\ \quad\bigl(F_3(qw_L)|\beta|\\ \qquad F_2(qw_R)\bigr).\end{gathered} \tag{C.71.6} \]

If a positive word contains a scalar-component or a third-component \(R\) basis letter, \(q\) kills that source input. Since \(H_G(E_{ye})=E_{fe}\), its bare component is

\[ \begin{gathered}\alpha_0=\operatorname{Id}_R\\ \quad+M_{ye}-Z_{fe}.\end{gathered} \tag{C.71.7} \]

The four second-section values needed for its first component are

\[ \begin{gathered}j_2(E_{ye},E_{ef})=-Z_{fy},\\ j_2(E_{ef},E_{ye})\\ \quad=-S-Z_{fy},\\ j_2(E_{yf},E_{ye})=Z_{fe},\\ j_2(E_{ye},E_{yf})=0.\end{gathered} \tag{C.71.8} \]

For completeness, apply the obstruction formula (C.68.8) and the kernel contraction \(k_q(f,0,a)=(\beta_{\rm lin}(a),0,-H_G(a))\), where \(\beta_{\rm lin}(a)=a_{ee}\). The third-component obstructions on those four inputs are respectively \(Z_{ff}+Z_{yy},-Z_{ee}\), \(-Z_{ye},\ 0\). Their contractions are exactly the four values displayed: \(H_G(E_{ff}+E_{yy})=E_{fy}\), \(H_G(E_{ee})=-E_{fy}\), and \(H_G(E_{ye})=E_{fe}\). This computes every required matrix entry directly.

Conjugation gives \(F_t(E_{ef})=E_{ef}+tE_{yf}\). The suspended source degree of \(M_{ef}\) is zero, so the two cuts in the marked formula have positive signs. Their sum is

\[ \begin{gathered}j_2(E_{ye},E_{ef}+2E_{yf})\\ \quad+j_2(E_{ef}+3E_{yf},E_{ye}).\end{gathered} \tag{C.71.9} \]

It follows that

\[ \begin{gathered}\alpha_1(M_{ef})\\ \quad=-S-2Z_{fy}+3Z_{fe}.\end{gathered} \tag{C.71.10} \]

The marked postcomposition functor carries the closed \(\beta q\) to a closed full \(\alpha\). Its \(q\) projection is exactly \(\beta q\) because qj is the identity full functor, and normalized units are retained by Section C.69. These statements also follow by inserting the displayed entire marked formula into its full Nat equation with source functor \(T_{2}\) and target functor \(T_{3}\).

To see a concrete failure of truncation, keep \(\alpha_0\) and discard its positive components. On source \(M_{ef}\) the differential of that bare cochain is

\[ \begin{gathered}Z_{ee}-Z_{ff}-Z_{yy}\\ \qquad+3Z_{ye}\ne0.\end{gathered} \tag{C.71.11} \]

Indeed it is \(T_3(M_{ef})\alpha_0-\alpha_0T_2(M_{ef})\), using the third-component bridge multiplication sign. The differential of \(-S-2Z_{fy}+3Z_{fe}\) is its negative, since \(DS=Z_{ee}+Z_{ff}+Z_{yy}\), \(DZ_{fy}=-Z_{ff}-Z_{yy}\) and \(DZ_{fe}=-Z_{ye}\). The remaining source unary term on this input is zero: \(dM_{ef}=-Z_{ef}\), and \(\alpha\)'s positive values on that \(q\)-kernel source vanish. Thus the actual first component cancels the explicit bare defect.

The bare map has the actual inverse \(\operatorname{Id}_R-M_{ye}+Z_{fe}\): its nonidentity part \(N=M_{ye}-Z_{fe}\) has \(N^2=0\) by the same bridge product formula. Let \(a_0\) be the bare cochain \(\alpha_0\), let \(a_0^{-1}\) be that bare inverse, and put \(n=a_0^{-1}\alpha-1\) in the graded full Nat composition. It has positive original source length. Therefore

\[ \begin{gathered}\alpha^{-1}\\ \quad=(1-n+n^2-\cdots)\\ \qquad a_0^{-1}.\end{gathered} \tag{C.71.12} \]

is a finite two-sided full inverse on each original word. The full dg product derivation rule makes it closed. Its \(q\) projection is \(\beta^{-1}q\), because \(q\) preserves full Nat products and exact inverses. This is an actual inverse cochain, retaining every higher term of \(\alpha\), rather than only an inverse cohomology class. \(\square\)

Theorem C.71.1.1 gives the normalized full native transport and its exact whole comparison. Exercises C.71.2.1–C.71.2.2 retain the parallel index labels and compute the necessary positive Taylor component of the native comparison. Editable SVG source.

C.72. Normalized unital cobar models

Actual dg categories need not have augmentations. Their unital cobar model retains coefficient outputs as constants, admits its actual counit contraction, and gives strict dg models of normalized unital functors. The canonical full unit retains every higher component under composition.

C.72.1. The normalized quotient and its actual counit

Let \(A\) be a unital dg category over its split coefficient category \(S\). The coefficients have degree zero and zero differential; all tensor products below are balanced over them. Start with the full tensor bar \(B_{\rm full}A\) on all mapping spaces, including ordinary coefficient and identity letters. Use the suspension degree \(|sa|=|a|-1\) and the conventions of Theorem C.67.1.1:

\[ \begin{gathered}b_1(sa)=s(da),\\ b_2(sa|sb)\\ \quad=(-1)^{|a|-1}s(ab),\\ D(\mathsf tc)=\mathsf t(bc)\\ \quad-\sum_{c=c_L|c_R}(-1)^{|c_L|}\\ \qquad(\mathsf tc_L)(\mathsf tc_R),\end{gathered} \tag{C.72.1} \]

where \(\mathsf t\) is the degree-one cobar generator map. These equations define the ordinary full augmented cobar before imposing the following unit relations. There is no quasi-isomorphism claim for its ordinary unreduced counit.

Let \(J_{\rm unit}\) be the two-sided ideal generated by

\[ \begin{gathered}\mathsf t(su)-u\quad(u\in S),\\ \mathsf t(sa_1|\cdots|sa_r),\\ r\geq2,\quad a_i\in S,\\ \text{for some }i.\end{gathered} \tag{C.72.2} \]

Define \(Q^{\mathrm u}(A)=\Omega B_{\rm full}A/J_{\rm unit}\), with its original object labels. The relations identify one-letter coefficient generators with the actual coefficients and kill higher degenerate unit blocks. They do not kill scalar outputs of the original products or unary differential.

Theorem C.72.1.1 (the actual normalized unital resolution). \(J_{\rm unit}\) is a differential ideal. The quotient is a unital dg category. On its nonzero identity sector it is graded free over \(S\) on the nonempty words in the graded quotient \(A/S\), with one desuspension per block. Its generator differential retains the full original unary complex and has all other terms in the algebra on shorter generators, including constant terms.

The actual unital counit

\[ \epsilon_A:Q^{\mathrm u}(A)\longrightarrow A, \tag{C.72.3} \]

is graded-surjective and a quasi-isomorphism on each mapping complex. It has an actual normalized linear mapping SDR, finite on every original reduced-letter input. On zero-identity objects the incident mapping spaces are zero on both sides. The construction therefore also retains any actual zero objects, without a false nonzero identity inclusion there.

Proof. First check the unit ideal. A one-letter coefficient relation has zero differential, since its coefficient is closed. In a higher generator with a coefficient argument, unary terms remain degenerate and vanish modulo \(J_{\rm unit}\). If that argument is internal, the two neighboring binary source compositions cancel with opposite suspended signs: \(S\) balancing makes their remaining word equal. Other source compositions still leave a degenerate coefficient argument. At an outer boundary the single neighboring source-composition term cancels the cut term with its one-letter coefficient block, because \(\mathsf t(su)=u\). All other cuts leave a higher degenerate block. These checks also apply if several coefficient arguments occur; at length two the product of their one-letter blocks equals the coefficient obtained by the single source composition. Thus the full differential of every ideal generator is zero modulo that ideal. The derivation rule proves stability of the whole ideal. Its quotient inherits \(D\) squared zero and the original coefficient units.

Choose a graded \(S\)-bimodule splitting \(A=S\oplus\overline A\), on each nonzero identity sector, using Section C.30.1. The displayed ideal puts every one-letter \(S\) component into the coefficients and kills every higher block with an \(S\) argument. The remaining words in \(\overline A\) have no other graded algebra relations. Thus their arbitrary nonempty cobar blocks freely generate the quotient. The projected unary differential on \(A/S\) is a genuine differential because \(S\) is a closed subcomplex. At generator length \(r\), its unary part keeps that length. A reduced binary composition has length \(r\)-1. Splitting a generator gives a product of two generators each of smaller length. A scalar unary output contributes a coefficient only for a one-letter block; inside a longer block it is degenerate. A scalar binary output contributes a coefficient only for a two-letter block; inside a longer block it too is degenerate. These are exactly the constant terms claimed. This proves the stated generator-complex filtration, without assuming an augmentation of A.

The counit fixes the coefficients, sends a one-letter block to its actual A mapping, and kills any higher block. On a product of one-letter blocks it gives their ordered product in A. The defining unit relations vanish under it. It commutes with the differential: on a one-letter generator this is the actual unary equation; on a two-letter generator its source composition cancels the product at the single cut, including its scalar part; on longer generators every surviving bar or cut term still contains a higher block and has zero counit. It is therefore a unital dg functor. Its coefficient and one-letter values give graded surjectivity.

For its mapping contraction count the total number \(r\) of original \(\overline A\) letters in a cobar word, rather than the number of its bar blocks. Let \(D_0\) retain projected source-unary differentials and cuts. For \(r\geq2\) define \(H_0\) to remove the first boundary when the first block has one letter; merge that first block with the next. Otherwise give zero. Its coefficient is \((-1)^{|a_1|}\), where \(a_1\) is the first original letter in target-to-source order. It is zero on \(r\)=0,1.

The first-cut coefficient is also \((-1)^{|a_1|}\). Adding that cut and removing it gives the identity. All other cut insertions cancel in opposite pairs by the tensor derivation sign, and the unary differential on \(a_1\) changes that removal coefficient by a minus sign. Unary terms on other letters cancel by the Hom tensor sign. Consequently \(D_0H_0+H_0D_0\) is the identity off the coefficient and single-letter complex, and \(H_0\) is normalized. This is the direct first-boundary calculation of Theorem C.67.1.1, now on \(A/S\) words.

Every term of \(\delta=D-D_0\) strictly decreases total \(r\): a nonconstant binary composition lowers it by one, a scalar two-letter output by two, and a scalar one-letter unary output by one. Hence

\[ \begin{gathered}H_\epsilon\\ \quad=H_0(1+\delta H_0)^{-1},\end{gathered} \tag{C.72.4} \]

is finite on each original word. Apply the finite SDR identity of Lemma C.35.1.1. The inclusion \(I_0\) of A's graded \(S\) plus \(\overline A\) space into coefficients and one-letter generators is unchanged, since \(H_0\delta I_0=0\): its only new perturbation output can be a coefficient. The induced differential on that retract is exactly \(d_A\), including its scalar unary component. Thus \(I_0\) is the actual unital linear chain section, with \(\epsilon_AI_0=\operatorname{Id}_A\).

Every term of \(H_\epsilon\) ends with \(H_0\) and therefore contains a higher block. Its counit is zero. The perturbed SDR identity has form

\[ \begin{gathered}DH_\epsilon+H_\epsilon D\\ \qquad=1-I_0P.\end{gathered} \tag{C.72.5} \]

Applying the actual dg counit gives \(0=\epsilon_A-P\). Hence its projection is the actual \(\epsilon_A\), and the identity proves the claimed quasi-isomorphism. The normalized side conditions follow from the same finite SDR identity. This argument accommodates scalar unary outputs and scalar products; none was silently projected away.

Finally, if \(1_x=0\) in A, the ordinary unit axiom already makes all mappings incident to \(x\) zero. In \(Q^{\mathrm u}(A)\), \(\mathsf t(s1_x)-1_x=-1_x\) is a defining relation, so its identity and every incident mapping vanish there too. Its mapping comparison is the isomorphism of zero complexes. One can equivalently construct the displayed free model on the remaining identity sector and then adjoin these zero objects. This proves the full assertion. \(\square\)

The normalized quotient and actual counit commute with strict unital dg maps, full object restrictions and field extension. The auxiliary graded splittings used to display \(H_\epsilon\) may be chosen once by endpoint and then restricted; no naturality of an arbitrary splitting under unrelated input maps is required.

C.72.2. Strict operator models for all normalized unital functors

Let \(F:A\to B\) be a normalized uncurved unital \(A_\infty\) functor preserving the indicated coefficient maps. Its full bar map \(BF\) has every original Taylor component, including its coefficient-valued outputs.

Theorem C.72.2.1 (composition and the full natural unit). The full cobar map \(\Omega BF\) induces a strict unital dg functor

\[ \begin{gathered}Q^{\mathrm u}F:\\ Q^{\mathrm u}(A)\longrightarrow Q^{\mathrm u}(B).\end{gathered} \tag{C.72.6} \]

These operator models compose exactly:

\[ \begin{gathered}Q^{\mathrm u}(GF)\\ \quad=(Q^{\mathrm u}G)(Q^{\mathrm u}F),\\ Q^{\mathrm u}(\operatorname{Id})=\operatorname{Id}.\end{gathered} \tag{C.72.7} \]

There is a normalized unital \(A_\infty\) quasi-equivalence

\[ \iota_A:A\longrightarrow Q^{\mathrm u}(A), \tag{C.72.8} \]

with Taylor value on a word equal to its corresponding one cobar block modulo \(J_{\rm unit}\). Its exact entire identities are

\[ \begin{gathered}\epsilon_A\iota_A=\operatorname{Id}_A,\\ (Q^{\mathrm u}F)\iota_A\\ \qquad=\iota_BF.\end{gathered} \tag{C.72.9} \]

In particular \(\epsilon_B(Q^{\mathrm u}F)\iota_A=F\), including every higher Taylor component. For a strict dg \(F\) the ordinary counit square is a strict dg square as well. Coefficient-valued higher outputs of a general \(F\) are retained as actual coefficients, not discarded as degenerate higher blocks.

Proof. If a source higher block has a coefficient argument, expand its \(BF\) image by all consecutive partitions. A partition putting that argument inside a longer \(F\) component has zero value by normalized unitality. A surviving partition isolates it in \(F_1\), whose value is the corresponding target coefficient. If there is more than one output block, the single cobar generator on that bar word is therefore degenerate in the target and is zero modulo its \(J_{\rm unit}\). If there is just one output block, the whole original source word has been put into one longer \(F\) component, already zero at that coefficient argument. One-letter coefficient relations map to target coefficient relations. Thus \(\Omega BF\) preserves the unit ideal and descends to the stated strict dg functor.

Full bar maps compose exactly by the consecutive-partition formula for \(A_\infty\) composition. Cobar maps compose exactly on their free generators and products. Their quotients consequently satisfy both exact composition and identity equations. A higher \(F\) component that itself has a coefficient value is different from a coefficient input: in the single-output partition its one-letter cobar generator is identified with that coefficient. Such a value survives, exactly as claimed.

The canonical coaugmented coalgebra unit from \(B_{\rm full}A\) to \(B_{\rm full}(\Omega B_{\rm full}A)\) sums over all consecutive cobar blocks. Compose it with the quotient's full bar map. Its one-letter component on each original word is \(\mathsf t(\text{that word})\) modulo \(J_{\rm unit}\), so it is exactly the asserted \(\iota_A\). The unit is a chain coalgebra map: splitting a consecutive partition is its coalgebra equation, while the internal bar differential and its splitting terms give its chain equation, as in Section C.39.4. It is strictly unital after quotienting: its one-letter coefficient component is the coefficient itself and every longer block with a coefficient argument vanishes. The counit kills its higher blocks and preserves its one-letter component, proving \(\epsilon_A\iota_A=\operatorname{Id}_A\) as an entire \(A_\infty\) functor. Since \(\epsilon_A\) is a mapping quasi-isomorphism, the first component of \(\iota_A\) is one too.

The consecutive-partition coalgebra unit is natural for every original coalgebra map \(BF\). The normalized quotient is natural for \(\Omega BF\) by the first paragraph. Their composite therefore gives the exact whole identity \((Q^{\mathrm u}F)\iota_A=\iota_BF\). Applying \(\epsilon_B\) gives the last asserted equation. If \(F\) is strict dg, its bar map applies \(F_1\) separately to every letter; counit of each one-letter block is \(F_1\) of the original letter, and a higher block still has zero counit. That proves the strict dg counit square in this case. All statements retain the original objects, unit outputs and word labels. \(\square\)

C.72.3. Solved constant-term calculations

Use \(A=\operatorname{End}(V)\) from Exercise C.68.5.1, where \(V=ke^0\oplus kf^{-1}\oplus ky^0\) and \(df=y\). Use the linear unit retraction \(\beta(g)=g_{ee}\). The eight matrix units other than \(E_{ee}\) form \(\overline A\); \(E_{ee}=1-E_{ff}-E_{yy}\). They are a chain complement of k1, but not an augmentation ideal. At total original reduced letter count \(r\leq3\), all cut/block words give \(1+8+128+2048=2185\) basis elements.

Exercise C.72.3.1 (omitting a scalar product breaks the differential; advanced). Put \(a=E_{ef},\ b=E_{fe},\ c=E_{ye}\). Write \(x_z=\mathsf t(sz)\) and \(h_{u_1,\ldots,u_r}=\mathsf t(su_1|\cdots|su_r)\), with coefficient unit 1. Remove just the constant binary-product terms from the differential of \(Q^{\mathrm u}(A)\), retaining all its source unary, nonconstant binary and cut terms. Compute the square of the resulting operator on \(h_{a,b,c}\).

Solution. The product \(ab=E_{ee}\) has the actual decomposition

\[ ab=1-E_{ff}-E_{yy}. \tag{C.72.10} \]

Its coefficient part is 1. The constant contribution on \(h_{a,b}\) has sign \((-1)^{|a|-1}=1\), so it is +1. Let \(C\) denote the derivation consisting of all these constant binary terms, so that the operator in the question is \(D^{\prime}=D-C\). The term \(Ch_{a,b,c}\) is zero, since a scalar output inside a three-letter block is a degenerate two-letter block and vanishes.

The cut at \((a,b)|c\) contributes \(-h_{a,b}x_c\) to \(Dh_{a,b,c}\). Applying \(C\) there gives -\(x_c\). The other cut is \(-x_a h_{b,c}\), and \(bc=0\), so it gives zero. More explicitly, the full differential is

\[ \begin{gathered}Dh_{a,b,c}=h_{a,c,c}\\ \quad-h_{E_{ff},c}-h_{E_{yy},c}\\ \quad-x_a h_{b,c}-h_{a,b}x_c.\end{gathered} \tag{C.72.11} \]

The two displayed nonconstant binary products have no coefficient part. The source unary term remains a three-letter block and also has zero \(C\). Thus

\[ CDh_{a,b,c}=-x_c. \tag{C.72.12} \]

Since \(D\) squared zero and \(Ch_{a,b,c}\)=0, one obtains

\[ \begin{gathered}(D^{\prime})^2h_{a,b,c}\\ \qquad=x_c\ne0.\end{gathered} \tag{C.72.13} \]

The generator \(x_c\) is a nonzero element of the graded free algebra. This is a concrete differential failure, not merely a failure of a desired augmentation. Restoring the actual coefficient contribution +1 on the two-letter block cancels it exactly. The counit contraction in Theorem C.72.1.1 retains that contribution at every original word length.

A scalar unary output is allowed as well. For \(A=k1\oplus kh\) with \(|h|=-1\), \(dh=1\) and \(h^2=0\), the normalized model has \(Dx_h=1\). Both A and \(Q^{\mathrm u}(A)\) are contractible: left multiplication by \(h\) or \(x_h\) respectively satisfies the contracting equation by the dg Leibniz rule. This shows explicitly that the coefficient identity may be a boundary; no chain retraction from A onto its coefficient line was assumed in Theorem C.72.1.1. \(\square\)

Exercise C.72.3.2 (a coefficient-valued higher functor component survives; advanced). First consider strict conjugation \(F_{t}\) by \(U_t=1+tE_{ye}\). Compute the coefficient part of \((Q^{\mathrm u}F_t)(x_{E_{ey}})\). Then take the nonlinear \(F=vw\), where \(w:A\to k\) is Exercise C.68.5.1's full normalized functor and v sends scalars to scalar identities. Compute the value of its strict model on \(h_{E_{ef},E_{ye}}\), and explain why omitting that higher coefficient value breaks the dg functor equation on \(h_{E_{ey},E_{ye}}\).

Solution. Since \(E_{ye}\) squared zero, \(U_{t}\) inverse is \(1-tE_{ye}\). Direct matrix multiplication gives

\[ \begin{gathered}F_t(E_{ey})=E_{ey}-t1\\ \quad+tE_{ff}+2tE_{yy}\\ \quad-t^2E_{ye}.\end{gathered} \tag{C.72.14} \]

Consequently its one-letter model value is

\[ \begin{gathered}(Q^{\mathrm u}F_t)(x_{E_{ey}})\\ \quad=x_{E_{ey}}-t1\\ \quad+t x_{E_{ff}}+2t x_{E_{yy}}\\ \quad-t^2x_{E_{ye}}.\end{gathered} \tag{C.72.15} \]

The scalar \(-t1\) is present. It is the image of a single coefficient-output letter, whose normalized cobar generator is the coefficient itself. There is no augmentation-preserving assertion for this map.

For \(F=vw\), every higher output is a scalar identity. In the full \(BF\) partition formula, any partition with at least two output letters is a degenerate target higher block and vanishes after normalization. The one-output partition survives as its actual coefficient. Thus the strict model on a generator \(h_{z_1,\ldots,z_r}\) is \(w_r(z_1,\ldots,z_r)\) times the unit. By (C.68.10) this gives

\[ \begin{gathered}(Q^{\mathrm u}F)(h_{E_{ef},E_{ye}})\\ \qquad=-1.\end{gathered} \tag{C.72.16} \]

Now put \(A_1=E_{ey}\) and \(B_1=E_{ye}\). Their degrees are zero, \(dA_1=-E_{ef}\), \(dB_1=0\), and \(A_1B_1=1-E_{ff}-E_{yy}\). The complete generator differential is

\[ \begin{gathered}Dh_{A_1,B_1}\\ \quad=-h_{E_{ef},B_1}-1\\ \quad+x_{E_{ff}}+x_{E_{yy}}\\ \quad+x_{A_1}x_{B_1}.\end{gathered} \tag{C.72.17} \]

The model sends every one-letter \(\overline A\) generator to zero, since \(w_1=\beta\) and \(\beta\) vanishes on \(\overline A\). It sends \(h_{E_{ef},B_1}\) to -1. Applying the model to the displayed differential therefore gives \(+1-1=0\). Its value on \(h_{A_1,B_1}\) is zero by degree, so \(D\) of that image is zero as well.

If only the linear component \(w_1\) is used, the image of the first term is zero while the constant term still gives -1. The difference \(DQ_{\rm lin}-Q_{\rm lin}D\) on this generator is therefore +1, a nonzero violation of the dg functor equation. Both the original source unary differential and the higher coefficient output are essential to the cancellation.

Finally \(wv\) is exactly the identity scalar functor by normalized unitality. Thus \(F^2=F\), and Theorem C.72.2.1 gives \((Q^{\mathrm u}F)^2=Q^{\mathrm u}F\) exactly on the entire normalized cobar. The entire unit naturality equation from that theorem retains all consecutive block partitions, including those with ordinary identity output letters. None of these full statements is inferred just from the scalar value computed here. \(\square\)

Theorems C.72.1.1–C.72.2.1 give the actual unital counit resolution and strict operator models with their full natural unit. Exercises C.72.3.1–C.72.3.2 compute the necessary scalar differential terms and coefficient-valued higher functor component. Editable SVG source.

C.73. Full transformation complexes under the normalized unit

Restriction along the canonical normalized cobar unit has an exact section and a contracted kernel on full transformation complexes. Its mixed horizontal homotopy keeps all degrees and higher source components. The resulting operator comparison has an exact projected horizontal law.

C.73.1. An exact section and the actual restriction kernel

Work over the split degree-zero coefficient categories of Section C.30.1. Let \(q:R\to A\) be a strict unital dg functor with identical object labels, graded-surjective quasi-isomorphisms on mappings, and a normalized unital \(A_\infty\) section \(j:A\to R\) with \(qj=\operatorname{Id}_A\). Put \(E=jq\). Theorem C.70.2.1 supplies a closed normalized full transformation

\[ \begin{gathered} u:\operatorname{Id}_R\longrightarrow E,\\ u_0=1,\\ qu=1_q,\quad uj=1_j. \end{gathered} \tag{C.73.1} \]

Here and below a subscript zero denotes the bare component at every object. In particular its units are the actual mapping identities. Let \(D\) be a dg target. Functors and transformations are uncurved and normalized unital; full Nat complexes include all source lengths.

Theorem C.73.1.1 (full source restriction with a contracted kernel). On any chosen labelled family of functors \(F:R\to D\), restriction

\[ \begin{gathered} r:\operatorname{Nat}(F,G)\\ \longrightarrow\operatorname{Nat}(Fj,Gj). \end{gathered} \tag{C.73.2} \]

is a graded-surjective quasi-isomorphism and part of an actual linear SDR. Its section preserves vertical products and identity transformations exactly. Its kernel, with the full Nat differential, has a square-zero contraction. These statements apply to the complete transformation complexes, without an augmentation of \(R\) or \(A\).

Proof. Precomposition by any entire \(A_\infty\) functor is a strict dg functor on full Nat categories: substitution of its consecutive bar partitions commutes with the differential and deconcatenation; the latter gives the vertical product. This is the one-empty-level case of Theorem C.69.2.1. All sums are finite on each original word.

Postcomposition on one mark gives closed transformations

\[ U_F=F_{*,1}(u):F\longrightarrow FE. \tag{C.73.3} \]

Their bare components are actual identities, since \(F_1(1)=1\) and a one-mark evaluation on the empty original source word has no other arguments. The positive-source-length remainder is locally nilpotent under vertical composition. Its finite geometric inverse therefore gives an actual closed full Nat inverse, as in Theorem C.70.2.1. The exact evaluation identity of Theorem C.69.2.1 and \(uj=1_j\) give \(U_Fj=1_{Fj}\), including every positive component.

For \(\psi:Fj\to Gj\) define

\[ \begin{gathered} s(\psi)\\ \quad=U_G^{-1}(\psi q)U_F,\\ rs=1,\qquad P=sr,\\ P\phi\\ \quad=U_G^{-1}(\phi E)U_F. \end{gathered} \tag{C.73.4} \]

The middle expression has source \(FE\) and target \(GE\), so all types match. Closedness of the two units proves the chain equation for \(s\). In the product of two such expressions the intervening \(U_GU_G^{-1}\) cancels exactly. Thus \(s\) preserves vertical products and identities. Restriction gives the identity because \(qj=1\) and both restricted units are identities. Consequently \(P\) is an actual dg projector.

We now construct the homotopy, rather than infer acyclicity of a whole Nat complex. For a homogeneous full cochain \(\phi:F\to G\) of degree \(r\), let \(K_r(\phi)\) be the one-output part of the entire horizontal map of Theorem C.69.2.1 on \(s\phi\otimes su\). It has degree \(r-1\). Its complete two-output part is

\[ \begin{gathered} s(\phi E)|sU_F\\ \quad+(-1)^{r-1}sU_G|s\phi. \end{gathered} \tag{C.73.5} \]

Indeed, the first cut keeps the two suspended marks in their original order; the second interchanges suspended degrees \(r-1\) and \(-1\). The input differential is \(s(d\phi)\otimes su\), since \(du=0\). The binary target bar sign on the first displayed word is \((-1)^{r-1}\); on the second it is \(-1\). Taking the one-letter part of the chain equation therefore gives

\[ \begin{gathered} dK_r(\phi)-K_{r+1}(d\phi)\\ \quad=(-1)^r\bigl((\phi E)U_F\\ \qquad-U_G\phi\bigr). \end{gathered} \tag{C.73.6} \]

This also proves the signs for cochains that are not closed, not just the degree-zero closed case of Lemma C.69.3.1. Define

\[ \begin{gathered} h_r(\phi)\\ \quad=(-1)^{r+1}\\ \qquad\cdot U_G^{-1}K_r(\phi),\\ dh+hd=1-P,\\ rh=0. \end{gathered} \tag{C.73.7} \]

The homotopy equation follows directly from (C.73.6). For the last equation, precompose its entire evaluation with \(j\). The inner parameter is now \(uj=1_j\). A mixed positive component with an identity parameter vanishes by the unit normalization proved in Theorem C.69.2.1. Equivalently, its one-output expression inserts that actual identity into a positive normalized Taylor component of \(\phi\), which is zero. Thus \(K_r(\phi)j=0\), proving \(rh=0\).

The subcomplex \(N=\ker r\) is stable under \(h\), and (C.73.7) restricts there to \(dh+hd=1_N\). This is the specific kernel that is contractible. Normalize its homotopy by \(H_N=hdh\). On \(N\), the equation implies \(dh^2=h^2d\); it also implies that \(dh\) and \(hd\) are idempotent. It follows by direct multiplication that

\[ \begin{gathered} dH_N+H_Nd\\ \quad=(dh)^2+(hd)^2\\ \quad=1_N,\\ H_N^2=h(dh^2d)h\\ \quad=0. \end{gathered} \tag{C.73.8} \]

Set \(H=H_N(1-P)\) on the whole Nat complex. Its image lies in \(N\); \(dH+Hd=1-sr\), \(H^2=0\), \(rH=0\), and \(Hs=0\). Together with \(rs=1\) these are the asserted SDR identities. Each operation uses the finite marked evaluation bound of Theorem C.69.2.1 and the finite inverse series above. Even an empty input piece for \(u_0\) causes no infinite sum: the number of marks here is fixed, and an inserted bare unit in a positive normalized Taylor component vanishes. Complete cochain products therefore cause no convergence assumption. This proves every assertion. \(\square\)

C.73.2. The entire normalized operator comparison

Write \(Q_A=Q^{\mathrm u}(A)\), with \(\epsilon_A\) and \(\iota_A\) from Theorems C.72.1.1 and C.72.2.1. For a native functor \(F:A\to B\) retain its labelled strict dg model \(QF:Q_A\to Q_B\).

Theorem C.73.2.1 (full operator lifts and the projected horizontal equation). On each such labelled operator category there is a normalized unital \(A_\infty\) map \(\mathcal Q_{A,B}\) whose object value is \(QF\). Restriction along \(\iota_A\) has a contracted full Nat kernel and satisfies the exact entire identities

\[ \begin{gathered} r_{A,B}\mathcal Q_{A,B}=(\iota_B)_*,\\ (\epsilon_B)_*r_{A,B}\mathcal Q_{A,B}=1. \end{gathered} \tag{C.73.9} \]

Horizontal substitution of these lifted operators has the exact restriction

\[ \begin{gathered} r_{A,C}M(\mathcal Q_{B,C}\otimes\mathcal Q_{A,B})\\ \quad=(\iota_C)_*M_{A,B,C}\\ \quad=r_{A,C}\mathcal Q_{A,C}M_{A,B,C}. \end{gathered} \tag{C.73.10} \]

Every expression here denotes its full bar map, so (C.73.10) retains all mixed parameter components. It does not assert that the two lifts before restriction are equal.

Proof. Apply Theorem C.73.1.1 to \(q=\epsilon_A\), \(j=\iota_A\), and target \(Q_B\). The hypotheses hold by Theorems C.72.1.1 and C.72.2.1; the relative unit (C.73.1) is the one constructed in Theorem C.70.2.1. The exact object equation \((QF)\iota_A=\iota_BF\) identifies the restriction objects. If two labels determine the same underlying functor, retain both labels; this makes no change to any mapping complex or proof.

Let \(s_{A,B}\) be the strict dg section of Theorem C.73.1.1 and define the entire operator map

\[ \mathcal Q_{A,B}=s_{A,B}(\iota_B)_*. \tag{C.73.11} \]

Postcomposition \((\iota_B)_*\) includes all its Taylor operations by Theorem C.69.2.1. Composing with a strict dg functor therefore yields the asserted normalized unital \(A_\infty\) map. The equation \(rs=1\) proves the first identity (C.73.9). The full counit-unit equation \(\epsilon_B\iota_B=1\) proves the second, using the exact full evaluation identity, not only its linear component.

To prove (C.73.10), evaluate on an original \(A\)-word and arbitrary consecutive words of both parameter levels. After restricting the innermost input along \(\iota_A\), the entire inner lifted evaluation is the \(B\)-evaluation followed by \(B\iota_B\), by (C.73.9). The outer lifted evaluation on that whole output is then the native outer evaluation followed by \(B\iota_C\), again by (C.73.9). The exact nested evaluation identity of Theorem C.69.2.1 identifies this with the middle expression of (C.73.10). One-output projection and cofree uniqueness give the equality on the entire parameter bar, with the same cuts and signs. The last equality is (C.73.9) for \((A,C)\), precomposed with native horizontal substitution. The object equation \((QG)(QF)=Q(GF)\) is exact by Theorem C.72.2.1, so both lifted mapping targets have the same types. Their possible differences consequently lie in the specific contracted restriction kernels of Theorem C.73.1.1. No acyclicity of an entire Nat space or automatic compatibility of independent face lifts was used. \(\square\)

C.73.3. Solved kernel calculations

Use the actual 19-dimensional bridge \(R\), 9-dimensional dg algebra \(G=\operatorname{End}(ke^0\oplus kf^{-1}\oplus ky^0)\), and \(df=y\) of Exercises C.68.5.1 and C.70.4.2. The bridge projection \(q:R\to G\), its higher section \(j\), and the relative unit \(u\) are their entire maps. For \(F=G=q\) as operator objects, \(U_q=1_q\). Thus the section in (C.73.4) is precomposition by \(q\), and its projector is precomposition by \(E=jq\). All scalar and ordinary identity outputs must be retained; normalization only quotients identity inputs.

Write \(S=(1,0,0)\), \(M_{ij}=(0,E_{ij},0)\), and \(Z_{ij}=(0,0,E_{ij})\) in this bridge, with the same order \(e,f,y\) as the target matrices. Its actual unit is

\[ \begin{gathered} 1_R=S+M_{ee}\\ \quad+M_{ff}+M_{yy}. \end{gathered} \tag{C.73.12} \]

Exercise C.73.3.1 (the actual kernel and an absolute cohomology class; advanced). In the quotient retaining normalized source inputs of length at most two, find the total dimensions of both full transformation spaces and the restriction kernel. Explain why this kernel result does not make the whole Nat complex contractible.

Solution. A graded complement to the bridge unit has the eighteen \(M_{ij},Z_{ij}\); normalization evaluates an \(S\) input as minus the sum of the three diagonal \(M\) inputs. A complement to the target unit has the eight matrix units other than \(E_{ee}\). In source inputs, \(E_{ee}\) evaluates as \(-E_{ff}-E_{yy}\). These choices only normalize inputs: all nine matrix outputs, including actual unit outputs, remain. The numbers of source words, including the empty word, are therefore \(1+18+18^2=343\) and \(1+8+8^2=73\). Thus

\[ \begin{gathered} \dim\operatorname{Nat}_{\leq2}(q,q)\\ \quad=3087,\\ \dim\operatorname{Nat}_{\leq2}(qj,qj)\\ \quad=657,\\ \dim\ker r_{\leq2}=2430. \end{gathered} \tag{C.73.13} \]

The last subtraction is justified by the exact section in (C.73.4), not by an assumption about numerical ranks. Substitution and the homotopy never require a positive cochain component longer than its current original input: the apparent extra letter from \(u_0\) is an actual unit and vanishes in a normalized positive input. Consequently the SDR descends to this finite length quotient. It contracts this entire 2430-dimensional kernel as a graded complex.

In contrast the bare identity transformation is a closed full cochain on both absolute spaces. The functional \(\beta(T)=T_{ee}\) is zero on every unary boundary in \(\operatorname{End}(V)\), since \(dV\) has only the entry \(f\mapsto y\), while \(\beta(1_V)=1\). The bare component of a full Nat boundary is such a unary boundary: the source bar of an empty word is zero and there is no uncurved positive-input term on it. The identity transformation is consequently not a full Nat boundary. This proves the asserted distinction for the entire spaces as well as their finite quotients. \(\square\)

Exercise C.73.3.2 (a higher unit component is needed in the contraction; advanced). Let the degree-one normalized cochain \(\phi:q\to q\) have only its length-one component, with \(\phi_1(M_{ee})=E_{ee}\), zero on the other seventeen chosen complement basis elements, and zero bare and higher components. Compute the contraction equation on \((M_{ef},M_{ye})\). Compare it with the formula that omits \(u_2\) while retaining \(u_0,u_1\).

Solution. Normalization and (C.73.12) give \(\phi_1(S)=-E_{ee}\). The previously calculated actual section and unit have values

\[ \begin{gathered} j_2(E_{ef},E_{ye})\\ \quad=-S-Z_{fy},\\ u_2(M_{ef},Z_{ye})\\ \quad=-S-Z_{fy},\\ d_RM_{ye}=-Z_{ye}. \end{gathered} \tag{C.73.14} \]

The first is the higher section value of Exercise C.71.2.2; the other two follow from Exercise C.70.4.2 and the bridge differential in Theorem C.68.3.1. Applying the first value to \(\phi\) gives \((P\phi)_2(M_{ef},M_{ye})=E_{ee}\). For the mixed homotopy, the second value, followed by \(\phi_1\), gives \((h\phi)_2(M_{ef},Z_{ye})=E_{ee}\). Its sign is positive in (C.73.7), since \(|\phi|=1\). All other terms contributing to the following displayed input vanish by their matrix indices. Set \(w=(M_{ef},M_{ye})\); the third value gives

\[ \begin{gathered} (dh\phi)_2(w)=-E_{ee},\\ (hd\phi)_2(w)=0,\\ ((1-P)\phi)_2(w)\\ \quad=-E_{ee}. \end{gathered} \tag{C.73.15} \]

These are the degree-one contraction equation on that input. If the mixed construction instead uses only \(u_0,u_1\), both left-hand terms at this input are zero. Its defect relative to \(1-P\) is then \(+E_{ee}\ne0\). Dropping a higher source component loses the actual homotopy, even though the bare unit is the identity and its projection under \(q\) is unchanged. The full kernel cochain is defined by \((1-P)\phi\); the few components displayed here are not a definition that truncates that cochain at all higher source lengths. \(\square\)

Theorem C.73.1.1 gives the full source-restriction SDR; Theorem C.73.2.1 gives the entire lifted operator comparison and its projected horizontal law. Exercises C.73.3.1–C.73.3.2 distinguish the actual kernel from the absolute transformation space and compute the necessary higher unit term. Editable SVG source.

C.74. Normalized tensor parameters and relative coherent cells

Full tensor bars give unital free parameter categories that retain the original unary generator complexes and all tensor cuts. Relative cube extensions through an actual contracted mapping kernel preserve entire compatible boundaries and already prescribed parameter faces.

C.74.1. The full tensor-parameter cobar

Let \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\) be unital dg categories over split degree-zero coefficient categories, as in Section C.30.1. Keep their literal product object labels. Put \(K=\bigotimes_i B_{\rm full}A_i\), using all ordinary mapping letters in each full bar, including units. A generator is a tuple \(c=(w_1,\ldots,w_m)\) of factor words, not all empty. Write \(N(c)=\sum_i\ell(w_i)\) and use the suspended degrees \(|sa|=|a|-1\). Empty factor words have degree zero.

In \(\Omega K\), impose the following ideal \(J\). A generator on a single coefficient letter in one factor is its actual coefficient, with the other factor identities understood. A generator of total length at least two with a coefficient argument in any factor is zero. Define

\[ T(A_1,\ldots,A_m)=\Omega K/J. \tag{C.74.1} \]

This notation refers to the parameter category, not an ordinary tensor product of the categories \(Q^{\mathrm u}(A_i)\).

Theorem C.74.1.1 (the normalized tensor-parameter category). The ideal is differential-stable. On its nonzero identity sector, \(T\) is a free relative graded category on the nonempty tuples of reduced factor words in \(A_i/S_i\), with one cobar desuspension for the entire tuple. Its generator differential is the full projected source-unary differential plus terms involving generators of strictly smaller total length, including the possible scalar constants. It therefore satisfies the nonminimal relative lifting hypotheses of Theorem C.46.2.1.

Full normalized unital factor functors induce strict dg maps of \(T\), retaining all their higher coefficient outputs where they survive the displayed relations. The maps compose exactly. Coordinate factor faces are included as actual differential-stable free-generator faces. Their compatible unions have the same property. For zero factors \(T\) is the coefficient category. No comparison with an ordinary tensor product is asserted by this theorem.

Proof. In target-to-source tensor order, write every factor cut as \(w_i=l_i|r_i\). The full cobar splitting term on \(c\) is

\[ \begin{gathered} -\sum_{l,r}(-1)^{|l|+\chi(l,r)}\\ \qquad\cdot(\mathsf t l)(\mathsf t r),\\ \chi(l,r)=\sum_{i<j}|r_i||l_j|. \end{gathered} \tag{C.74.2} \]

The sum includes all tuples of cuts except the two coaugmentation cuts; neither output tuple may be entirely empty. The second exponent is the actual interchange of the right part of an earlier factor with the left part of a later factor. The other part of the differential is the full tensor bar differential, with its preceding-factor sign. The two coalgebra identities for tensor deconcatenation prove that this cobar derivation squares to zero, by the same cut cancellation as C.39.4.

Here is the unit-ideal check, including the extra tensor case. Unary differentials of coefficient inputs vanish. Other unary terms retain that input and remain degenerate. Inside a factor word, two neighboring unit bar multiplications cancel, as in Theorem C.72.1.1. At its first position a unit's single neighboring bar term has coefficient \(-(-1)^a\), where \(a\) is the sum of the degrees of all preceding factor words. The cut isolating that unit on the left has coefficient \(+(-1)^a\) in (C.74.2), so the two terms cancel after \(\mathsf t(s1)=1\). At its last position let \(p\) be the degree of its remaining factor word. The neighboring bar term has coefficient \((-1)^{a+p}\); isolating the unit on the right has its negative. All cuts that retain a unit in a higher output tuple vanish modulo \(J\).

There remains the case that the unit is its factor's only letter, while some other factor word is nonempty. There is no neighboring bar term. The only potentially nondegenerate cuts isolate this single unit on one side and put all the other factor words on the other side. If \(b\) is their degree sum after the unit's factor, their two cobar coefficients are respectively \(+(-1)^a\) and \(-(-1)^{a+b+b}=-(-1)^a\). Their products agree by coefficient balancing, and cancel. This check also handles several unit factors, with any remaining degenerate output zero. If a length-two factor consists of two coefficients, its bar product cancels its coefficient cut product. Single-letter coefficient relations have zero differential. These cases cover every ideal generator, proving stability.

Choose graded coefficient-linear complements to each \(S_i\). Expanding each letter into its coefficient and complement parts shows that every remaining generator is exactly a tuple of reduced words; no additional graded relation involves these generators. The relative algebra on them is free. Its source-unary part is the tensor differential on the quotient complexes \(A_i/S_i\), with their full original unary maps. It squares to zero because each coefficient subspace is a closed subcomplex.

A reduced binary bar product lowers total length by one. A scalar binary output survives as a constant only when its entire tuple had two letters in that factor and all others empty; otherwise its coefficient argument is degenerate. A scalar unary output likewise survives as a constant only at total length one. Every proper tensor cut gives a product of two generators of smaller individual length. Thus the differential has exactly the filtered generator form of Theorem C.46.2.1, including the constants.

For factor functors, apply their entire bar maps and tensor them, including the tensor interchange signs. A coefficient input inside a longer Taylor piece gives zero; if isolated it gives a coefficient output. In a surviving multi-output tuple that output is degenerate. A single coefficient output from a higher Taylor piece can instead survive as an actual coefficient when all other factor words are empty. These are precisely the same unit relations as above, so the cobar map descends. Entire factor bar maps compose exactly; their tensor, cobar and quotient maps consequently do too.

Fixing all factor words outside a coordinate subset to be empty is a coalgebra inclusion and preserves all displayed relations. Its free generators are a subset of the reduced tuples. The unary differential keeps that subset; every other differential term lies in its generated algebra. The union for any family of coordinate subsets has the same properties, and its relative free algebra has no further relations between the faces. Compatible prescribed dg maps on those faces therefore give a dg map on their generated union. With no factors there are no positive generators. Zero-identity objects are treated by killing their identities and incident mappings, exactly as in Theorem C.72.1.1. This proves all the statements. \(\square\)

C.74.2. Full relative cubes through an actual mapping kernel

Let \(p:E\to D\) be a strict unital dg functor on a fixed object family, with graded-surjective mapping quasi-isomorphisms. Let its actual mapping kernel \(N(x,y)\) have a coefficient-linear contraction \(h_N\). The restriction map of Theorem C.73.1.1 is one such functor, with its explicit contraction; no acyclicity of absolute Nat is assumed.

Use the cohomologically graded interval coalgebra \(I\) of C.36: vertices \(v_0,v_1\) have degree zero, \(e\) has degree minus one, \(de=v_1-v_0\), and

\[ \begin{gathered} \Delta v_i=v_i\otimes v_i,\\ \Delta e=e\otimes v_1+v_0\otimes e,\\ \epsilon(v_i)=1,\quad\epsilon(e)=0. \end{gathered} \tag{C.74.3} \]

For \(n\geq1\), the full cube is \(I^{\otimes n}\), with its tensor coproduct, every cell and every ordinary face. Let \(\partial I^n\) be the span of all cells except \(e^{\otimes n}\). It is the union of the coordinate endpoint faces, and is a dg subcoalgebra. On each fixed mapping pair use the convolution differential and product on \(\operatorname{Hom}(I^n,E(x,y))\). In particular the product has the Koszul sign for moving the right cochain across the left coalgebra piece.

Let \(\mathcal E_n\) consist of pairs \((d,\phi)\) with \(d\in D(x,y)\) and \(p\phi=\epsilon(-)d\). Let \(\mathcal B_n\) have the same definition on \(\partial I^n\). Their object families are the fixed object labels of \(E\).

Theorem C.74.2.1 (relative coherent cell extension). Boundary restriction \(\mathcal E_n\to\mathcal B_n\) is a strict unital dg functor, graded-surjective and a quasi-isomorphism on each mapping complex. Its kernel is the actual complex below, where \(C_n=I^n/\partial I^n\):

\[ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{Hom}(C_n,N(x,y))\\ \qquad\cong N(x,y)[-n]. \end{gathered} \tag{C.74.4} \]

Postcomposition with \(h_N\) contracts it. Consequently a whole compatible cubical boundary of strict dg maps from the parameter category of Theorem C.74.1.1, with one common projected dg map, extends across the cube. The extension retains any already prescribed whole cube on compatible free-generator faces. It retains the complete source-unary complex and all constant terms, in every parameter degree.

Proof. The interval diagonal is a chain map: on \(e\), the two middle vertex terms cancel and the result is \(v_1\otimes v_1-v_0\otimes v_0\). Both iterated diagonals on \(e\) are \(e\otimes v_1\otimes v_1+v_0\otimes e\otimes v_1+ v_0\otimes v_0\otimes e\). This proves coassociativity and the vertex counit equations directly. Tensoring with the Koszul permutation proves the same identities for the full cube. Its differential replaces an \(e\) by vertices, and a diagonal of a boundary cell keeps its fixed vertex in both outputs. Thus its boundary is indeed a dg subcoalgebra.

Convolution is associative because the cube diagonal is coassociative; its Hom differential obeys the product rule because the diagonal is a chain map and the target composition obeys that rule. Its unit is the cube counit followed by the actual identity. The condition \(p\phi=\epsilon(-)d\) is stable under both differential and product, since \(p\) is strict dg and the counit is a coalgebra map to the coefficient field. This proves all dg assertions and boundary functoriality.

Every proper cube cell lies in a boundary face. Compatible boundary values therefore prescribe it exactly once, regardless of which face contains it. Extend a graded boundary cochain by value zero on the unique interior cell. Its projection there must be zero as well, since \(\epsilon(e^{\otimes n})=0\); so this is a graded lift in \(\mathcal E_n\). It need not be a chain lift yet. The kernel has zero boundary values and zero \(d\) component, and its remaining interior value lies in \(N\). This identifies it with (C.74.4). The quotient cube has one basis cell in degree \(-n\) and zero differential, proving the stated graded shift. For the standard cohomological shift differential, the actual chain isomorphism sends a degree-\(r\) cochain to \((-1)^{nr}\phi(e^{\otimes n})\); its sign in the next degree differs by \((-1)^n\), precisely the shift's differential sign. In Hom coordinates the differential is the target unary differential, so postcomposition with \(h_N\) gives the contraction. In standard shifted coordinates it is \((-1)^nh_N\), consistently with that chain isomorphism. The kernel is consequently acyclic, and graded surjectivity and this contraction prove the mapping quasi-isomorphism.

A supplied common projected functor and compatible boundary functors package into a strict dg map from \(T\) to \(\mathcal B_n\). Use the just proved surjective mapping quasi-isomorphism as the target projection in Theorem C.46.2.1. The free-generator and full unary hypotheses were proved in Theorem C.74.1.1. That theorem gives a strict dg lift to \(\mathcal E_n\), with exactly the supplied boundary and projection. If full cubes are already assigned on parameter faces, their compatible union is precisely the relative free-generator subcomplex proved in Theorem C.74.1.1; the relative clause of C.46.2.1 retains it. This constructs the entire cell, not only an edge or a primitive after forgetting its other boundary faces. \(\square\)

At dimension one the same signs have a concrete path form. If a degree \(r\) cochain has vertex values \(f=\phi(v_1)\), \(g=\phi(v_0)\), write \(a=(-1)^r\phi(e)\). Its formulas are

\[ \begin{gathered} D(f,g,a)\\ \quad=\bigl(df,dg,\\ \qquad-da+f-g\bigr),\\ (f_2,g_2,a_2)\\ \qquad\cdot(f_1,g_1,a_1)\\ \quad=\bigl(f_2f_1,g_2g_1,\\ \qquad a_2f_1\\ \qquad+(-1)^{r_2}g_2a_1\bigr). \end{gathered} \tag{C.74.5} \]

Here \(r_2\) is the degree of the second path. These formulas follow by evaluating the differential and the two terms of \(\Delta e\); they agree with the identity-comparison path convention of Section C.53.4. In these regraded path coordinates the kernel contraction on \(a\) has the sign \(-h_N\), rather than an unjustified positive sign.

C.74.3. Solved unit and path calculations

Exercise C.74.3.1 (an isolated factor unit needs both tensor cuts; advanced). Take two copies of the actual unaugmented dg algebra \(A=\operatorname{End}(ke^0\oplus kf^{-1}\oplus ky^0)\), with \(df=y\). Let \(a=E_{ye}\), so \(|a|=0\) and \(da=0\). Compute the differential of the degenerate parameter generator \(z=\mathsf t(s1\otimes sa)\). Explain what fails if only one of its nontrivial tensor cuts is retained.

Solution. There are no unary or binary bar terms on these two one-letter factor words. In the tensor coproduct the two nontrivial terms are

\[ \begin{gathered} (s1\otimes1)\otimes(1\otimes sa),\\ -(1\otimes sa)\otimes(s1\otimes1). \end{gathered} \tag{C.74.6} \]

The minus sign interchanges two suspended degree-minus-one letters. Both left output tuples have degree minus one, so the additional cobar coefficient \(-(-1)^{|l|}\) is positive. After the single unit generator is identified with the coefficient, the two products consequently give

\[ \begin{gathered} Dz=\mathsf t(1\otimes sa)\\ \quad-\mathsf t(1\otimes sa)=0. \end{gathered} \tag{C.74.7} \]

This is required because the normalized relation itself sets \(z=0\). Keeping either cut alone gives a nonzero generator, with one of the two signs. That clipped differential does not preserve the defining unit ideal. The cancellation concerns actual ordinary identity outputs; it does not authorize deleting one of the tensor cuts before normalization. \(\square\)

Exercise C.74.3.2 (an actual relative path and its kernel sign; advanced). Use the actual 19-dimensional bridge \(R\to\operatorname{End}(V)\) of Section C.68.5, with \(S,M_{ij},Z_{ij}\) as in Exercise C.73.3.2. Let \(b=Z_{ee}\) and \(c=S+Z_{fy}\). Construct a relative dg path between the maps from the free unital dg algebra \(k\langle x\rangle\), \(|x|=1\), \(dx=0\), that send \(x\) respectively to \(b\) and zero. Also contract the closed path-kernel element with third coordinate \(b\).

Solution. The bridge formulas give

\[ \begin{gathered} |b|=1,\quad |c|=0,\\ db=0,\quad dc=b,\\ q(b)=q(c)=0,\\ h_N(b)=c. \end{gathered} \tag{C.74.8} \]

Indeed \(dS=Z_{ee}+Z_{ff}+Z_{yy}\) and \(dZ_{fy}=-Z_{ff}-Z_{yy}\). The kernel contraction in Theorem C.68.3.1 has the displayed value, also calculated in Exercise C.70.4.2. Map the free generator to the degree-one path

\[ x\longmapsto(b,0,c). \tag{C.74.9} \]

Its differential is \((0,0,-dc+b)=0\) by (C.74.5), so extension by products is a strict unital dg functor on the entire free algebra. Both endpoint projections to the quotient are zero, and the path is relative there too. In interval Hom coordinates its values are \(b\) at \(v_1\), zero at \(v_0\), and \(-c\) at \(e\); these obey the entire Hom differential. Omitting \(c\) leaves the nonzero third defect \(b\).

The separate kernel element \(k=(0,0,b)\) has degree two. Its contracted primitive is \((0,0,-c)\), of degree one, since its path differential is \((0,0,dc)=k\). A positive \(c\) would instead differentiate to \(-k\). This verifies the negative kernel-contraction sign in the path coordinates, while the un-regraded cube Hom contraction remains ordinary postcomposition with \(h_N\). \(\square\)

Theorem C.74.1.1 constructs the normalized full tensor-parameter category; Theorem C.74.2.1 extends compatible relative cube boundaries through an actual contracted mapping kernel. Exercises C.74.3.1–C.74.3.2 calculate the isolated-unit cancellation and the actual path contraction sign. Editable SVG source.

C.75. Actual normalized tensor comparison

The normalized tensor-parameter category maps to the tensor of the actual unital resolutions by a graded-surjective quasi-isomorphism with a finite kernel contraction. Its full shuffle gives a second quasi-isomorphism to the unital resolution of the tensor, with the actual counit square.

C.75.1. The normalized Milgram projection without augmentations

Let \(A,B\) be unital dg categories over the split coefficients of Section C.30.1. Write \(Q_A=Q^{\mathrm u}(A)\) and \(T=T(A,B)\) for the actual normalized models of Theorems C.72.1.1 and C.74.1.1. All tensor products keep their literal ordered object and matrix labels.

Define \(\rho:T\to Q_A\otimes Q_B\) on a generator \(\mathsf t(w_A\otimes w_B)\) by its pure-factor value when exactly one word is nonempty, and by zero when both are nonempty. Extend by the actual graded tensor product, with the other factors' coalgebra counits. These are the counits of the full bar coalgebras, which exist without augmentations of the original dg categories.

Theorem C.75.1.1 (the actual binary tensor projection). The map \(\rho\) is a strict unital dg functor, graded-surjective and a quasi-isomorphism on every mapping complex. Its actual kernel has a normalized linear contraction finite on each original reduced-letter word. The projection is strictly natural for full normalized unital factor functors, where their strict models on the right are \(QF\otimes QG\).

Proof. For a pure generator, the chain equation is the ordinary factor cobar equation. On a mixed generator every unary or bar-product term remains mixed, or is killed by its coefficient-input relation. The only cut products whose projection can be nonzero put the entire first word on one side and the entire second word on the other. Their coefficients in equation (C.74.2) are \(-(-1)^{|w_A|}\) and \(-(-1)^{|w_B|+|w_A||w_B|}\). Reordering their pure cobar generators in the graded tensor target contributes \((-1)^{(|w_A|+1)(|w_B|+1)}\) to the latter. Thus the two resulting coefficients are opposite. This proves the full chain equation on mixed generators. Single coefficient generators have the actual coefficient image, and higher unit-degenerate generators have zero image, so the map descends through the normalized relations. Every product of pure-factor generators in the target has a preimage, proving graded surjectivity. More precisely, the linear section \(s_\rho\) puts all first-factor cobar blocks before all second-factor blocks. The derivation rule on this ordered word is exactly the tensor differential, including scalar outputs in either factor. Thus \(s_\rho\) is an actual linear chain section and \(\rho s_\rho=1\). This statement concerns a linear section; no multiplicativity of this chosen normal ordering is required.

For the quasi-isomorphism, retain the original reduced-letter counts \((p,q)\). Let \(D_0\) keep source-unary terms on the quotient complexes and all cobar cuts, on both sides. Bar products and scalar outputs are the remaining perturbation \(\delta\). The projection preserves these counts and intertwines the leading differentials. We prove its leading quasi-isomorphism with the full unary complexes present.

Fix the ordered original factor words. A source cobar word with \(k\) blocks is exactly a strict chain of \(k-1\) interior grid points between \((0,0)\) and \((p,q)\) in the coordinatewise ordered grid. A block records the nonzero monotone step between consecutive points. Every factor letter appears in its original order. Refining a step adds one interior point; these are exactly the leading cobar cuts.

Here are explicit signs for that grid identification. In block \(i\) let \(a_i,b_i\) be its suspended first and second factor words. Set \[ \begin{gathered}\pi=\sum_{i<j}|b_i||a_j|,\\ \lambda=(-1)^{\pi+k-1+\sum_vd(v)},\end{gathered} \tag{C.75.1} \] where the sum is over internal chain vertices, and \(d(v)\) is the degree of the original suspended factor prefixes ending there. Rescale the chain's source basis by \(\lambda\). Inserting a vertex into step \(i\), numbered from zero, changes this exponent by \(1+d(v)+\chi\), with \(\chi\) the tensor-cut interchange exponent of equation (C.74.2).
